ET POPULIS AUGUSTANAM CONFESSIONEM PROFITENTIBUS DICATA SUNT, SINE PRÆIUDICIO, ET ABSQUE ANIMI ACERBITATE, LEGENDA, EXPENDENDA, ET IN LEGITIMO TANDEM CONVENTU COMMUNI, LIBERO, ET LEGITIMO, QUUM DEDERIT DOMINUS, EX PURO DEI VERBO DIIUDICANDA.
units.tr: These writings, as they proceed from a sincere heart and a candid zeal for the peace of the Churches, are dedicated to all the most illustrious princes of Germany, to the other most noble orders, the magistrates of the Churches, the ministers, the teachers and the peoples who profess the Augsburg Confession. Let them be read and weighed without prejudice and without bitterness of spirit, and at length, when the Lord grants it, be judged from the pure Word of God in a lawful, common, free and lawful assembly.

units.la: DE CONTROVERSIIS IN COENA DOMINI, PER NONNULLOS nuper in Germania partim novatis, partim auctis, Christiana & perspicua disputatio.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE CONTROVERSIES ON THE LORD'S SUPPER, RAISED BY CERTAIN PERSONS RECENTLY IN GERMANY, partly new, partly enlarged: a Christian and clear disputation.

units.la: INTER eos, qui contra omnem Ecclesiae Christianae verae consuetudinem & expressum Apostoli interdictum 1.Corint. 1.12. & 13. Lutheranos sese inscribere non verentur, & nos, quos nulla neque ratione recta, neque satis sana conscientia olim quidem Zuinglianos, nunc vero Calui-nistas appellant: plurima, de quibus scribere nunc constitui, in negotio de sacra Domini Coena controvertuntur:errore, sicut fit, errorem cumulante, quoties inter aliquos non sincero veritatis inveniendę studio, sed odiis, ambitione, vel etiam zelo absque scientia non disceptatur, sed decertatur. Quandoquidem vero istis dissidiis sancto & legitimo conven-tu componendis, nulli magis adversantur, quàm ij ipsi Theologi, quos tamen in hoc in primis negotium totis animis incumbere oportuit: utinam tandem nobis concedat Do-minus, ut penes utros stet veritas, piorum Principum & Magistratuum auctoritate, in-ter verae pacis Ecclesiarum studiosos, abactis ambitiosis & turbulentis ingeniis, ex puro puro Dei verbo decidatur, vsitato ab ipsis vs-que Apostolorum temporibus totius ortho-doxæ Ecclesiæ Christianæ, in obruendis hæ-resibus, exemplo. Quod enim ait de sui temporis Synodis Nazianzenus, minimè sic accipiendum est, quasi ista per Synodos afferendæ veritatis ratio vt inutilis, vel etiam noxia, re-prehendatur: sed eò spectat, partim vt falsi conuentus, quos propterea Græci ληστικὰς[?] Synodos appellarunt, quasi latronum inter se ad opprimendam veritatem coniurantium cœtus, à vere & sincere conuocatis & habitis Ecclesiarum quasi comitiis discernantur: partim ne pendentibus huiusmodi controuersiis, homines suspensis animis hærentes expectent Synodorum iudicia, quasi ab illis proprie pendeat veritas: sed vt iam nunc potius de sua ex verbo Dei certioranda conscientia sedulo laborent, sicut nos monet Apostolus Rom.14.5. Sed mihi nunc quidem consilium non est hoc persequi. Ad illa igitur hu-ius controuersiæ capita accedo.
units.tr: Among those who, contrary to all the true custom of the Christian Church and the express prohibition of the Apostle (1 Cor. 1.12 and 13), do not hesitate to call themselves Lutherans, and us, whom neither right reason nor a sufficiently sound conscience has ever called Zwinglians, but who are now called Calvinists: many matters, about which I have now decided to write, are being disputed in the controversy over the Lord's Supper. Error, as usually happens, compounds error whenever people argue among themselves not with a sincere zeal to find the truth, but out of hatred, ambition, or even zeal without knowledge; they do not debate, they fight. Since, however, no one opposes the settling of these disagreements by a holy and lawful assembly more than those very theologians, whose duty above all was to give their whole minds to this business, may the Lord at last grant us that, on whichever side the truth stands, it be decided from the pure Word of God, by the authority of pious princes and magistrates, among those who sincerely seek true peace of the Churches, with ambitious and turbulent wits set aside. This is the method the whole orthodox Christian Church has used from the very times of the Apostles in overthrowing heresies. For what Nazianzen says about the synods of his own time is by no means to be taken as condemning this way of asserting truth through synods as useless or even harmful. Rather, he aims partly to distinguish false assemblies, which the Greeks therefore called robber [ληστικὰς] synods, as gatherings of robbers conspiring together to suppress the truth, from those truly and sincerely convened and held as, so to speak, the assemblies of the Churches. He aims partly so that, while such controversies are pending, people do not stand in suspense, waiting for the judgments of synods as if truth depended entirely on them, but rather that they should now diligently labour to make their conscience certain from the Word of God, as the Apostle admonishes us (Rom. 14.5). But it is not my intention to pursue this further now. I therefore come to the heads of this controversy.

units.la: Ad illa igitur huius controuersiæ capita accedo, quæ mihi quidem videntur ad quin-que quæstiones posse reuocari, vnam, de signis, alteram, de rebus significatis, tertiam de Sacramentali signorum & rerum significatarum coniunctione, quartam, de rerum significatarum perceptione, quintam denique, de proprio Cœnæ Domini fine & visu, & quidem posito de quo arbitror inter nos non concontrouerti, nempe constitui Sacramenta ex Dei ordinatione,tribus istis,nimirum Signis, Rebus significatis,&verbo Sacramentali,quo duo illa fiunt quod sunt,& inter se Sacramen-taliter copulantur.
units.tr: I therefore come to the heads of this controversy, which seem to me can be reduced to five questions: first, concerning the signs; second, concerning the things signified; third, concerning the sacramental conjunction of the signs and the things signified; fourth, concerning the perception of the things signified; and fifth, finally, concerning the proper end and use of the Lord's Supper. This being granted, and I think there is no dispute among us about it, namely that sacraments are constituted by God's ordinance from three things: the signs, the things signified, and the sacramental word, by which those two become what they are and are sacramentally joined to each other.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: De signis Sacramentalibus,& eorundem cum rebus significatis analogia.
units.tr: On the sacramental signs, and their analogy with the things signified.

units.la: ANTEQVAM vero quænam hæc signa sint dicamus, statuendum est in primis, non de vulgaribus signis, sed diuinitus ad magna illa nostræ salutis mysteria significanda constitutis, hic agi: ac proinde ad hoc vt hæc vere signa esse in hac actione sacra censeantur, præsupponi diuinæ illius ordinationis legitimam obseruationem.
units.tr: Before we say what these signs are, it must first be established that we are not dealing here with ordinary signs, but with signs divinely appointed to signify those great mysteries of our salvation. Therefore, for these to be counted as true signs in this sacred action, the lawful observance of that divine ordinance must be presupposed.

units.la: Secundò sciendum est res istas non simpliciter idcirco signa fieri & dici, quòd in oculos nostros incurrētes, instar picturæ quędam nostræ recordationi suggerant: sed vt res per illas significatæ, & per fidem apprehensæ, intrà nos,verè diuina virtute,obsignentur: quo discrimine signa ista ab illis, recordationis tantùm causa,constitutis signis,& Sacramentalis significatio ab aliis simplicioribus dis-cernuntur.
units.tr: Second, it must be understood that these things are not made and called signs merely because, falling under our eyes, they suggest something to our memory like a picture. Rather, the things signified by them, and grasped by faith, are truly sealed within us by divine power. By this distinction these signs are set apart from those established merely as an aid to memory, and sacramental signification is distinguished from other simpler kinds.

units.la: His positis, signorum appellatione primum omnium intelligimus res illas duas materiales, panem videlicet illum, & vinum illud, quibus adhibitis, Christo visum est nouum suum foedus cum Ecclesia sua pacisci: panem videlicet, vt veri illius corporis sui pro nobis in mortem traditi, & vinum, vt veri sui sanguinis pro nobis effusi, signum Sacramentale, sicuti modò diximus, definitum.
units.tr: With these points laid down, by the name of signs we first of all understand those two material things, namely that bread and that wine, which Christ chose to use when he made his new covenant with his Church: the bread, as the sign of his true body, given for us to death, and the wine, as the sign of his true blood, poured out for us, defined as a sacramental sign, as we have just said.

units.la: Secundo loco signa vocamus, sacros actio-num Sacramentalium ritus, quos & ipsos Christus, his verbis vtens (Hoc facite) diserte imperauit, vt & ipsi in sensus externos incurrentes, credentium menti res alias plane cœlestes & spirituales, intelligendas, credendas, & per fidem obsignandas, proponant.
units.tr: Secondly, we call signs the sacred rites of the sacramental actions, which Christ himself expressly commanded, using the words Do this. They too, falling upon the external senses, set before the mind of believers other things that are entirely heavenly and spiritual, to be understood, believed, and sealed by faith.

units.la: Eorum autem rituum alij iis conueniunt, à quibus mandato & nomine Christi agenti-bus quod agunt, ista administrantur: alij au-ditoribus ad Domini mensam accedentibus præscripti sunt, quos sigillatim explicabi-mus.
units.tr: Of these rites, some belong to those by whose mandate and in whose name Christ's agents do what they do and administer these things. Others are prescribed for the hearers who approach the Lord's table, which we will explain one by one.

units.la: Generaliter igitur dicimus in hac tota actione Sacramentali sursum, atque adeò supra ipsos cœlos, vbi Christus secundum carnem nunc est, & vnde reuersurum illum expectamus, tota mente, veluti per fidei scalam, esse fideli mente assurgendum. In Pastorum igitur persona debent qui ad Domini mensam accedunt, ipsum Christum oculis fidei intueri, & illius perpessiones, licet iam pera-ctas, & nunquam in æternum repetendas, menti suæ repræsentare.
units.tr: In general, therefore, we say that in this whole sacramental action the faithful mind must rise upward, and indeed above the very heavens, where Christ now is according to the flesh and whence we await his return, with the whole mind, as if by the ladder of faith. In the person of the ministers, therefore, those who approach the Lord's table ought to gaze with the eyes of faith upon Christ himself, and to set before their minds his sufferings, though already accomplished and never to be repeated for eternity.

units.la: Primum quidem in panis fractione, & vini in poculum infusione, ac deinceps in ipsa panis ac vini distributione. Panis enim illius fractio, & illius vini in poculum infusio, veluti limpidissima quædam specula sunt, mentibus fide præditis proposita, in quibus Christum quasi in cruce, inenarrabilibus animi & corporis cruciatibus fractum, & usque ad spiritus à corpore violentissimam separationem discerptum, & tanquam adhuc sanguinis grumos stillantem, fidelis mentis oculis intueantur.
units.tr: First, indeed, in the breaking of the bread and the pouring of the wine into the cup, and then in the distribution of the bread and wine itself. For the breaking of that bread and the pouring of that wine into the cup are like most clear mirrors, set before minds endowed with faith, in which the faithful eyes of the mind may behold Christ as if on the cross, broken with unspeakable anguish of soul and body, torn by the most violent separation of spirit from body, and still dripping clots of blood.

units.la: In panis autem illius & illius vini distributione, ipsos eundem Christum, eadem mente fideli, considerare oportet, perinde ac si illum sese, cum vita æterna, sua ipsius manu utendum fruendum, ipsis tradentem cerne-rent. Solus enim Christus is est, qui Spiritus sancti sui virtute interiore, homini reipsa communicat, quod externa illa panis & vini à Pastoribus corporali præbitione, σχηματικῶς[?] fideli menti repræsentatur. Et hæ quidem sunt Pastorum in illa sacra actione partes.
units.tr: In the distribution of that bread and that wine, one must consider the same Christ with the same faithful mind, just as if they saw him offering himself to them, with eternal life, to be used and enjoyed by his own hand. For Christ alone is the one who, by the inner power of his Holy Spirit, really communicates to man what the external giving of bread and wine by the ministers represents to the faithful mind figuratively [σχηματικῶς]. And these are indeed the ministers' parts in that sacred action.

units.la: Reliqui verò ritus Sacramentales, accedentibus ad mensam Domini præscripti, hi sunt, σχηματικῶς[?] itidem considerandi, id est, quatenus significandis & obsignandis spiritualibus rebus, ut illarum ex divina ordinatione σημεῖα[?], & σφραγῖδες[?] adhibentur. Primum panis illius & illius vini in manus receptio, per quam tum ipsius Christi tum omnium ipsius ad salutem nostram necessariorum beneficiorum spiritualis per instrumentum Fidei intra nos obsignatio:tam vera significatur, quàm vera & certa est signorum istorum naturalis & sen-sibilis,intrà acceptantium manus receptio.
units.tr: The remaining sacramental rites prescribed for those approaching the Lord's table are likewise to be considered figuratively [σχηματικῶς], that is, insofar as they are used as signs [σημεῖα] and seals [σφραγῖδες] of spiritual things, to signify and seal them according to divine ordinance. The first is the receiving of that bread and that wine into the hands, by which the spiritual sealing within us, through the instrument of faith, both of Christ himself and of all the benefits necessary for our salvation, is signified as truly as the natural and sensible reception into the hands of those who accept these signs within is true and certain.

units.la: Hanc autem signorum in manus traditionem & eorundem distributionem,& prehen-sionem, sequitur externa siue corporea huius panis & huius vini, in nostrum corpus per manducationem & haustum traductio: accommodatissima & manifestissima analogia mentibus fidelium testificans, sicut naturales illi cibus & potus naturalibus organis sumpti,& naturali calore concocti,digesti & tandem nostris corporibus assimilati, mortalem hanc vitam, ex Dei Creatoris ordinatione, nutriunt & foueŋt:ita Iesum Christum θεάν-θρωπον [?],per fidei instrumentum, diuina virtute,ex noui fœderis pacto perceptum,vsque adeo nostrum fieri cum suis beneficiis saluificis omnibus, ut,incomprehensibili mysterio, ad spiritualem vitam [?] in nobis obsignandam, velut in nos transeat, & nos vicissim in illum transeamus. Nulla tamen hic imaginanda est illarum substantiarum traductio. Manet e-nim ille semper ὑφισταμένον [?] a nobis non tantum distinctum, sed etiam, quòd ad sui substantiam attinet, separatum, & nos vicissim nostris hypostasibus ab illo distincti & separati: & cibus iste, ut scite scribit Augustinus, non dentis est, sed mentis. Sed hæc mutua illius in nos & nostri in illum velut transitio intelligitur, quatenus ille quidem nos, quòd ad luendas nostrorum peccatorum pœnas, & diuinæ legis præstatione attinet, in sese quodammodo traduxit: & nos vicissim, quatenus ipsius, ad mortem usque crucis, obedientiam gratuita imputatione obtinemus, in ipsum traducimur, ut in eo iustificati, tum ab omnibus peccatis absoluamur, tum ius ad obtinendam vitam æternam adipiscamur. Sed & præterea, sicut naturalis facultas, diuinitus cibo & potui indita est, hominibus in hac vita, tum ad iustam staturam sensim euehendis, tum in illa postea coseruandis:ita, & quidem multò magis, assumptæ pro nobis à Filio Dei humanitati inexistit subiectiuè perfectissima tum naturæ nostræ sanctitas, tum perennis illius ac cœlestis vitæ fons inexhaustus:ut inde ἐνεργητικῶς[?] in omnes, diuina virtute, per fidei instrumentū ipsi adhærentes, & ita ipsi paulatim συμμορφωμένως[?] & συσχηματιζομένας redundet, illa intra nos cœpta Sanctificatio nostra, tum in anima, tum in corporibus nostris ultimo illo die consummanda.
units.tr: Next to this handing over, distribution and grasping of the signs in the hands, there follows the external or bodily conveyance of this bread and this wine into our body by eating and drinking. This offers a most fitting and manifest analogy, testifying to the minds of the faithful, that just as natural food and drink, taken by the natural organs and digested by natural heat, are at last assimilated to our bodies and by the ordinance of God the Creator nourish and sustain this mortal life, so Jesus Christ, the God-man, received through faith as the instrument, by divine power, from the covenant of the new testament, is made ours, with all his saving benefits, to such a degree that, by an incomprehensible mystery, he passes into us to seal the spiritual life within us, and we in turn pass into him. Yet no conversion of those substances is to be imagined here. For he always remains distinct from us, and indeed separate as regards his substance, and we likewise remain distinct and separate from him in our own persons. And this food, as Augustine wisely writes, is not for the teeth but for the mind. But this mutual passing of him into us and of us into him is understood insofar as he indeed, as far as paying the penalties of our sins and fulfilling the divine law is concerned, has in a manner transferred us into himself; and we in turn, insofar as we obtain his obedience, even to the death of the cross, by free imputation, are transferred into him, so that being justified in him we are absolved both from all sins and obtain the right to attain eternal life. Moreover, just as the natural faculty is divinely implanted in food and drink, for men in this life both to be raised gradually to a full stature and afterwards to be preserved in it, so, and much more so, there inheres in the humanity assumed for us by the Son of God, as its subject, the most perfect holiness of our nature and the inexhaustible fount of its perennial and heavenly life. Thence it overflows, actively, by divine power, through the instrument of faith, into all who cling to him, and so our sanctification, begun within us, is gradually conformed to him, to be brought to completion in our souls and in our bodies on that last day.

units.la: Cæterùm Christus cum his suis beneficiis, nō tunc primùm credentibus donatur, sed antea per fidem receptus, intra credentes magis ac magis obsignatur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ with these benefits is not given to believers only then for the first time, but, having been received previously through faith, is more and more sealed within believers.

units.la: Deinde præter ingens illud, tum inter corporalem & spiritualem vitam, tum inter corporalem generationem, & spiritualem regenerationem discrimen, quædam etiam maxidissimilitudo & imparitas in istis occurrit, summopere a nobis obseruanda. Nam in naturali quidem nutritione, cibus & potus iis corporibus assimilantur, a quibus sumuntur & concoquuntur: in ista vero spirituali alimonia, quae manducationis & potus nominibus metaphoricè intelligendis, extra haec etiam mysteria adumbratur, contrario prorsus ordine, animus primum noster, diuinitus, quod ad intelligentiam attinet, illustratus, & in voluntate ad recte volendum & agendum idoneus factus, Christo per fidei instrumentum apprehenso συμμορφωτάι, & συσχηματίζε-ταὶ: hic quidem renascens & sensim adolescens, in coelis vero, vltimo demum die, in aeternum vna cum corpore spiritualem vitam victurus: quum Deus videlicet erit omnia in suis omnibus. Nec aliter etiam intelligenda est, metaphoricè sic appellata Insitio. Nam in illa quidem naturali arborum insitione, olea cui surculus inseritur, vim suam in illius surculi sibi insiti naturam transformat: in ista vero spirituali credentium in Christum insitione contrario itidem ordine euenit, vt surculi in naturam eius cui insiti sunt transmutentur.
units.tr: Then, beyond that great difference both between bodily and spiritual life and between bodily generation and spiritual regeneration, there is also a certain very great likeness and unlikeness in these things, which we must observe with great care. For in natural nourishment, food and drink are assimilated to the bodies from which they are taken and digested. But in that spiritual nourishment, which is figured by the metaphorically understood names of eating and drinking, and which is also shadowed forth outside these mysteries, the order is entirely reversed: our mind is first enlightened by God as regards understanding, and made fit to will and act rightly, and then, having apprehended Christ through the instrument of faith, it is conformed [συμμορφωτάι] and fashioned [συσχηματίζεται] to him. The mind is reborn here and gradually grows, and in heaven at last, on the final day, it will live a spiritual life for ever together with the body, when God will be all in all. Nor is the metaphorically so-called grafting to be understood otherwise. For in that natural grafting of trees, the olive into which a shoot is grafted changes its own power into the nature of the shoot grafted into it; but in the spiritual grafting of believers into Christ, the order is likewise reversed, so that the shoots are transformed into the nature of that into which they are grafted.

units.la: Et haec quidem in nostris Ecclesiis, minimè profecto ex cuiusquam hominis quantumuis excellentis Christi serui placitis, sed ex Propheticis & Apostolicis scriptis, perpetua Ecclesiae totius veteris orthodoxae consuetudine, desumpta proponuntur.
units.tr: These things are set forth in our Churches, not at all from the pleasure of any man, however excellent a servant of Christ he may be, but drawn from the Prophetic and Apostolic writings and from the perpetual custom of the whole ancient orthodox Church.

units.la: Qui vero nos, vt de rebus istis non recte sensentientes insectantur, videamus quo iure id faciant. Primum igitur, ut ab illis materiali-bus signis incipiamus, si ex Pontificiorum doctrina, panis ille & vinum illud in corpus & sanguinem Domini, verè ac reipsa trans-substantiantur, certè amplius non existunt, ac proinde ne signa quidem sunt. Quòd si signa non sint, quînam, posita transsubstantiatione, non tolletur tota Sacramenti definitio? Neque ullus relinquitur huic Pontificiorum exceptioni locus, quòd videlicet ipsa panis & vini accidentia permaneant. Hoc enim si verum est, certè hæc accidentia, vel nulli subiecto, vel ipsi Christi corpori & sanguini inerunt. Si nulli, ergo accidentia non erunt. Sin verò ipsi Christi corpori & sanguini, ut alia absurdissima præteream, ubi iam erit analogia illa signorum & rerū significatarum? quæ, sicut rectè scribit Augustinus, si abest, Sacramenta nulla fuerint? Substantiis enim significandis, substantiæ suis accidentibus vestitæ, non autem nuda accidentia conveniunt: ut-pote quæ, ne subiici quidem sensibus absque substantia possint, cui insint & inhæreant.
units.tr: But as for those who harass us as if we thought wrongly about these matters, let us see by what right they do so. First, to begin with those material signs: if, according to the doctrine of the Papists, that bread and that wine are truly and in reality transubstantiated into the body and blood of the Lord, then they certainly no longer exist, and so they are not even signs. But if they are not signs, what then, once transubstantiation is posited, will not be taken away from the whole definition of the Sacrament? Nor is there any room left for this exception of the Papists, that the accidents of bread and wine remain. For if this is true, these accidents will either inhere in no subject or in the very body and blood of Christ. If in no subject, then they will not be accidents. But if in the very body and blood of Christ (to pass over other most absurd consequences), where then will be that analogy between signs and things signified? And, as Augustine rightly writes, if this is absent, there would be no sacraments. For substances are signified by substances clothed with their accidents, not by bare accidents, which cannot even be perceived by the senses without a substance in which they inhere and to which they adhere.

units.la: Ritus autem Sacramentales quo tandem iure, ab aliis quidem pessimè deprauatos, ab aliis verò penitus abolitos, censebimus? Nam ut à panis fractione exordiar, (cuius ritus analogia Christi quasi adhuc in cruce animam pro nobis exhalantis imaginem pœnè viuam nobis ob oculos subiicit,) cur illam bis in institutione Coenæ Domini, nēpe verbo ἔκλασε[?] & participio κλώμενον[?], expressam, perpetuo consensu ab ecclesia vetere obseruatam, & invecta demum sacrorum symbolorum idololatria abolitam, illi non modò non restituunt, sed nec restitui quidem patiuntur? Immò cur illam non modò sic expungunt, verùm etiam in contrarium prorsus ritum transformant, quum pro fracto pane, accedentibus omnibus, totidem numero integros, & separatos paruulos panes singulis accedentibus distribuunt? Hac enim sui cuique particularis integri panis praebitione, praeter illam abolitam fractionis panis pretiosissimam analogiam, de qua diximus, illud quoque credentium & ex uno fracto pane edentium, mutuae cum uno & eodem Christo & inter se communicationis spiritualis symbolum aboletur. Quid autem huic tam audaci facto praetexitur? Frangere panem, inquiunt, apud Hebræos, idem declarat atque panem distribuere. adeò quidem ut ipsa Cœnæ Domini administratio fit fractionis panis nomine intellecta, ut Act. 2.42. & 46. & 20.7. & 11. & 1.Cor.10.20. Fateor,
units.tr: But by what right shall we judge the sacramental rites, which some have utterly depraved and others entirely abolished? To begin with the breaking of bread (whose analogy, as if Christ were still on the cross breathing out his soul for us, sets almost a living image before our eyes): why do they not only refuse to restore it, though the ancient Church observed it with perpetual agreement, and though it is expressed twice in the institution of the Lord's Supper, namely by the verb ἔκλασε [éklase] and the participle κλώμενον [klṓmenon], and was abolished only when the idolatry of sacred symbols was introduced; but they do not even allow it to be restored? Indeed, why do they not only erase it in this way, but even transform it into the completely opposite rite, since, instead of broken bread, they distribute to each of those approaching as many whole, separate little loaves as there are communicants, one to each? For by this giving to each person a whole particular bread, that most precious analogy of the breaking of bread, of which we have spoken, is lost, and with it also that symbol of the spiritual communion of believers, who eat from one broken bread, both with the one and same Christ and with one another. What is offered as a pretext for so bold a deed? "To break bread," they say, "among the Hebrews means the same as to distribute bread." So much so that the very administration of the Lord's Supper is understood under the name of the breaking of bread, as in Acts 2.42, 46; 20.7, 11, and 1 Cor. 10.20. I grant it.

units.la: Sed συνεκδοχικῶς[?]: quoniam videlicet Hebræis, qui non ita spissis ut nos panibus utebantur, mos fuit cibi sumptionem à panis, non scissione, sed fractione inchoare. Hinc enim factum est, ut ab eo quod antecedebat, totum quod consequebatur Epulum hanc appellationem sumpserit, ut apparet etiam ex panum miraculo multiplicatorum historia, & Luc. 24.30. Sublata verò, ut isti faciunt, panis fractione, ctione, quisnā fuerit isti synecdochæ relictus locus? Sed quorsū hoc?Duas enim numero & ordine distinctas actiones istas fuisse liquet, ex his duobus verbis, Fregit, Dedit. Neque Lucas scripsit, τὸ διδόμενον ὑμῖν, quod datur vobis, sed τὸ διδόμενον ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, quod datur pro vobis, apertissimè ostendens hanc donationē à præbitione discipulis facta distinctam, alió spectare: nempe ad factam patri à Christo pro nobis corporis sui oblationē. Neq; verò Paulus temere participium illud διδόμενον, quod generalius erat à Luca scriptū, in κλώμενον mutauit. Et de fractione quidem panis hactenus.
units.tr: But this is by synecdoche: namely, because it was the custom of the Hebrews, who did not use bread as thick as ours, to begin the taking of food from the bread not by cutting but by breaking it. Hence it came about that the whole feast which followed took this name from that which came first, as is also apparent from the history of the multiplied loaves, and from Luke 24.30. But if, as they do, the breaking of bread is taken away, what place is left for that synecdoche? But to what end is this said? For it is clear from these two words, "He broke, he gave," that these were two actions distinct in number and order. Nor did Luke write τὸ διδόμενον ὑμῖν [to didomenon hymin], "which is given to you," but τὸ διδόμενον ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν [to didomenon hyper hymōn], "which is given for you," most plainly showing that this giving, distinct from the distribution made to the disciples, looks elsewhere: namely, to the offering of his body which Christ made to the Father for us. Nor did Paul rashly change that participle διδόμενον [didomenon], which Luke had written more generally, into κλώμενον [klṓmenon]. And so much for the breaking of bread.

units.la: Iam verò quòd ad traditionem in manus,& illi ex aduerso respondentem manuum prehensionem attinet: iidem vtrumque sa-cramentalem ritum, ne restitui quidem sustinent. Non rectè primùm, retenta duntaxat panis & vini oralí sumptione. Con-venit enim illæ [?]cibi & potus ore ipso sumendi mos, non adultis, & grandioribus, id est, iis qui sensus habent ad discretionē boni & mali exercitatos, Hebr.5.14. quales esse oportet, quoad fieri poterit, eos omnes qui sese iubentur explorare, priusquàm ad Domini mensam accedant: sed vagientibus adhuc infantibus, & qui dextram à sinistra discernere nequeunt. Deinde cui tándem homini licuit, quod Christus & fecit & disertè faciendum præcepit, (non tantum illo generali mandato Hoc facite, sed speciatim λάβετε dicens, & quidem imperandi modo) abrogare? Hoc enim verbum de prehenfione per manus, ac proinde verbum ἔδωκεν[?] de traditione in manus intelligendum esse, non tantum ostendit propria verbi λαμβάνειν notatio: sed etiam ex eo liquet quod alioqui manifesta foret in Christi verbis ταυτολογία[?], quum oris fumptio ex verbis φάγετε & πίνετε per se necessario intelligatur. Sed & hoc demonstrat ipsa institutionis Cœnæ Domini narratio, si spectetur epulantium cum Domino discipulorum discubitus. Nam alioqui profecto singulos illos oportuisset, relicto suo loco, ad Dominum accedere, & ei porrigenti panem & vinum os apertum exhibere: quod neque factum fuisse narrat historia, neque verisimiliter opinari quisquam possit. Merito igitur quum in Africa maximus ille præbendæ mortuis etiam Eucharistiæ, ac proinde istius in os ingestionis abusus inolevisset, Synodus Carthaginiensis tertia, Can.6. quanvis alia quibus ista profanatio refellere-tur argumenta non deessent, verbum tamen λάβετε[?] arripuit. Dictum enim est, inquit, a Domino, accipite, edite, Cadavera vero mortuorum nec accipere possunt nec edere. Ad hæc accedit, quod ista in os panis ac potus ingesti receptio, non est oris actio, sed potius πάθος[?]: ac proinde nequit ἀναλόγως ad certissimam illam & supernaturalem Fidei in Christo apprehendendo energia accommodari. Sed istud, inquiunt adversarij, est syllabas aucupari, & pæne de nihilo controversiam movere. Mihi vero prorsus nefarium esse videtur sacramentales istos ritus, diuinitus tam expresse institutos, præceptos, & veteris totius Ecclesiæ iudicio & auctoritate confirmatos abrogare.
units.tr: Now as for the handing over into the hands, and the corresponding taking with the hands, they do not even allow either sacramental rite to be restored. First, they are wrong in retaining only the oral taking of bread and wine. For that manner of taking food and drink with the mouth suits not adults and grown people, that is, those whose senses are trained to discern good and evil (Heb. 5.14), such as all those who are bidden to examine themselves ought to be, as far as possible, before they approach the Lord's table; it suits infants still crying, who cannot tell right from left. Then, by what right has any man been permitted to abrogate what Christ both did and expressly commanded to be done, not only by that general command "Do this," but specifically saying λάβετε [labete], "take," and that in the imperative mood? That this word refers to taking by the hands, and so the word ἔδωκεν [edōken] to giving into the hands, is shown not only by the proper meaning of the word λαμβάνειν [lambanein], but also by this: otherwise there would be a manifest tautology in Christ's words, since the taking into the mouth is already necessarily understood from the words "eat" and "drink." This too is shown by the very narrative of the institution of the Lord's Supper, if one considers the reclining of the disciples at table with the Lord. For otherwise each of them would have had to leave his place and approach the Lord, and present an open mouth to him as he held out the bread and wine; which the history does not relate was done, nor can anyone reasonably suppose it. Rightly, therefore, when that great abuse of offering the Eucharist even to the dead had grown up in Africa, and with it this abuse of putting it into the mouth, the Third Council of Carthage (canon 6), although other arguments by which this profanation might be refuted were not lacking, nevertheless seized upon the word λάβετε [labete]. "For it has been said by the Lord," it says, "take, eat; but corpses can neither take nor eat." To this is added that this reception of bread and drink put into the mouth is not an action of the mouth but rather a passion, and therefore cannot be fitted in proportion to that most certain and supernatural energy of faith in apprehending Christ. But this, the opponents say, is to hunt for syllables and to stir up a controversy almost out of nothing. To me, however, it seems utterly wicked to abrogate those sacramental rites, so expressly instituted by God, commanded, and confirmed by the judgment and authority of the whole ancient Church.

units.la: Supersunt actiones duæ Sacramentales, & quidem maximi momenti: panis videlicet illius externa & naturalis manducatio, & illius vini itidem externus, & naturalis potus: quibus signis illa interna & spiritualis alimonia, & quasi (sicut supra diximus) Christi in nos, & nostra vicissim in illum transitio efficacissima repræsentatur. In his vero, partim depra-vandis, partim abolendis, quis explicare satis possit, quæ ab aliquot seculis fuerit, & nunc adhuc sit, spiritus erroris efficacia? Primùm enim, ecce Pontificij altera harum actionum, solis suis sacrificis concessa, reliqua Ecclesiam priuant: alteram verò, id est, Man-ducationem, quæ proprie vnius panis est, nec attribui Christi corpori, aliter quàm metaphoricè potest, retinent quidem, sed quàm non ad panem, quem sua transsubstantiatio-ne, abolent, sed ad ipsum Christi corpus referunt, dentibus etiam ipsis, (sic enim loquitur illorum Papa Nicolaus) atterendum: ut jam causa nulla sit, cur Christiani Iudæis sæui-tiam illam exprobrent, quam aduersus Christum exercuerunt. Sed ista, scilicet plusquam Cyclopica immanitas, ferri facilè potest, mo-dò per aliud scelus, Christi corpore sua visi-bilitatis essentiali proprietate spoliato, inui-sibilis hæc σαρκοφαγία statuatur.
units.tr: Two sacramental actions remain, and indeed of the greatest importance: the external and natural eating of that bread, and the likewise external and natural drinking of that wine. By these signs that inward and spiritual nourishment is represented, and, as we said above, the most efficacious transition of Christ into us and of ours in turn into him. But in these, partly depraving and partly abolishing, who can sufficiently explain how great has been, for some centuries and is still now, the efficacy of the spirit of error? For first, behold: the Papists, granting one of these actions to their priests alone, deprive the rest of the Church of it. The other, namely the eating, which properly belongs to bread alone and can be attributed to the body of Christ only metaphorically, they indeed retain, but refer not to the bread, which they abolish by their transubstantiation, but to the very body of Christ, which is to be ground even with the teeth (for so their Pope Nicholas speaks). So there is now no reason why Christians should reproach the Jews for the savagery they exercised against Christ. But that monstrous cruelty, more than Cyclopean, can easily be borne, provided that by another crime the body of Christ, stripped of the essential property of its visibility, is made the object of this invisible sarcophagy.

units.la: Alij nonnulli dum illud utrumque malum vitare studeant, restituto poculi usu, & corporali panis esu, videant tandem, rogo & obtestor, an non unicam & eandem statuentes significationum & rerum significatarum mandationem, ex Scylla in Charibdin incidat. Nam, ut alia praeteream, de quibus alibi dicemus, quum in his mysteriis constare debeat Corpus & sanguinem Domini, non simpliciter & per se, quatenus, & ipsæ sunt substantiæ corporeæ, & sensibus ipsis perceptibiles, sed ut res, sicut recte loquitur Irenæus, cælestes, ac proinde fideli demum mente magis ac magis intelligendas, credendas, & ad spiritualis vitæ incrementum spirituali modo in nobis obsignandas proponi: quis sapientissimis etiam Theologis, persuaderi potuisse facile credat, ut repugnante ipsa rerum istarum natura, & ipso Sacramentorum usu sic euerso, una & eadem naturali in os præbitione externa, res illas sumendas præberi, & proinde una & eadem naturali, orali manducatione, & sensibili oris esu & potu sumi existimarent, ac proinde duas tam diversas personas, (Pastorem videlicet id quod exterius agitur, agentem, & Christum suo Spiritu sancto id quod intus fit, efficientem) velut in unam personam conflarent? duas tam diversas præbitiones, unam videlicet externam & sensibilem signorum sensibilium, alteram internam, & supernaturaliter intellectualem rerum significatarum, non aliter quam fidei oculo perceptibilium, in unam & quidem oralem, naturalem & sensibilem lem praebitionem redigerent? &, vt paucis omnia complectar, coelum in terram aduocarent? non minus id quidem absurde, quam si quis Circumcisionem externam praeputij, & internam cordis Circumcisionem, vt vnicam eamque simplicem actionem, ad vnum eundemque sacerdotem referendam fuisse existimaret:aut in Baptismo, Pastorem hodie aqua baptizantem, & Christum suo Spiritu intus baptizantem, vnam & eandem esse personam, & vnam simplicem hic esse actionem habendam opinetur. Hoc enim vsque adeo falsum est, vt & istae personae (Christus videlicet & Pastores) & externa corporalis actio Ba-ptismi, & altera interna & spiritualis Ba-ptismi actio, non tantum inter se diseernantur,sed etiam in nonnullis seiungantur, vt in hypocritis & iis omnibus accidit, quos nunquam fuisse intus Spiritu baptizatos, perpetuus eorum vitae cursus ostendit.Hoccine vero est, doctrinam de Sacramentis,ab Antichri-stianis tam foedis & horrendis corruptelis as-serere?
units.tr: Others, while they try to avoid both of those evils, restore the use of the cup and the bodily eating of the bread. I beg and urge them to consider whether, in holding a single and identical mandate for the signs and the things signified, they do not fall from Scylla into Charybdis. To pass over other points, which I will discuss elsewhere: since in these mysteries the body and blood of the Lord must be understood not simply and in themselves, insofar as they are corporeal substances perceptible to the senses, but as heavenly things, as Irenaeus rightly says, which are to be grasped and believed more and more by the faithful mind and sealed upon us spiritually for the growth of spiritual life, who could easily believe that even the wisest theologians could be persuaded to do this: that, though the very nature of these things and the very use of the sacraments resist it, these things are offered to be taken by one and the same natural external presentation to the mouth, and so they judge that they are received by one and the same natural, oral eating and by the sensible eating and drinking of the mouth? And so they would fuse two such different persons into one: the minister, who performs the outward action, and Christ, who by his Holy Spirit effects what happens inwardly. Would they reduce two such different presentations, one outward and sensible of sensible signs, the other inward and supernaturally intellectual of the things signified, which are perceptible only to the eye of faith, into one presentation that is oral, natural and sensible? And, to sum up everything briefly, would they bring heaven down to earth? That would be no less absurd than if someone thought that the outward circumcision of the foreskin and the inward circumcision of the heart were one simple action, to be attributed to one and the same priest; or if someone held that in Baptism the minister who baptizes today with water and Christ who baptizes inwardly by his Spirit are one and the same person, and that there is here one simple action. For it is so far from true that these persons (namely Christ and the ministers), the outward bodily action of Baptism and the other, inward and spiritual action of Baptism, are not only distinguished from one another but in some cases are even separated, as happens in hypocrites and in all those whom the continual course of their life shows never to have been baptized inwardly by the Spirit. Is this really how one should teach the doctrine of the sacraments, given such foul and horrible corruptions by the Antichristians?

units.la: Et de ritibus quidem illis plane diuinis, partim miserè corruptis, partim abolitis ha-ctenus dictum esto. Illas autem commentitias innumerabiles ceremonias, falsa religionis specie introductas, mihi vel nominare re-ligio est. Nam si Pontificij istarum rerum doctoribus fides habenda est,nihil est in toto ipsorum apparatu, ne ipso quidem Sacerdotum illorum habitu excepto, quod spirituale & religiosum quidpiam spectatoribus non figuret. Sed, quo auctore, quo sponsore? non certè Christo, nisi nos hæc arcana celarunt Euangelistæ & Apostoli. Non itidem Spiritu sancto, Ecclesiæ quidem, minimè tamen ad aliquod ἄγραφον verbum aut Sacramentum excogitandum, promisso. Quinam autem acceptam illi tulerimus istam ex abolito Iudaismo, & profanissimo Paganismo, longè maxima ex parte, cōflatam istarum ceremoniarum farraginem? Scilicet ille addendum aliquid ad simplices illos ritus, tum in Baptismo, tum in sacræ Cœnæ mysteriis docuit, vt augustiorem & spectabiliorem aliquam formam induceret?
units.tr: So much for those rites that are truly divine, some of them wretchedly corrupted and some abolished until now. As for those innumerable invented ceremonies, introduced under a false appearance of religion, I scruple even to name them. For if the Papists are to be believed by their teachers of these matters, there is nothing in their whole apparatus, not even the very dress of their priests, that does not suggest something spiritual and religious to the onlookers. But by whose authority, by whose guarantee? Certainly not Christ's, unless the evangelists and apostles hid these secrets from us. Nor the Holy Spirit's, who promised the Church indeed, but by no means that it should devise any unwritten word or sacrament [ἄγραφον]. And who are we to credit with this huge hodgepodge of ceremonies, largely cobbled together from the abolished Judaism and the most profane paganism? Did he, perhaps, teach that something should be added to those simple rites, both in Baptism and in the mysteries of the holy Supper, in order to introduce some more majestic and showy form?

units.la: Quasi vero quanto illa simpliciora sunt, tanto non sint rebus spiritualibus repræsentandis accommodatiora, & novo Testamento convenientiora Sacramenta. Hoc enim nisi concedamus, longè potior fuerit patrum sub lege conditio quàm nostra: vt qui tam multa, & tam operosa Sacramenta præ nobis habuerint. Neque id mirum, quum pluribus & crassioribus quàm nos adminiculis indiguerit eorum fides, quibus Euangelij lux illa plena nondum affulserat.
units.tr: As though the sacraments, the simpler they are, were not for that very reason more suited to representing spiritual things and more fitting to the New Testament! For unless we grant this, the condition of the fathers under the law would be far better than ours, since they had so many and such laborious sacraments before them. Nor is this surprising, since their faith, to whom the full light of the gospel had not yet shone, needed more and coarser supports than ours do.

units.la: Num vero nos ab illo, vt loquitur Petrus, tam oneroso iugo, & quidem diuinitus imposito, liberati per Christi aduentum sumus, vt aliud multò grauius, nobis hominum arbitrio imponeretur? Neque hanc iniuriam, Ecclesiæ factam, plerique patrum, & quidem in primis Augustinus Ianuario cuidam scribens, dissimularunt: rectius tamen facturi si huic malo, quod semper deterius factum est, promptum remedium adhibuissent. Sed de istis postea quoque, quum ad Sacramentorum finem & usum ventum erit, Deo fauente, dis-seremus.
units.tr: Have we really been freed by the coming of Christ from that yoke so burdensome, as Peter calls it, and imposed by God himself, only to have another, much heavier one laid upon us by human judgement? Most of the fathers, and especially Augustine in his letter to a certain Januarius, did not ignore this wrong done to the Church. Yet they would have acted more rightly if they had applied a ready remedy to this evil, which has always got worse. But, God willing, we will discuss these matters again later, when we come to the purpose and use of the sacraments.

units.la: Denique signa illa omnia superstruimus in primis ipsi Institutionis Cœnæ Domini historiæ, diligentissimè à tribus Euangelistis perscriptæ, & ab Apostolo repetitæ: ac præsertim verbis ipsius [illegible, ~8 letters], nempe, Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis frangitur, siue datur. Hoc est sanguis meus Noui Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur. Vtpote quibus Euangelica salutis promissio, adhibitis certis tum corporeis rebus, tum ritibus religiosis, Christo sic nobiscum paciscente, magis ac magis, intelligenda, credenda, & per fidem apprehendenda, menti fideli proponitur. Hoc igitur est Domini verbum illud, quod propterea Sacramentale vocamus: à simplici verbo Euangelico, non re significata, sed notis illis externis adiunctis distinctum. Christus enim θεάνθρω-πος & unicus ille Mediator noster, utrobique totus & idem, cum omnibus suis beneficiis, sese fide, spiritualiter, magis ac magis apprehen-dendum, fideli menti præbet.
units.tr: Finally, we build all those signs first on the very history of the institution of the Lord's Supper, recorded most carefully by three evangelists and repeated by the apostle, and especially on his words [illegible]: This is my body, which is broken or given for you. This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many. By these words the promise of evangelical salvation is set before the faithful mind, with certain bodily things and religious rites added, as Christ thus covenants with us, to be understood, believed and grasped by faith more and more. This, then, is the word of the Lord which for that reason we call sacramental, distinguished from the plain gospel word not by the thing signified but by those outward signs added to it. For Christ, the God-man and our one Mediator, whole and identical in both, with all his benefits, offers himself to the faithful mind, to be grasped spiritually by faith more and more.

units.la: Quum autem ab huius verbi legitima prædicatione pendeant, vt ab instrumentali cau-sa συςτατικῇ[?] Sacramenta: viderint quinam hoc Sacramentum penitus non subvertunt, qui hoc eius fundamentum saluum & integrum non retinent: & an non illud quod Corinthiis Apostolus 1.ad Corin.11.20. infinitè leuiorem ob causam, exprobrat, (quòd videlicet Dominicam Cœnam non ederent) multò magis ipsis conueniat.
units.tr: Since the sacraments depend on the lawful preaching of this word, as on an instrumental cause, constitutive [συστατικῇ], let those consider who do not keep this foundation whole and intact whether they are utterly subverting this sacrament. And let them consider whether the reproach that the apostle directs at the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 11:20, for a far slighter reason (namely that they did not eat the Lord's Supper), applies much more to them.

units.la: Peccant verò hac in re omnium grauissimè & manifestissimè qui in huius actionis celebratione, verbum quidem Sacramentale non aperte expungunt, sed illo nonnisi peregrina lingua & plerunque ne iis quidè à quibus pronunciantur cognita, vtuntur. Quid quòd iidem hoc verbum, quod ab omnibus & singulis intelligi & credi oportuit, ne effantur quidem, sed in sinu demurmurant? Et quid hoc rei est, si non est Deum ipsum & Ecclesiam ludibrio habere? testante eodem Apostolo 1.ad Cor.14. eos in aërem loqui, qui in sacro cœtu, sermonem εὐσημον[?] no edant? Idem autem est de ritibus essentialibus neglestis statuendum.
units.tr: Those who, in celebrating this action, do not openly strike out the sacramental word, but use it only in a foreign tongue, and mostly one not even known to those who pronounce it, sin in this matter most gravely and most manifestly of all. What is more, do they not even utter this word, which ought to be understood and believed by each and every one, but mutter it into their bosoms? And what is this, if it is not to make a mockery of God and the Church, since the same apostle, in 1 Corinthians 14, testifies that those who in a sacred assembly utter speech that is not intelligible [εὔσημον] speak into the air? The same must be said of essential rites that are neglected.

units.la: Peccant quoque, etsi valdè grauiter, non tamen pariter, qui verbum quidem Sacramentale pronuntiant εὐσήμως[?], sed interpola-tum, & salsissimis interpretationibus adul-teratum, siue prudentes, siue per ignorantiam hoc agant: leuiore tamen quàm priores idcirco abusu, quòd, si modò alioqui hæc actio ritè, & ex Dei ordinatione exerceatur, persona-le Pastoris erratum integritate ipsam Sacramenti non aboleat: nec meliùs sentietis quàm Pastorem loquentem audiat, conscientiam rectiùs rectius instructam viciet. Sic enim sancti Pa-tres,& tum Christus ipse tum discipuli externo cultui diligenter interfuerunt, quanuis & tota doctrina in synagogis, & quaecunque in templo gerebantur, essent salsissimis interpretationibus contaminata. Hæc tamē etiam tunc adhibenda cautio est, vt infirmorum aliorum fratrum conscientiæ, quoad eius fieri potest, caueatur, sicut nos idem Apostolus monet 1.ad Cor.10.29. & quidem de rebus indif-ferentibus agens.
units.tr: Those also sin, though not equally, and yet very gravely, who pronounce the sacramental word intelligibly [εὐσήμως] but corrupted by interpolation and adulterated by most insipid interpretations, whether they do this knowingly or through ignorance. Their abuse is nonetheless lighter than that of the former, because, provided that this action is otherwise performed lawfully and according to God's ordinance, an error of the minister in his person does not abolish the integrity of the sacrament itself. Nor will those who hear a minister speaking worse understand or have their conscience more rightly instructed. For so the holy fathers, and Christ himself and his disciples, diligently took part in the outward worship, although all the teaching in the synagogues, and whatever went on in the temple, was contaminated by most insipid interpretations. Yet even then this caution must be observed, so far as it can be, so that the consciences of other weak brothers are spared, as the same apostle warns us in 1 Corinthians 10:29, and indeed when speaking of indifferent things.

units.la: Summa autem horum omnium hæc est, Quum sacra Domini Cœna, ex pactione Dei cum sua Ecclesia verbo Sacramentali testata, constet signis & rebus significatis, & hæc duo in mutua relatione consistant, vix dici posse Cœnam Dominicam edere (vt de Corinthiis loquitur Paulus) qui verbo Sacramentali non nisi peregrina lingua abutuntur, vt perinde faciant ac si semel esset expunctum: qui panem illum & vinum illud abolent transsub-stantiationis commento:qui denique ritibus Sacramentalibus sublatis, actionem hanc to-tam miserè mutilant.
units.tr: Now the sum of all these points is this. Since the holy Supper of the Lord, attested by the sacramental word in God's covenant with his Church, consists of signs and the things signified, and these two stand in mutual relation, it can hardly be said that those celebrate the Lord's Supper (as Paul speaks of the Corinthians) who abuse the sacramental word with a foreign language, so that they act as if it had been once for all struck out; who abolish that bread and that wine by the invention of transubstantiation; and who, finally, with the sacramental rites taken away, mangle the whole action wretchedly.

units.la: CAPUT II. De rebus Sacramentaliter in sacra Domini Cœna significatis & sub fidei conditione præbitis.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. Of the things sacramentally signified in the Lord's Supper and offered under the condition of faith.

units.la: Q[?]VÆ res in sacra Domini Cœna, partim materialibus illis signis duobus, partim ritibus illis religiosis, diuinitus mandatis Sacramentaliter, id est, addita illarum verę præbitionis promissione, significetur, ex superiore tractatione intelligi plenissimè potest: Christus ipse nimirum, sese, cum suis omnibus beneficiis, spiritualiter mentibus nostris, per fidem magis ac magis apprehendendum, & vtendum fruendum, non minus verè præbens, quàm verè signa illa corporaliter & organis corporeis percipienda traduntur.
units.tr: Which things are signified sacramentally in the Lord's Supper, partly by those two material signs and partly by those religious rites divinely commanded, that is, with the promise of their true giving added, can be fully understood from the preceding treatment. Christ himself, with all his benefits, is offered to our minds spiritually, to be apprehended more and more through faith, and to be used and enjoyed, no less truly than the signs are handed over to be received bodily by bodily organs.

units.la: In hanc veritatem peccant,& quidem gravissimè,qui pro ipsa essentiali Christi humanitate ( quæ est omnium quæ pro nobis redimendis subiit,subiectum,& per quam nobis, sicuti suo loco explicabimus, communicata vita illa spiritualis in credentes defluit) solum ipsius obedientiæ meritum, contendunt in sacra Domini Cœna, pane illo & vino illo,significari.Verètur enim ne si ipsum illud corpus, & ipsum illum Christi sanguinem, in hac actione significari,& nobis verè præberi, statuatur,realis quoq; in terris Christi humanitati,tum præsentia, tum cum panis & vini substantiis coniunctio, atque adeò in ipsa corpora nostra traiectio,ponantur. Et fatendum quidem est, hæc monstra necessario Transsubstantiationis &Consubstantiationis dogma consequi.Sed non propterea fuit ipse ChriChristus & eius obedientia, ab eius merito, & fructu separandus, quum agitur de re, quæ in hac actione Sacramentaliter significatur: sed naturalis quidem ille & corporeus rerum cum signis coniunctionis modus, vt salsissimus est tollendus: & eius loco, vera illa Sacramentalis & σχετικὴ[?] connexio statuenda, ex qua nullum tale monstrum nascitur, & tamen vera ipsiusmet quoque Christi, & eius beneficiorum Sacramentalis coniunctio statuitur, sicut sequenti tractatione ostendemus.
units.tr: Those who contend that in the Lord's Supper only the merit of Christ's obedience, and not his very essential humanity (which is the subject of everything he underwent for our redemption, and through which that spiritual life, as we shall explain in its place, flows into believers), is signified by that bread and that wine, err in this truth, and very gravely. They fear that if it is affirmed that his very body and his very blood are signified in this action and truly offered to us, then a real presence of Christ's humanity on earth will be posited, and a conjunction with the substances of bread and wine, and so a passage into our very bodies. And it must indeed be admitted that these monsters necessarily follow from the dogma of Transubstantiation and Consubstantiation. Yet for that reason Christ and his obedience ought not to be separated from its merit and fruit, when we are dealing with the thing that is signified sacramentally in this action. Rather, that natural and corporeal mode of conjunction of things with signs must be removed, as most absurd, and in its place that true sacramental and relative [σχετική] connection must be established, from which no such monster arises. Yet by it a true sacramental conjunction is established both with Christ himself and with his benefits, as we shall show in the following treatment.

units.la: Nec enim temere Christus ipse requirit à patre vt vnum cum ipso fiamus: & ipsa corporis pro nobis traditi, & sanguinis pro nobis effusi, nomina signis illis tribuit. Et huc quoque respicit similitudo illa palmitum in illam vitem Insitionis, per quam postea, causarum ordine, palmites illius succo alantur & fructificent: itidemque illa capitis & membrorum σῶμα[?]: & illud In Chri-sto, toties ab Apostolo inculcatum: & quod idem Apostolus diserte Sacram hanc Cœnam, à præcipuo effecto describens, pani quidem illi, Corpo-ris, vino autem illi, Sanguinis communio-nem adscribit.
units.tr: For Christ did not lightly ask of the Father that we should become one with him, and he gives the names of his body given for us and his blood shed for us to those signs. To this also refers the likeness of the branches to that vine of ingrafting, by which afterwards, in the order of causes, the branches are nourished and bear fruit from its sap; likewise the body [σῶμα] of the head and the members; and that phrase In Christ, so often urged by the Apostle; and also the fact that the same Apostle, describing this Holy Supper by its principal effect, ascribes to that bread the communion of the body, and to that wine the communion of the blood.

units.la: Sed infinitè certè grauior est eorum lapsus, quos si à spiritu erroris, incredibili pœnè efficacia, fascinatos fuisse dixero, dixero certè quod res est. Illos autem cum grauissimo, cu-ius mihi Deus testis est, gemitu, & sincero pe-ctore, per illius Seruatoris nostri nomen pre-cor & obsecro, vt rem hanc totam malint sine præiudicio placidoq; animo nobiscum con-siderare, quàm in isto contendendi proposi-to perseverare. Quorsum igitur, quæso, Corporis & Sanguinis Domini vocabula jactantur, nisi salva prorsus, & perpetua illorum quantumvis glorificatorum definitio, tum in ipsa eorum substantia, & ut in scholis loquuntur, Quidditate, tum etiam in essentialibus eius proprietatibus inviolabiliter servetur? An autem id fieri possit, posita reali, & essentiali, Humanitatis Christi, sive per Transsubstantiationem, sive per Consubstantiationem, sive omnibus, sive in, sub, vel cum tot panibus & tot poculis, in terris præsentia, sequente tractatione quæretur.
units.tr: But the fall of those men is certainly infinitely more grievous, and if I should say that they have been bewitched by a spirit of error, with an almost incredible efficacy, I would certainly be saying what is the truth. Yet with the deepest groaning, and with a sincere heart, God being my witness, I pray and beseech them, in the name of our Saviour, that they would rather consider this whole matter with us calmly and without prejudice, than persist in the purpose of contending. Why, then, I ask, are the words of the Lord's Body and Blood bandied about, unless the definition of those things, however glorified, remains wholly safe and perpetual, both in their very substance, and, as they say in the schools, in their quiddity, and also inviolably preserved in their essential properties? Whether this can be done, given a real and essential presence of Christ's humanity on earth, whether by Transubstantiation or by Consubstantiation, whether in, under, or with so many breads and so many cups, will be inquired into in the following treatment.

units.la: Ad hunc errorem alius, & quidem grauissimus, accedit, in eo positus, quòd nonnulli, Corpus & sanguinem, sic præcisè & restrictè solet urgere, ut ne levissime quidem ipsius a-nimæ Christi meminerint, cuius tamen, vel in primis habenda fuit ratio. Quum enim o-bedientiæ Christi per quam & à peccatis ab-solvimur, & æternæ vitæ ius adipiscimur, partes præcipuas subierit anima Christi: efficitur animam quoque Christi oportere nobis spiritualiter communicari, id est, nostram fie-ri, non minus, imò etiam multò magis, quàm ipsius corpus & sanguinem, ut in ipsius morte, in qua proprie & præcipuè, ipsius lucta-ta, ut ex ipsius agone apparet, tum remissionem peccatorum, tum vitæ æternæ ius, tum spiritualis vitæ, ultimo demum die consummandæ primitias non aliter nanciscamur ex Euangelico fœdere, quàm huius nostræ cum toto Christo spiritualis vnitionis beneficio, cuius specialis est σφραγίς hæc sacra Domini Cœna.
units.tr: To this error another, and a most grievous one, is added, consisting in this: that some press the body and blood so exclusively and narrowly that they do not so much as lightly remember the soul of Christ, though that soul should above all have been taken into account. For since the soul of Christ undertook the principal parts of that obedience of Christ through which we are absolved from sins and acquire the right to eternal life, it follows that the soul of Christ also must be spiritually communicated to us, that is, made ours, no less, indeed much more, than his body and blood. In his death, in which above all and especially he struggled, as is clear from his agony, we obtain by the covenant of the gospel the remission of sins, the right to eternal life, and the firstfruits of spiritual life, to be consummated on the last day, in no other way than by the benefit of this spiritual union of ours with the whole Christ. Of this benefit the Lord's Holy Supper is a special seal [σφραγίς].

units.la: Itaque corporis & sanguinis appellatione, in his mysteriis totam Christi humanitatem, & ὅλως & καθ' μέρη consideratam συνεχδοχι-ικῶς [?] intelligimus: imò etiam totam Christi personam, seruato tamen communicationis Deitatis discrimine, quod suo loco explicabimus. Nam vt recte scribit Augustinus, nec ipsius humanitas sine Deitate, per fidem videlicet, in simplici verbo, tum in Sacramentis apprehensa, nobis esse potest Mediatrix. Causa vero istius synecdoches, in hac sacræ Cœnæ institutione, ab ipso Christo vsurpatæ, hæc est: quòd licet vnus & idem ille, qui passus est pro nobis, sit Deus & homo, vivifica alioqui non futura ipsius morte, passus est tamen, non ipsa Deitate, sed in carne, vt loquitur Petrus: & idcirco, Christus volens nostræ totius salutis mysterium, nobis hac sacra actione, in Christo quasi adhuc præsente, &, vt barbarè in scholis loquuntur, in ipso fieri visibiliter quodammodo repræsentare, visibilem illam Humanitatis suæ partem exprimens, alteram tamen & quidem præcipuam, nō magis omittere voluit, quàm quum dicitur, verbum Caro factum, & Christus passus in carne, & nos sanguine ipsius redempti dicimur. Sic etiam scribens Apostolus, nos in istis mysteriis fieri membra corporis eius, ex eius carne, & ex eius ossibus, de spirituali tamen Christi & Ecclesiae connubio loquens, minime certe expungere voluit, quod alibi nempe, i.ad Corinth.6.17. declarat, eum videlicet qui Christo adhaereat unum esse cum ipso spiritum.
units.tr: Therefore, by the term body and blood in these mysteries we understand the whole humanity of Christ, considered both wholly and in its parts [ὅλως καὶ καθ' μέρη], by synecdoche [συνεχδοχικῶς]; indeed, even the whole person of Christ, while preserving the distinction of communication of the Deity, which we shall explain in its place. For, as Augustine rightly writes, neither can his humanity be our Mediator without the Deity, that is, apprehended by faith in the simple word, as well as in the sacraments. The cause of this synecdoche, used by Christ himself in the institution of this Holy Supper, is this: although that one and the same man who suffered for us is both God and man, his death, which would otherwise not be life-giving, was suffered not in the Deity itself but, as Peter says, in the flesh. Therefore Christ, wishing to represent to us, in this holy action, the mystery of our whole salvation, as though he were still present in Christ, and, to use the barbarous scholastic phrase, in some way visibly made in him, expressing that visible part of his humanity, yet did not wish to omit the other part, and that the chief one, any more than when we say, the Word was made flesh, and Christ suffered in the flesh, and we are said to be redeemed by his blood. Likewise, when the Apostle writes that we in these mysteries become members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones, speaking of the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church, he certainly did not wish to erase what he declares elsewhere, namely, i. ad Corinth. 6.17., that he who cleaves to Christ is one spirit with him.

units.la: Restat tertius alius, & quidem multiplex error sane pudendus, cuius emendationem mirum est multos etiam grauissimos Theologos ferre non posse. Nam profecto quum mutua sit & reciproca Relatorum natura, sublata panis fractione, tollitur animae Christi a suo corpore per inenarrabiles cruciatus se-parationis, iconica quodam modo repraesentatio. Sic etiam commentitia illa, & à fi-gnorum idololatrica adoratione profecta, integrorum panum seperatim singulis accedentibus praebitorum distributio, illi omnium ex uno pane vescentium, cum uno & eodem Christo, & mutuae inter se fratrum coniun-ctioni ex diametro repugnat. Sic abrogata panis & vini in manus traditione, deleta est illa pulcherrima Christi, quasi sensibiliter, fe-fe suaque omnia, nobis velut in ipsas manus tradentis pictura. Sic denique abolita signorum per manus prehensione, mirifica illa fidei in Christo spiritualiter apprehendendo, vis & energia tollitur.
units.tr: There remains a third, and manifold, error, truly shameful, the correction of which it is astonishing that many even very grave theologians cannot bear. For since the nature of correlatives is mutual and reciprocal, when the breaking of bread is removed, there is removed, by the unspeakable torments of separation, a kind of iconic representation of the soul of Christ from his body. Likewise that invented distribution of whole breads, offered separately to each of those who approach, which arose from the idolatrous adoration of the signs, is diametrically opposed to the communion of all who eat from one bread with one and the same Christ, and to the mutual fellowship of the brethren among themselves. Thus, with the handing of the bread and wine into the hands abolished, that most beautiful picture of Christ, as it were sensibly presenting himself and all that is his to us as one handing them into our very hands, has been destroyed. Thus finally, with the taking of the signs by the hand abolished, the wonderful power and energy of spiritually apprehending Christ by faith is taken away.

units.la: His autem sic, nisi potius ipse videbor aliis falli, recte & vere confirmatis, rursum ex iis qui errores istos tuentur, quaero, quod Corinthiis[?] ex probrat Apostolus: nempe hoccine sic Coenam Dominicam edere, in qua neque signa,neque res signatæ, permaneant?
units.tr: Since these things have been confirmed rightly and truly, unless I myself perhaps seem to be deceived by others, I ask again of those who defend these errors, what the Apostle reproaches the Corinthians for: namely, whether they may celebrate the Lord's Supper in such a way that neither the signs nor the things signified remain.

units.la: CAPUT. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De signorum sacramentalium, & rerum per ea sacramentaliter significatarum mutua coniunctione.
units.tr: On the mutual conjunction of the sacramental signs and the things sacramentally signified by them.

units.la: MIRUM profecto videri meri-tò potest, de rerum Sacramen-taliter significatarum cum si-gnis coniunctione disceptari cum iis qui maximam Signo-rum partem, ritus videlicet Sacramentales manifestè partim aboleuerút, partim depra-varunt: immo etiam qui præcipua signa, pa-nem illum videlicet & vinum illud,in hac sacra actione, vel in nihilū redigi, vel in ipsum corpus & sanguinem domini transsubstan-tiari tantopere contendunt, ut nos ab ipsis hac in re dissentientes, tanquam omnium he-reticorum pessimos abominentur. Sed tamē, eò res sensim deuenit:animaduertente nimi-rum istud erroris spiritu, nisi in subsidiū ad-vocato & posito, externo & orali, quem vo-cant, ipsius corporis domini esu, & sanguinis potu, non potuisse initio persuaderi, & post-ea in hominum animis confirmari, realem il-lam, adhuc in terris, humanitatis Christi præsentiam[?] Hac autem concessa, obtinuit certè, impurus ille Spiritus quod volebat, nempe: veræ,tum incarnationis,tum ascensionis,tum è cœlis futuræ reversionis Christi destructionem, si non verbo & directè, ut volebat Marcionat certè reipsa ex necessario consequente: quum ἀμέσως[?] contradictoria, nec apud Deum nec in rerum natura simul vera esse possint: qua de re,te, lector, quisquis es, obsecro ut me placidè, & collatis non manibus, sed rationibus,disputantem benignè audias.
units.tr: It may well seem strange that we should dispute about the conjunction of the things sacramentally signified with the signs, with men who have openly abolished or corrupted most of the signs, that is, the sacramental rites. Even those who so earnestly insist that the chief sign, that bread and that wine in this sacred action, is either reduced to nothing or transubstantiated into the very body and blood of the Lord, abhor us as the worst of all heretics because we dissent from them on this point. Yet matters have gradually come to this. That spirit of error, seeing that the external and oral eating of the Lord's body and drinking of his blood, as they call it, could not at first be urged as a support, and afterwards be fixed in men's minds, perceived that this real presence of Christ's humanity on earth must be established. Once this was granted, that unclean spirit certainly obtained what it wanted, namely the destruction of the true incarnation, ascension, and future return of Christ from heaven. If not in words and directly, as Marcion wanted, it did so in fact, by a necessary consequence, since things [ἀμέσως] immediately contradictory cannot both be true, either before God or in the nature of things. Therefore, reader, whoever you are, I beg you to listen kindly to me as I dispute calmly, with reasons rather than with hands brought together.

units.la: Utrique igitur,id est,tum qui Transsubstan-tiationem tuentur, tum qui, illa deserta, ad Consubstantiationem refugerunt, vacuum, & inane quiddam fore totam hanc sacram actionem, sibi & aliis persuadent, nisi nunc quo-que ipsummet illud Christi corpus, & ille ipse sanguis, etsi alio quodam modo tamè tà vere & proprie, adsit adhuc in terris, quàm quū inter homines versaretur. Sed tum in hoc, tū in aliis quibusdam quæ suo loco attingemus, isti ab illis sic differunt, quòd Transsubstantia-tores quidem, illa in terris, non pani, & vino, inexistere (utpote quæ vel iam in nihilum e-vanuerint, vel in ipsum corpus & sanguinem illum sint essentialiter transmutata) sed sub accidentibus panis & vini, sine subiecto, (id est, quæ ne accidentia quidem sint) delitescere contendunt; Consubstantiatores verò, alij quidem, corpus & sanguinem Domini, non ubique, sed duntaxat in, sub, vel cum illo pane & vino ex quo demum tempore sacram Coenam instituit, alij vero ubique & à sua incarnatione, sua substantia ad fuisse & adesse, doceant: sed in sacra Cœna peculiari quodam fine adesse, nempe ut ibi demum nobis ore sumendum præbeatur: quarum trium sententiarum communia hæc sunt principia.
units.tr: Both parties, then, that is, those who defend transubstantiation and those who, abandoning it, have fled to consubstantiation, persuade themselves and others that this whole sacred action would be empty and void unless that very body of Christ and that very blood, though in some other manner, yet truly and properly, were still present on earth, as they were when he lived among men. But these parties differ from each other in this and in certain other matters which we shall touch on in their place. The transubstantiationists contend that the body and blood do not exist on earth in the bread and wine, since these have already vanished into nothing or have been essentially changed into that very body and blood, but lie hidden under the accidents of bread and wine, without a subject, that is, under what are not even accidents. The consubstantiationists, some teach that the body and blood of the Lord are present not everywhere but only in, under, or with that bread and wine, from the time he instituted the Holy Supper; others teach that he has been and is present everywhere, from his incarnation, in his own substance, but that he is present in the Holy Supper for a particular purpose, namely that there he may at last be offered to us to be eaten by the mouth. These are the common principles of these three opinions.

units.la: Aiunt igitur constare Sacramenti integritatem ex re terrena & re cœlesti. Agnosco & probo Irenæi verba, quò etiam respiciens Augustinus, plurimis locis, planius etiam locutus, duo in Sacramentis considerat, nempe, id quod videtur, & id quod intelligitur. Sed quod illi adiiciunt de suo, nempe, nisi & quæ videntur, & quæ intelligitur, simul in terris essentialiter, per inexistentiam, vel indistantiam sint connexè præsentia, suam Sacramentis integritatem non constare, illis magnis & orthodoxis patribus manifestè assingitur.
units.tr: They say, therefore, that the integrity of the sacrament consists of an earthly thing and a heavenly thing. I acknowledge and approve the words of Irenaeus, to which Augustine also, looking back at them in many places and speaking more plainly, considers two things in the sacraments, namely that which is seen and that which is understood. But what they add of their own, namely that the integrity of the sacraments does not consist unless both the things seen and the things understood are present together on earth, essentially, by inexistence or indistance, is clearly attributed to those great and orthodox Fathers, but falsely.

units.la: Nam quum distinctè rem terrenam à re cœ-lesti, & id quod videtur ab eo quod intelligitur discernant: quis merito existimare possit illos idem præsentiæ genus utrisque attribuere voluisse? Sicut enim profectò, quæ audiuntur, auditu: & quæ videntur, visu: ita quæ intelliguntur, intellectu, & quæ creduntur fide percipientur. Nec ista similiter suis obiectis sunt præsentia: sed essentia quidem sua, oculis: sonitu verborum, auribus: interiore rerum ipsarum natura, intellectui: quæ vero creduntur, fidei, res promissas ita ut promissæ sunt, in Dei verbo, tum simplici, tum Sacramentali, intuenti, sese repræsentant, quoniam necessario rerum praesentia, & apprehensio, ἀναλο- γως, inter se conuenirent.
units.tr: For since they distinctly separate the earthly thing from the heavenly thing, and that which is seen from that which is understood, who could reasonably think that they meant to attribute the same kind of presence to both? For just as things heard are perceived by hearing, and things seen by sight, so things understood are perceived by the understanding, and things believed by faith. Nor are these present to their objects in the same way. The essence of the visible things is present to the eyes, the sound of the words to the ears, the inner nature of the things themselves to the understanding. But the things that are believed present themselves to the eye of faith, as they are promised, in God's word, both plain and sacramental; for the presence and apprehension of things must necessarily correspond to each other [ἀναλόγως] in proportion.

units.la: Dico praeterea rem terrenam, siue ea quae videntur, male ad solum panem illum & solum vinum illud, restringi, quum ritus quoque Sacramentales ita notentur. Itidem dico rem coelestem, perperam de solo corpore & sanguine Domini ab iisdem intelligi, quum non minus, nec sane aliter quam corpus & sanguis Domini per panem illum & vinum illud, res quoque per ritus illos Sacramentales, quas suo loco declarauimus, menti significentur, & fide apprehendendae proponantur.
units.tr: I say further that the earthly thing, that is, the things that are seen, is wrongly restricted to that bread alone and that wine alone, since the sacramental rites are also designated in this way. Likewise I say that the heavenly thing is wrongly understood by the same men as the body and blood of the Lord alone, since the things also which we have explained in their place are signified to the mind through those sacramental rites, no less, and indeed in no other way, than the body and blood of the Lord are signified through that bread and that wine, and are set forth to be apprehended by faith.

units.la: tur. Cur autem, obsecro, corpus quidem illud & sanguinem illum Domini, essentialiter, & reali inexistentia, siue indistantia, oportuerit ad constituendam Sacramenti integritatem vel illi pani & illi vino (vt consubstantiationis dogma postulat) adesse : vel, (vt transubstantiatores volunt,) sub vanis illis speciebus, id est accidentibus sine subiecto, delitescere? Quoniā (fortassis inquiunt illi) corpus quidem & sanguis Domini sunt substantiae permanentes: psius vero παθήματα[?] nō ite:quae vero ritibus Sacramentalibus significantur, sunt potissima ex parte παθήματα[?], quae praeterierunt nec vnquam repetentur. Futilis autem est haec obiectio ad stabiliendam illorum sententiam. Nam ne corpus quidem illud, nec sanguis ille Domini in hac actione Sacramentali, simpliciter vt res substantiales, sed corpus quidem, vt pro nobis fractum & traditum, sanguis ille ut pro nobis effusus, consideranda: ac proinde non corpori sed menti & ut cœlestis & spiritualis alimonia, præbentur.
units.tr: But why, I ask, should that body and that blood of the Lord, essentially and by real inexistence or indistance, have to be present to constitute the integrity of the sacrament, either in that bread and that wine (as the doctrine of consubstantiation demands), or lie hidden under those empty appearances, that is, accidents without a subject (as the transubstantiationists want)? Because, perhaps they will say, the body and blood of the Lord are permanent substances, but the things signified by the sacramental rites are for the most part [παθήματα] sufferings, which have passed away and will never be repeated. But this objection is worthless for establishing their view. For in this sacramental action the body of the Lord and his blood are not to be considered simply as substantial things, but the body as broken and given for us, and the blood as poured out for us. Accordingly they are offered not to the body but to the mind, as heavenly and spiritual food.
