units.la: Itaque sicut nec panis ille, nec vinum illud, à ritibus Sacramentalibus separari, in vera cœna dominica, possunt: ita non alia est corporis & sanguinis Domini cum pane illo, & vino illo, quàm rerum per ritus illos Sacramentales significatarum, cum ipsis ritibus præsentia & præbitio intelligenda.
units.tr: Therefore, just as neither that bread nor that wine can be separated from the sacramental rites in the true Lord's Supper, so the presence and offering of the body and blood of the Lord with that bread and that wine must be understood as no other than the presence and offering, together with the rites themselves, of the things signified through those sacramental rites.

units.la: Quæro & illud, si talis inexistentia, & indistantia, ad Sacramentorum integritatem requiritur, quinam integra, ac non potius ludicra & inania fuerint, veteris fœderis Sacramenta: quæ tamen recte profecto Augustinus adversus Manichæos tuetur, signis quidem fuisse à nostris diversa, re verò nostris paria? Cedo verò qua re? certè ipsomet illo Christo ϑεανθρώπω, qui est utriusque illius fœderis subiectum, & velut ipsa materia & substantia: propterea vocante Apostolo Circuncisionem σημεῖον [?] τομῆς σφραγῖδα Iustitiæ fidei. Ergo & ipsiusmet Christi. Circumcisionem enim cordis, partim in remissione peccatorum, per nascituri Christi sanguinem: & in eiusdem Iustitiæ imputatione, per eius obedientiā: partim denique in spirituali regeneratione, per Christi Spiritum, in morte & resurrectione ipsius posita: ab ipso horuo mnium subiecto spiritualiter præbito diuellere, merum est profecto somnium.
units.tr: I ask this too: if such inexistence and indistance is required for the integrity of the sacraments, which of the sacraments of the Old Testament were whole and not rather playful and empty? Yet Augustine rightly defends them against the Manichaeans, holding that they differed from ours in sign but were equal to ours in the thing signified. On what grounds, I ask? Certainly on account of Christ himself, the God-man [θεάνθρωπω], who is the subject of both covenants, and as it were their very matter and substance. That is why the Apostle calls circumcision the sign of the cutting off [σημεῖον τομῆς] and the seal of the righteousness of faith [σφραγῖδα δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως]. Therefore it is also of Christ himself. For to separate the circumcision of the heart, which lies partly in the forgiveness of sins through the blood of the Christ who was to be born, and in the imputation of his righteousness through his obedience, and partly finally in spiritual regeneration through the Spirit of Christ, grounded in his death and resurrection, from that very subject of all these things, which is spiritually offered, is surely mere dreaming.

units.la: Verum est igitur Christum secundum carnem, neque in veteris Testamenti simplici verbo, nec in umbris illis (quarum tamen iam tum Christus corpus erat) nec in veteribus Sacramentis, ea quam hi requirunt inexisten-tia vel indistantia, praeberi patribus illis po-tuisse, corporeis organis sumendum: non mo-do ea qua hi monetur ratione, quia nimirum Christi humanitas in rerum natura nondum erat: verum etiam in primis, quoniam talis praebitio nihil ad Sacramentorum usum & finem, utpote spiritualem, facit, ideoque, ne nunc quidem requiritur. Sed inde colligi debuisse nego, Christum etiam secundum carnem, licet nondum creatam, menti & fidei patrum non fuisse verissimè & efficacissimè, tum in simplici verbo, tum in umbris illis, tum in Sacramentis repraesentatum. Hoc e-nim qui negat, Christi quoque personam, in fidei patrum mysterio, dividit: negat patres, eundem atque nos, (non certè signis, sed quòd ad generalem Sacramenti definitionem & conditionem attinet) cibum ac potum spiritualem habuisse: negat Petram illam spiritua-lem, (id est, non qualis erat sui natura, sed quatenus Sacramentum erat) fuisse Sacramentaliter Christum ipsum, & quidem totum ac θεάνθρωπον[?]. Hoc tamen Paulus expressis verbis affirmat, & nisi illud agnoscamus, consequetur Christum fuisse patribus sola Deitate Mediatorem, ac proinde aliam reipsa fuisse patrum fidem, & Ecclesiam, quàm nostram: Christum adhuc venturum, à Christo exhibito eo to eo modo differre quo dimidium à Toto: patrum fidem vera ὑποστάσει[?] caruisse: qui tamen si verè dicitur fuisse heri & hodie, atque adeo ab origine mundi occisus (apud Deum patrem videlicet, & in mentibus[?] fidelium spiri-tualiter, iam tum patribus, ut & nunc nobis) certè fuit quoque illis, necessaria conse-quutione, natus, passus, mortuus, sepultus, & à mortuis excitatus: quamuis, hæc suo demum tempore fuerint naturali, & sensibus ipsis perceptibili modo implenda: quæ propterea dicuntur patres eminus, fidei videlicet oculis, contemplati.
units.tr: It is true, then, that Christ according to the flesh could not be offered to the Fathers, in the plain word of the Old Testament, nor in those shadows (of which, however, Christ's body already then was), nor in the old sacraments, by that inexistence or indistance which these men require, so that it might be received by bodily organs. This is not only because, as they are warned, Christ's humanity did not yet exist in the nature of things; but chiefly because such an offering contributes nothing to the use and purpose of the sacraments, which are spiritual, and therefore is not required even now. But I deny that it should be inferred from this that Christ, even according to the flesh, though not yet created, was not most truly and most effectively represented to the mind and faith of the Fathers, in the plain word, in those shadows, and in the sacraments. For whoever denies this divides the person of Christ in the mystery of the Fathers' faith. He denies that the Fathers had the same spiritual food and drink as we do (not indeed in the signs, but as far as concerns the general definition and condition of a sacrament). He denies that the spiritual rock (that is, not as it was in its own nature, but as far as it was a sacrament) was sacramentally Christ himself, and indeed the whole God-man [θεάνθρωπον]. Yet Paul affirms this in express words, and unless we acknowledge it, it will follow that Christ was to the Fathers a Mediator by his Deity alone, and that therefore the faith and Church of the Fathers were in fact different from ours: that Christ was still to come, and differs from Christ already exhibited as a half differs from the whole; and that the faith of the Fathers lacked a true [ὑποστάσει] substance. Yet if it is rightly said that he was yesterday and today, and so slain from the foundation of the world (namely before God the Father, and spiritually in the minds of believers, both then for the Fathers and now for us), then he certainly was also born, suffered, died, was buried, and raised from the dead for them, by necessary consequence. Although these things were to be accomplished in their own time, in a natural way perceptible to the senses, the Fathers are therefore said to have contemplated them from afar, namely with the eyes of faith.

units.la: Sed & hodie, quamuis illa Christi huma-nitas reipsa extet, tamen ne nunc quidem, in terris, aliis, quàm eiusdem fidei oculis, à no-bis intelligitur & creditur: & illius πα̇θήμα-τῷ[?], ritibus nostris Sacramentalibus significata, utpote res præteritæ, & nunquam repeten-dæ, dici nequeunt aliter nunc nobis, quàm olim patribus, adesse. Nimis autem pudendum fuerit, menti à Spiritu sancto per fidem illustratæ, & tum, in simplici verbo divino, tum in Sacramentis, Christum, & omnia eius beneficia, ut spiritualiter sibi præsentissima intuenti, minus tribuere, quàm intellectus nostri naturalis facultati: utpote qui, nec falsò, nec inutiliter, res quoque nondum in rerum natura extantes, non minùs, imò etiam interdum certius, quàm sibi reipsa præsentes perspiciat ac diiudicet, ac etiam in suum usum applicet.
units.tr: But even today, although that human nature of Christ really exists, not even now on earth is it understood and believed by us except with the eyes of faith. His passion [πάθημα], signified by our sacramental rites, since it is a past event never to be repeated, cannot be said to be present to us now otherwise than it was to the fathers of old. Yet it would be very shameful to attribute less to a mind enlightened by the Holy Spirit through faith, which beholds Christ and all his benefits as most spiritually present to it, both in the simple divine word and in the Sacraments, than to the natural faculty of our understanding. That faculty, not falsely or uselessly, perceives and judges things not yet existing in nature no less, and sometimes even more certainly, than things actually present to it, and applies them to its own use.

units.la: Grauissimus igitur hac in re duplex error à nonnullis admittitur. Vnus, & is quidem Bla-sphæmia non carens, eorum qui mentis fide præditæ, & in Dei verbo, res quas ea fide amplectitur, intuentis, sanctos, & à Spiritu sancto insculptos conceptus, non alio loco habent, quàm naturales ratiocinantium, imò etiam quàm vanas deliratium imaginationes.
units.tr: Some therefore admit a most grave double error in this matter. The first, which is not free from blasphemy, belongs to those who, having a mind endowed with faith and beholding in God's word the things that faith embraces, regard the holy concepts engraved by the Holy Spirit as no better than the natural reasonings of men, indeed no better than the vain fancies of the deranged.

units.la: Alter, eorum qui veteris & noui Testamenti discrimen, in ipso utriusque subiecto constituunt, in Christo ipso videlicet, in quo tamen vnico promissiones omnes salutis nostræ semper fuerunt, sunt, & erunt, Etiam & Amen: quæ tamen duo Testamenta, quòd ad subiectum utrique commune attinet, non aliter, quàm, sicut in scholis loquuntur, secundum [?] plus & minus differunt: externa videlicet my-steriorum nostræ salutis manifestationis forma, & mensura.
units.tr: The second belongs to those who place the difference between the Old and New Testaments in the subject of each, namely in Christ himself, in whom alone all the promises of our salvation always were, are, and will be "Yea and Amen" (2 Cor. 1). Yet these two Testaments, so far as the subject common to both is concerned, differ only, as the schools put it, in more and less: namely in the external form and measure of the manifestation of the mysteries of our salvation.

units.la: Accedo nunc ad alterum, noui fœderis Sa-cramentum, nempe Baptismum: ad cuius in-tegritatem, quùm neque à Transubstantiato-ribus neque à Consubstantiatoribus essentialis illa cum aqua Bap-tismi, inexistentia, & indistantia requiratur, efficietur profectò (si fides illis habenda est) Baptismum à Cœna Domini, non modò si-gnis, & eorundem analogia cum rebus per il-la signa significatis, sed etiam re & substantia ipsa differre: quòd videlicet in Baptismo Christus ipse ἐνεργητικῶς[?] tantum, in sacra verò Cœna etiā οὐσιωδῶς[?] & ὑπαρξικῶς adsit. Quamobrem id vero? quoniam, inquient, Christus de aqua Baptismi, non dixit totidem verbis, hæc est sanguis meus. Atqui,sicut antea dixi-mus, beneficiorum Christi communionem ab ipsiusmet Christi, & eius perpessionum communione distrahere, nulla ratione, neque Physica neq; Theologica, fas est: & vitâ haurire nemo queat ex anima, nisi ea ipsa sit animat⁹[?]: nec eo cibo vel potu nutriri, quo nō utatur: nec aliter sese res habet in vita illa spirituali, ex Christo ipso, vt capite, in membra subiecta promanante. Et vt propius ad Baptri-smi analogiam accedam, sicut ablui corpus nequit, nisi ipsius aquæ applicatione: ita neque à peccatis ablui , nisi sanguinis ipsius Christi spirituali ῥανϑισμῷ[?] possumus, de quo loquitur Petrus. Et ne quis quod dicit A-postolus,nos per Baptismum Christo ipsi co-mori, & consepeliri peccato, & in vitam nouam, resurgere, interpretetur de solo ipsius mortis, sepulturæ & resurrectionis merito & fructu : meminerimus Apostolum præmittere,nos in ipsum Iesum Christum baptizari: immo ipsi implantari,&cū eo coalescere:deniq;,(quo nihil dici potuit expressius,)nos in unum corpus per unum spiritum Baptizari.
units.tr: I come now to the other sacrament of the New Covenant, namely Baptism. For its integrity, neither the Transubstantiators nor the Consubstantiators require that essential inexistence and indistance with the water of Baptism. Yet it will certainly follow, if they are to be believed, that Baptism differs from the Lord's Supper not only in its sign and in the analogy of the signs with the things they signify, but also in the thing and substance itself: namely that in Baptism Christ is present only energetically [ἐνεργητικῶς], whereas in the holy Supper he is present also essentially [οὐσιωδῶς] and by existence [ὑπαρξικῶς]. Why so? they will say: because Christ did not say of the water of Baptism, in so many words, "This is my blood." But surely, as I said before, it is never lawful, by any physical or theological reasoning, to separate the communion of Christ's benefits from the communion of Christ himself and of his sufferings. No one can draw life from a soul unless it is itself living, nor be nourished by food or drink he does not use; nor does it stand otherwise in that spiritual life which flows from Christ himself, as the head, into the members subject to him. And to come closer to the analogy of Baptism: just as the body cannot be washed except by the application of the water itself, so neither can we be cleansed from sins except by the spiritual sprinkling [ῥαντισμῷ] of Christ's own blood, of which Peter speaks. And lest anyone interpret what the Apostle says, that we are buried with Christ in death and rise to new life through Baptism, as referring only to the merit and fruit of his death, burial and resurrection, let us remember that the Apostle first says we are baptized into Jesus Christ himself: indeed, that we are implanted into him and grow together with him. Finally (nothing could be said more plainly) he says we are baptized into one body by one Spirit.

units.la: Nostra igitur illa, cum ipsomet Iesu Christo, spiritualis concorporatio, non est unius sacræ Cœnæ propria,sed utrique Sacramento communis: quanvis specialiter Christus in Baptismo, vt nos à peccatis abluens, & suo Spiritu, nova,in Christo spirituali creatione regeneransiin sacra vero Cœna, vt nos iam in Baptismo ablutos,& ipsi insitos ac regenerator sui ipsius alimonia spiritualiter pascens, Sacramentalibus peculiaribus signis repræsentetur.Nam quo iure istud Baptismo detraxerimus, quû Christus ipse, in simplici quoque verbo suo carne suam edi, & sanguinem suum bibi, apertissimè testetur: & quidem verbis non minus expressis, de fide ex verbi simplicis auditu differes, quàm quû sacrâ illâ Cœnam institueret,locutus? Quid igitur (inquiunt) amplius in sacra Domini Cœna accipimus? Respondeo ipsis Christi verbis fretus, vtrobique Christi carnem veram manducari, & verum sanguinem bibi, & quidem vno & eodem modo, spiritualiter nimirum per fidem, quam quisquis veram habet, Totum Christum, & Totû Christi est amplexus, vt qui nobis nonnisi totus sit saluificus.Sed vt caducam hanc vitam, primùm nascendo, deinde paulatim ab adolescentia ad virilem ætatem progrediendo,adhibitis cuique ætati cómodis cibis, vtiimus: ita nos diuini verbi quasi femine, ad vitam spiritualem, in Ecclesiæ vtero primùm ferì, cuius ortus peculiare sigillum est Baptismus: postea sensim,eiusdem verbi prædicati, & Christum nobis per fidem recipiendum prębentis,meditatione quotidiana, in ea vita foueri, & eius alimoniæ vi, adhibito huius nostræ cum Christo, in dies arctius & efficacius sese nobis adiungente, communionis Sacramento, adolescere scere[?], donec vltimo illo die, neque verbi neque Sacramentorum usu indigentes,toti in Christo, & cum Christo, reipsa nobis in cœ-lis præsente, sempiterna illa spirituali vita perfruamur. Viderint ergo illi quibuscum hic ago,quo tandem iure,aliam Christi in sacra Domini Cœna coniunctionem signorum cum rebus, per panem illum & vinum illud, & ritus eius actionis Sacramentales, significatis, quàm in Baptismo, vel in ipso quoque simplici verbo prædicato, requirant. Ita verò vt nos, tum de simplici verbo, tum de Baptismo sensisse & docuisse veteris Ecclesiæ doctores,negari satis recta conscientia non potest. Vt enim tam multa iampridem a nostris citata testimonia prætermittam., Hieronymus in tertium caput Eccles. Vescimur, inquit, carne eius & cruore potamur, non solum in mysterio, sed etiam in Scripturarum lectione. Et Augustinus (Beda illius verba in 1. ad Corinth.10.citante,) credentes, ait, per Baptismum fiunt corporis & sanguinis Christi participes, licet adhuc non peruenerint qui Baptizantur ad alterius Sacramenti perceptionem. Et certè perabsurdum est ipsis aliquorum etiam humanorum contractuum authenticis instrumentis,(qualis est multò magis veteris& noui fœderisScriptura,)minus aliquid tribuere quàm eorum cõtractuum sigillis, ad eorum confirmationem appensis, cuiusmodi sunt,Apostolo teste,Sacramenta.Quod si etiâ libeat hæc duo Sacramenta inter se conferre, tanto certè potior erit Baptismus, quanto maius quiddam est Nasci quàm Nutriri, siue quanto plus per generationem adipiscimur quàm Alimento.
units.tr: This spiritual union of ourselves with Christ himself is therefore not peculiar to the Lord's Supper but common to both sacraments. Christ is especially represented in Baptism as washing us from sins, and by his Spirit regenerating us in a new spiritual creation in Christ; in the holy Supper, as we are already washed and engrafted into him in Baptism, he is represented by its special sacramental signs, feeding us spiritually with the nourishment of himself, who is our regenerator. For by what right should we take this from Baptism, since Christ himself most clearly testifies, even in his simple word, that his flesh is to be eaten and his blood to be drunk? Does he not speak of faith arising from the hearing of the simple word in words no less express than when he instituted that holy Supper? "What, then," they say, "do we receive more in the holy Supper of the Lord?" I answer, relying on Christ's own words, that in both places the true flesh of Christ is eaten and his true blood drunk, and indeed in one and the same way, namely spiritually, through faith. Whoever has true faith embraces the whole Christ, and is embraced by the whole Christ, since to us he is wholly saving. But just as we sustain this fleeting life, first by being born and then gradually advancing from youth to manhood, taking foods suited to each age, so we are carried, as it were, by the divine word as by a mother, into spiritual life, first in the womb of the Church, whose birth is marked by the special seal of Baptism. Afterwards, little by little, by the daily meditation on that same preached word, which offers Christ to be received through faith, we are nurtured in that life. By the power of its nourishment, and with the sacrament of this communion with Christ joining itself to us ever more closely and effectively from day to day, we grow up, until on that last day, needing neither the use of the word nor of the sacraments, we wholly in Christ and with Christ, who is really present to us in heaven, enjoy that everlasting spiritual life. Let those with whom I am dealing here see, then, by what right they finally require, in the holy Supper of the Lord, another union of Christ with things through that bread and that wine and the sacramental rites of that action signified, than in Baptism or even in the simple preached word itself. That the teachers of the early Church thought and taught as we do, both about the simple word and about Baptism, cannot be denied with a sufficiently clear conscience. To pass over the many testimonies long since cited by our side: Jerome, on the third chapter of Ecclesiastes, says: We eat his flesh and drink his blood, not only in the mystery but also in the reading of the Scriptures. Augustine (as Bede, citing his words on 1 Corinthians 10, reports) says: believers, he says, through Baptism become partakers of the body and blood of Christ, although those who are baptized have not yet reached the reception of the other sacrament. And surely it is very absurd to attribute less to the authentic instruments of some human contracts (and this is far more true of the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments) than to the seals appended to those contracts for their confirmation, which, as the Apostle bears witness, are the sacraments. But if one likes to compare these two sacraments with each other, Baptism will certainly be the more excellent, by as much as being born is greater than being nourished, or as we obtain more by generation than by food.

units.la: Video tamen ipsius præsentiæ per inexi-stentiam & indistantiam essentialem & rea-lem,defensores (Vbiquitarios excipio)sese ad hæc Christi Cœnam instituentis verba,nem-pe Hoc est corpus meum, & Hoc est sanguis meus, recipere,de quorum recta & vera interpreta-tione ante quàm differam, videamus quæso, quàm aptas & certas Conclusiones illi ex his verbis eliciant.
units.tr: I see, however, that the defenders of his presence by inexistence and by essential and real indistance (I except the Ubiquitarians) take refuge in the words by which Christ instituted his Supper, namely "This is my body" and "This is my blood." Before I discuss their correct and true interpretation, let us see, I pray, how apt and certain are the conclusions they draw from these words.

units.la: Constat igitur, inter omnes rectè disputandi peritos,quoties de alicuius loci,qui varió sensu accipi potest, vera interpretatione controvertitur, non posse, ex eo ipso loco quem ad suum sensum quisque disputantium accommodet,tam certa peti argumenta,ut iis facilè tota controversia definiatur: sed tum oportere ut ex præcedentibus aut subsequentibus,vel ex aliorum locorum collatione:præcipue verò, in Theologicis, ex ipsa capitum Christianę Religionis analogia, eruatur vera eius loci de quo disceptatur, interpretatio.
units.tr: It is agreed among all who are skilled in disputing correctly that when the true interpretation of a passage capable of various senses is in controversy, arguments so certain cannot be drawn from that very passage, adapted by each disputant to his own sense, that the whole controversy is easily settled by them. Rather, the true interpretation of the passage in question must be drawn out from what precedes and follows it, from the comparison with other passages, and especially, in theological matters, from the analogy of the articles of the Christian religion itself.

units.la: At contrarium hic prorsus faciunt, & Transsubstantiatores, & Consubstantiato-res: ut qui illis Christi verbis, ad suam illam corporis & sanguinis Christi essentialem in terris præsentiam, sic abutantur, ut suam eo-rum verborum interpretationem quasi probatam assumant.Quid enim Transsubstantia-tores? Christum, inquiunt, illis verbis id quod prius erat panis, in illud ipsum corpus suum trans-substantiasse ex eo colligitur necessario, quoniam, ita ferente Disparatorum natura, panis ille esse essentialiter & vere panis, & verum illud ipsum Christi corpus nequiret. Itaque mutari illum reipsa oporteat in Christi corpus. Concedo antecedens,consequens nego esse necessarium: Nec enim mutatio Sacramentalis (quam ab-fit ut inficiemur) substantiam mutat, sed i-psum dutaxat eius rei usum, quae ex re commu-ni fit, per diuinā ordinationē, rei sacrae, nempe inuisibilis gratiae, signum Sacramentale.
units.tr: But the Transubstantiationists and the Consubstantiationists do exactly the opposite. They so abuse Christ's words, in support of their claim that his body and blood are essentially present on earth, that they take their own interpretation of those words as if it had been proved. For what do the Transubstantiationists say? Christ, they say, by those words changed into his own body what was previously bread. This follows necessarily, because, as the nature of opposites requires, that bread could not be essentially and truly bread and also the true body of Christ. Therefore it must really be changed into the body of Christ. I grant the antecedent but deny that the consequent is necessary. For sacramental change, which we are far from denying, does not change the substance but only the use of the thing. By divine ordination, what was a common thing becomes a sacramental sign of a sacred thing, namely invisible grace.

units.la: Addunt etiam,Enuntiata illa, Hoc est corpus meum, & hic est sanguis meus, eâdē ratione vera semper fuisse, & esse, qua vera fuerunt, quum à Christo sacra illam Coenam instituente, sunt pronuntiata: At Christus tunc erat essentialiter praesens, & hoc ipsum manibus tenebat, cui tribuit sui corporis & sanguinis appellationem. Ergo nunc quoque est praesens eâdem quâ prius ratione. Rur-sum antecedens concedo, consequens nego.
units.tr: They add also: The statements "This is my body" and "This is my blood" have always been true in the same way as they were true when they were pronounced by Christ instituting that sacred Supper. But Christ was then essentially present and was holding this very thing in his hands, to which he gave the name of his body and blood. Therefore he is now also present in the same way as before. Again I grant the antecedent and deny the consequent.

units.la: Fateantur enim oportet Transsubstantiato-res,Christum, quoquomodo ipsius verba accipiant, duplici ratione tunc praesentem suis-se:nempe Corporaliter quidem & Visibiliter apud mensam, & ante discipulorum suorum oculos,intelligibiliter vero & inuisibiliter in Sacramento. At illa prior praesentiae species desiit. Ergo ex illa peti non potest argumen-tum. Superest altera, nempe Sacramentalis, quam si isti essentialem & reale fuisse voluit, aut duo numero corpora tunc vni Christo tribuent, aut vnum idemque corpus, in eodem instanti, eadem essentiali & reali praesentia, tum corporaliter,& visibiliter apud Mensam, tum intelligibiliter & inuisibiliter, in iis quae manu sua praebebat, praesens fuerit. Horum autem duorum prius illud isti nunquam, vt opinor agnoscent: posteriusvero, non minus profecto falsum quàm illud, probet oportet, priusquàm illis assentiamur: aut nobiscum consentiant necesse est. Hinc enim verae Sacramentalis praesentiae ratio eruetur, eorum Transsubstantiationi & corporali praesentiae contraria, & ea ipsa quam profitemur: in eo videlicet posita, quòd in his mysteriis, verum illud essentiale Christi corpus, verè quidem adsit, at non hominum corporibus, vt quum in terris Coenâ instituisset, sed nunc in coelis, (inde quoque vltimo demum die reuersurum) spiritualiter,& nihilominus verissimè & efficacissimè mentibus fidelium repraesentatum, & ab iisdem, per fidem sese in coelos subuehentem, communicandum praebens.
units.tr: For the Transubstantiationists must admit that, however they understand his words, Christ was present in two ways at that time: corporeally and visibly at the table, before the eyes of his disciples, and intelligibly and invisibly in the sacrament. The first kind of presence has ceased, so no argument can be drawn from it. There remains the second, the sacramental presence. If they want this to be essential and real, they must either attribute two bodies to the one Christ, or else say that one and the same body, at the same instant, with the same essential and real presence, was present both corporeally and visibly at the table and intelligibly and invisibly in the things he handed out with his own hand. Of these two, they will never, as I think, admit the first. The second they must prove, though it is no less false than the first, before we assent to it; or else they must agree with us. For from this the true account of sacramental presence will be drawn. It is contrary to their transubstantiation and corporeal presence, and it is the very account we profess: that in these mysteries the true, essential body of Christ is truly present, but not in the bodies of men as it was when he instituted the Supper on earth. It is present now in heaven, whence he will return at the last day, spiritually represented to the minds of the faithful, and yet most truly and most effectively, and offered to be communicated by them, as they are lifted up to heaven by faith.

units.la: Sed age. Quid si (quod tamen absit) hanc substantiae panis in substantia corporis Christi transmutationem concederemus? minimè profecto inde consequeretur realis & essentialis illa veri corporis in terris praesentia, sed tum ipsius Sacramenti definitionis, tum veri corporis Christi destructio. Nam sublata panis substantia, tolletur quoque signum: ac proinproinde, huius Sacramenti fundamentum ruet,nisi hæc tria probarint. Unum,substantiam permanentibus suis accidentibus, interire posse: Alterum, accidentia dici posse quæ nulli subiecto insint. Tertio, Christi corpus illud verum & essentiale, & sub ratione coelestis alimoniæ in Cœna Domini spiritualiter repræsentatum, posse ἀναλόγως[?], per panis & vini accidentia, Sacramentaliter significari.
units.tr: But come now. Suppose (which God forbid) we granted this transmutation of the substance of bread into the substance of Christ's body. Nothing would follow from it except that real and essential presence of the true body on earth. What would follow is the destruction both of the definition of the sacrament itself and of the true body of Christ. For once the substance of the bread is removed, the sign is removed too; and so the foundation of this sacrament collapses unless they prove three things. First, that a substance can perish while its accidents remain. Second, that accidents can be spoken of as existing without any subject. Third, that the true and essential body of Christ, which in the Lord's Supper is spiritually represented under the aspect of heavenly food, can be signified sacramentally through the accidents of bread and wine, analogously [ἀναλόγως].

units.la: Deinde,sequetur etiam, veri illius corporis Christi,ex beatæ virginisMarię substantia, ante annos pęne mille sexcetos,Sacti Spiritus virtute desumpti,destructio, aut certè absentia ex hoc Sacramento: & eius loco alterum, inter Sacrificorum manus,recenter, ex panis & vini substantiis creatum, substituetur: nisi fortassis probarint isti,unum & idem corpus, tot ante seculis, verissimè creatum, & de quo quin expresse loquutus sit Christus negari nulla ratione potest: potuisse & posse toties rursum, & quidem ex diversissima materia verè creari, quot illic panes, & quot pocula consecrarunt, consecrant, &,nisi Deus obstiterit, consecrabunt.
units.tr: Further, it would also follow that the true body of Christ, taken from the substance of the blessed Virgin Mary nearly sixteen hundred years ago by the power of the Holy Spirit, is destroyed, or at least absent from this sacrament. In its place another body, recently created from the substances of bread and wine in the hands of the priests, would be substituted. The only escape would be if they could prove that one and the same body, created most truly so many centuries ago, and of which Christ certainly spoke expressly (which cannot be denied on any ground), could have been, and could be, created again and again from entirely different matter, as many times as they have consecrated, consecrate, and (unless God prevents it) will consecrate breads and cups there.

units.la: Qui vero Confubstantiationis dogma tue-tur,etsi panis & vini substantiæ mutationem recte condemnant, tamen itidem ut Trans-substantiatores,eandem præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi in terris, ex sua quadam interpretatione, nec probata nec concessa, sed ab ipsis præsumpta,sic colligunt. Christus dicens HOC est corpus meum, & HIC est sanguis meus,de vero & essentialisuo corpore & sanguine est loquutus. Concedo,& hoc ipsum ad-versus eos assumo.Nam si de vero & essentia-li corpore & sanguine hic agitur, ut sane agi-tur:non igitur de corpore cui veri & organiei[?] etiam post resurrectionem & ascensione cor-poris definitio essentialis non conueniat : id est,quod vel pluribus, vel omnibus simul lo-cis essentialiter adesse possit: siue de corpo-re non corpore,Christus est loquutus.
units.tr: Those who defend the doctrine of Consubstantiation, although they rightly condemn the change of the substance of bread and wine, nevertheless collect in the same way as the Transubstantiationists the presence of Christ's body and blood on earth, from an interpretation of their own that is neither proved nor conceded, but presumed by themselves. Christ, saying THIS is my body and THIS is my blood, spoke of his true and essential body and blood. I grant this, and I take it up against them. For if the words are indeed about his true and essential body and blood, as they certainly are, then he did not speak of a body to which an essential definition of a true and organic body, even after the resurrection and ascension, does not apply: that is, a body that can be essentially present in several places or in all places at once. Christ spoke either of a body that is not a body, or not of a body in that sense.

units.la: Significauit autem, aiunt, illis verbis Christus verum illud suum corpus, quum hanc Cœnam in-stitueret,in,sub, vel cum illo pane,& verum illum suum sanguinem, in,sub, vel cum illo poculo, qua tunc præsens in terris manibus suis tenebat& por-rigebat, adesse: nec aliter nunc quam olim verum est illud Christi enuntiatum. Ergo nunc etiam in terris essentialiter corpus illud,& illum sanguinem eredendum[?] est,in sub,vel cum illo pane & illo vino essentialiter adesse. De præsentia illa Christi Cœnam instituentis, paulò ante respondi. Concessi quoque, & concedo, qua ratione Christus verè loquutus est Cœnam illam suam instituens,ita quoque verum & firmum esse quod, ex ipsius mandato, nunc in hac a-ctione dicitur & geritur.Sed quod in hoc ar-gumento assumitur, tanquam probatum ex his ipsis Christi verbis, hoc illud est de quo controuertitur, & quod non debuit assumi, sed probari. Etsi enim corpus de quo hic agi-tur, est verum illud essentiale corpus, traditu pro nobis:& agnoscimus, hoc ipsum corpus esse alteram, & quidem longè potiorem: huius actionis Sacramentalis partem: immo etiam particulas illas non improbamus, modò rectè intelligantur, & quo sensu à patribus vsurpantur: non tamen propterea consequetur necessariò, rem significatam, in, sub vel cum signis, reali & actuali essentiæ suæ præsentia in terris adesse: quum hoc neque exprimatur Christi verbis, neque ex illis orthodoxè possit quidem elici, quòd Sacramé-torum[?],seu veterum, seu nouorum, nec integritas, nec vsus id efflagitet, sicut de veteribus Sacramentis & de Baptismo paulò ante demonstrauimus: nec corporis Christi, vera incarnatio, resurrectio, ascensio, & sperata è cœlis reuersio patiantur: atque adeò quòd nihil istud ad spiritualem carnis & sanguinis Domini communionem, & cœlestem inde exorientem vitam, faciat.
units.tr: "But," they say, "by those words Christ signified that his true body was present, in, under, or with that bread, and his true blood in, under, or with that cup, which he then held and offered in his hands while instituting this Supper on earth. Therefore that statement is true now as well as then. So now also, on earth, that body and blood are essentially present in, under, or with that bread and wine." I have already answered regarding the presence of Christ instituting the Supper. I have also granted, and still grant, that just as Christ spoke truly when instituting that Supper, so what is now said and done in this action by his command is true and firm. But what is assumed in this argument as proved from these very words of Christ is exactly what is in dispute, and it ought to have been proved, not assumed. For although the body spoken of here is the true essential body given for us, and we acknowledge that this same body is the other, and far more important, part of this sacramental action, and we do not disapprove of those particles, provided they are rightly understood and in the sense in which the Fathers used them, it does not follow necessarily that the thing signified is present on earth in the real and actual presence of its essence, in, under, or with the signs. This is not expressed in Christ's words, nor can it be rightly inferred from them. Neither the integrity nor the use of the sacraments, whether old or new, requires it, as we showed a little earlier concerning the old sacraments and Baptism. Nor do the true incarnation, resurrection and ascension of Christ's body, or its hoped-for return from heaven, permit it. And so this has nothing to do with the spiritual communion of the flesh and blood of the Lord, and the heavenly life arising from it.

units.la: Præterea certum est Christo non fuisse propositum istis verbis significare, ubi essentialiter suum illud corpus adesset, utpote ipsis discipulorum oculis apud mensam illam conspicuum: nec etiam an esset cum illo pane & vino essentialiter cohærens, utpote quæ ipse manu sua gestaret: sed certè voluisse cur & quorsum illis quæ gestabat & porrigebat, corporis & sanguinis sui appellationem tribueret, declarare: nempe quatenus excommuni usu Sacramentorum, (ac præsertim ex iis quæ discipulis suis, copiosè, expositerat, Iohannes 6.) ea quæ videntur corporis oculis.idipsum esse dicuntur, quod in illis intelligendum, & fide sumendum diuinitus praebetur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is certain that Christ did not intend, by those words, to signify where his body was essentially present, since it was visible to the disciples' eyes at that table. Nor did he intend to signify whether it was essentially joined to that bread and wine, which he himself was holding in his hand. But he certainly wished to declare why, and to what end, he gave the name of his body and blood to the things he held and offered. That is, insofar as, from the common use of the sacraments (and especially from what he had explained fully to his disciples, John 6), those things which seem to the eyes of the body are said to be that very thing which is divinely offered to be understood in them and received by faith.

units.la: Et hoc ita esse liquet, non tantum, ex ipsa generali Sacramentorum natura, sed maxime ex adiunctis illis, Quod pro vobis frangitur, &, Qui pro vobis effunditur, Quum enim ista inter se, inseparabili nexu cohaereat, certè, si ipsius corporis & sanguinis praesentia essentialis & actualis recte colligitur ex ipsis corporis traditi & sanguinis effusi nominibus, statuendum etiam necessario fuerit, in sub,vel cum, ritibus & actionibus Sacramentalibus, actuali-ter quoque tunc adfuisse, & adhuc adesse, illa Christi pro nobis πάθηματα[?], quae tamen tunc non extabant, & nunc praeterierunt, nec unquam repetentur. Itaque ista, ut & ipsum corpus, & ipse sanguis, non in terris, nec essentialiter, aut actualiter, sed intellectui & fidei spiritualiter, & equidem efficacissime re-praesentantur. Haec autem repraesentatio, quū a sola Dei rerum illarum communicationem promittentis voluntate, tum verbo, tum abditis vilibus signis testata pendeat: propterea Christus illam praesentis temporis participiis κλώμενον[?], & ἐνχωρούμενον[?], notavit, ut res illas intellectui fide praedito praebitas, doceret, discipulos quidem suos ut futuras, nos vero licet praeteritas, tamen ut praesentes fidei velut oculis intueri, & eiusdem velut manu in Sacramentis apprehendere.
units.tr: And that this is so is clear not only from the general nature of the sacraments, but especially from those additions, "which is broken for you" and "which is poured out for you." For since these are joined by an inseparable bond, if the essential and actual presence of the body and blood themselves is rightly inferred from the very names "body given" and "blood shed," then it must also necessarily be held that, in, under, or with the sacramental rites and actions, those passions of Christ for us [πάθηματα] were actually present at that time and are still present now, although they did not then exist, have passed away, and will never be repeated. Thus these things, like the body itself and the blood itself, are represented not on earth, nor essentially or actually, but spiritually to the understanding and to faith, and indeed most effectively. This representation, however, depends on the will of God alone, who promises the communication of those things, and it is attested both by the word and by hidden earthly signs. Therefore Christ marked it with the present participles [κλώμενον] and [ἐγχεόμενον], so as to teach that those things are offered to the understanding endowed with faith: his disciples were to see them as future, while we, although they are past, are to see them as present, as with the eyes of faith, and to grasp them in the sacraments as if by his hand.

units.la: Non possunt igitur profecto dici, qui hanc
units.tr: Therefore those who uphold this

units.la: verborum Christi interpretationem tuentur, τὸ ῥητὸν, in illorum enuntiatorum praedi-catis retinere, posita illa essentiali & actuali, in terris praesentia, nisi ab ipso Christo diuelant ipsius [illegible, ~9 letters], sine quibus tamen, caro illa non esset nobis aeternae vitae cibus, etiam millies reipsa, sive ore, sive Spiritu per fidem manducata.
units.tr: interpretation of Christ's words cannot indeed be said to keep the literal sense [τὸ ῥητὸν] in the predicates of those sentences, if they posit that essential and actual presence on earth, unless they tear away from Christ himself his (illegible), without which that flesh would not be food of eternal life for us, even though it were eaten a thousand times in reality, whether by the mouth or by the Spirit through faith.

units.la: Idem autem dico de ipso pronomine demonstrante, quod certè propria & sua natiua significatione acceptum, non potest accipi pro In, Sub vel cvm hoc, sed id demum significat, quod Christus manu acceptum, nempe panem illum, & vinum illud poculo comprehensum gerebat, & discipulis suis porrigebat. Hinc etiam Augustinus, Sacramentalem & spiritualem coniunctionem ab ista essentiali & actuali, cum signis recte discernens, addidit particulam QUODAM-MODO, quum diceret Christum corpus suum manibus gestasse: vt nimirum Sacramentalem significationem & praebitionem, minime vanam & inanem esse ostenderet. Christus igitur per Hoc pronomen, vel vnicam tantum substantiam, nempe, priore quidem praedicato panem: posteriore vero, vinum poculo comprehensum declararit, de quibus non dixit, in, sub, vel cum illis adesse suum corpus & sanguinem, sed illa esse suum corpus & sanguine. Quòd si malint illius interpretationis defensores Christum duas substantias, hoc vnico pronomine significasse, propter arctissimā & coessentialem, inter se cohærentiā: tunc fuerit hoc pronomen, non simpliciter κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν. sed κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν, & synecdoches tropo resoluendum, in Hic PANIS ET HOC CORPVS, HOC POCVLVM ET HIC SANGVIS. Quid autem fuerit absurdius, quàm illa duo dicere esse corpus suum & sanguinem suum, si τὸ ῥητὸν, vt illi volunt, simpliciter respiciamus: & execrabilis sit hæresis, tropum hic vllum constituere? Et hinc quidem, fa-teor,natum est istud, in,sub,vel cum, quod[?] sicut Sacramentaliter intelleƈtum non improbo, ita de essentiali & actuali præsentia per inexistentiam & indistantiam acceptum, minus profecto potest, illis Christi verbis κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν expositis, quàm Transsubstantiationis dogma, licet salsissimum, conuenire: vt cunctis nullum conceptæ opinionis præiudicium, sed solum cognoscendæ veritatis sincerum studium, ad hanc disceptationem afferentibus, sicuti spero, constabit.
units.tr: I say the same of the demonstrative pronoun itself. Taken in its proper and natural meaning, it cannot be understood as in, under, or "with this"; it signifies only that which Christ held in his hand, namely that bread and that wine contained in the cup, and was giving to his disciples. Hence also Augustine, rightly distinguishing the sacramental and spiritual union from that essential and actual one with the signs, added the particle "in a certain manner" when he said that Christ carried his body in his hands, so as to show that the sacramental signification and offering is by no means empty or vain. So Christ, by the pronoun This, declared only one substance, namely bread in the first predicate, and wine contained in the cup in the second; of these he did not say that his body and blood are present in, under, or with them, but that these are his body and blood. But if the defenders of that interpretation prefer to say that Christ signified two substances by this single pronoun, on account of their very close and co-essential cohesion, then the pronoun must be resolved by synecdoche, not simply according to the literal sense but according to the meaning, into "This bread is this body, this cup is this blood." But what could be more absurd than to say that those two things are his body and his blood, if we look simply at the literal words, as they wish? And is it not an execrable heresy to posit any trope here at all? I admit that the phrase "in, under, or with" has arisen from this. And although I do not disapprove of it understood sacramentally, yet taken as referring to an essential and actual presence by inexistence and indistance, it can agree with Christ's words expounded according to the literal sense even less than the dogma of transubstantiation, however very false that is. So that all who bring to this dispute no prejudice of an opinion formed beforehand, but only a sincere zeal to know the truth, will, as I hope, be established.

units.la: Restat in illis enuntiatis copula subiecto-rum, nempe in priore, panis & corporis cum prædicato corporis: & in posteriore, vini & sanguinis cum sanguinis prædicato copula, verbo, EST, expressa. Eam verò si natiua significatione, id est, ὑπαρξικῶς[?] accipiamus, vt & Transsubstantiatores & Confubstantiatores volūt, manifeste, quòd ad illos attinet, falsum fuerit illud enuntiatum: nisi panis in corpus Transsubstantiatus ponatur: quum nulla ratione prorsus, neque Physicè neque Theolo-gicè, disparatum de disparato verè dici possit ὑπαρχλικῶς [?], quòd nimirum vnaquæque species, ab altera per suam specificam differen-tiam differt: immò etiam, vnius & eiusdem speciei indiuidua, inter se proprietatibus suis indiuiduantibus ita discernantur, vt numero quoque multiplicentur. Confubstantiationi verò multò etiam minùs conueniet verbum EST, ὑπαρχλικῶς [?] intelligendum. Num enim, obsecro, duo ὑπαρχλικῶς [?] distincta manentia, quantumcunque suis essentiis cohærere existimentur, (vt panis ille & corpus illud: vinum illud, & sanguis ille.) vsque adeò vnum τὸδετι [?] esse, dici verè possint, vt vnum verè esse alterum ὑπαρχλικῶς [?] dicatur? Sumamus, pro huius rei exemplo, corpus & animam, ex quibus personaliter non tantùm coiunctis, sed etiam vnitis, constituitur HOMO. Num propterea a-nima verè dicetur esse corpus, aut corpus esse anima? Multò minùs igitur panis ille, idcircò ὑπαρχλικῶς [?] dicetur esse corpus Domini, etiàm essentia sua per indistantiam concedatur ade-sse, in, sub, vel cum illo pane. Nam alioqui vicissim, quum eadem sit panis cum corpore, atque corporis cum pane vnitio, corpus illud verè quoque esse ὑπαρχλικῶς [?] ille panis diceretur: quod tamen, opinor, Confubstantiatores non concesserint: licet istud ex posito antecedente illorum necessariò efficiatur. Immò si homo in illius hypostaticæ vnitionis exem-plo, quum sit tertium quiddam, ex hoc corpore & anima exsurgens, nec corporis nec animæ singulari appellatione definiri potest: multò minùs igitur pronomen hoc, etiamsi pro toto sacramento accipi concederetur, ὑπαρχικῶς dici debet Christi corpus. Denique ne in illa quidem peculiari, & omni exemplo carente humanæ naturæ vnitione per subsistentiam in filij Deitatis persona, cum Euthychete dicenda est Humanitas esse Deitas, vel contrà, aut concretis vocibus, Homo esse Deus sua Humanitate, aut Deitate sua Homo: sed alter de altero dicitur aduersus Nestorium per vnitatem personæ, & καὶ ἄλλο aduersus Eutychē. Abest autem vt Sacramentalem signorum & rerum significatarum coniunctionem (quam nonnulli hyperbolis quorundam patrum abutentes vnitionem malunt admodum improprié appellare) quantamcunque illam esse imaginentur, vel cum illa vel cum ista aurint comparare. Denique etsi recte Consubstantiatores sentiunt non de panis & vini accidentibus sine subiecto, sed de vere essentiali pane & vino, itidemq; de vere essentiali corpore & sanguine hic agi (quod tamen postea euertunt[?]) tamè illud, HOC EST, interpretantes per IN, SVB, vel, CVM HOC EST, nunquam euicerint verbum EST, à se ὑπαρχικῶς accipi in mutua istorum attributione, nisi simul ostenderint idem esse ALIQVID ESSE, & CVM SVB vel IN ALIQVO ESSE.
units.tr: There remains in those sentences the copula joining the subjects and predicates: in the first, of bread and body with the predicate "body," and in the second, of wine and blood with the predicate "blood," expressed by the verb "is." But if we take it in its natural sense, that is, substantially [ὑπαρξικῶς], as both the transubstantiators and the consubstantiators want, then, so far as they are concerned, that statement is plainly false, unless the bread is posited as transubstantiated into the body. For in no way, neither physically nor theologically, can a disparate thing be truly said of a disparate thing substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς], since each species differs from another by its specific difference; indeed, even individuals of one and the same species are so distinguished from one another by their individuating properties that they are multiplied also in number. Yet the verb "is" would fit even less, to be understood substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς], in consubstantiation. For, I ask you, can two distinct things remaining substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς], however much they are thought to cohere in their essences (such as that bread and that body, that wine and that blood), be truly said to be so one thing [τὸδετι] that one is truly the other substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς]? Let us take, as an example of this matter, body and soul, from which man is constituted, not only personally joined but also united. Will the soul therefore truly be said to be the body, or the body the soul? Much less, then, will that bread be called the body of the Lord substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς], even if its essence is granted to be present through indistance in, under, or with that bread. For otherwise, conversely, since the union of bread with body and of body with bread is the same, the body would also truly be said to be the bread substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς]; which, I think, the consubstantiators would not concede, although this follows necessarily from their own posited antecedent. Indeed, if man, in the example of that hypostatic union, since he is a third thing arising from this body and soul, cannot be defined by the singular name of body or of soul, then much less ought the pronoun this, even if it were granted to be taken for the whole sacrament, to be said substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς] to be the body of Christ. Finally, in that peculiar union of human nature, which lacks every example, by subsistence in the person of the Son of God, we must not say with Eutyches that the humanity is the deity, or the reverse, nor say in concrete terms that man is God by his humanity, or the deity is man; rather, one is predicated of the other, against Nestorius through the unity of the person, and "another" [καὶ ἄλλο] against Eutyches. Far from it, whatever they imagine that sacramental conjunction of signs and things signified to be (which some, abusing the hyperboles of certain Fathers, prefer to call a union, quite improperly), they cannot compare it either with that or with this. Finally, even if the consubstantiators rightly hold that what is meant here is not accidents of bread and wine without a subject but truly essential bread and wine, and likewise truly essential body and blood (which, however, they later overturn), yet, by interpreting "This is" as "in, under, or with this is," they will never prove that the verb "is" is taken substantially [ὑπαρχικῶς] in their mutual predication, unless they have at the same time shown that to be something is the same as to be with, or in or under, something.

units.la: Idem de altero enunciato HOC EST SANGVIS MEVS,siue,HIC (CALIX) EST SAN-GVIS MEVS, intelligendum est. Sic autem vertendum esse hunc locum apparet, tum ex Luca repetēte vocem [illegible, ~8 letters], tum ex reipsa: quoniam, si cum vulgato interprete Latino legatur apud Matthæum & Marcum, HIC EST SANGVIS MEVS, non repetita, vel subaudita Calicis voce, identica erit propositio, nec aliud demonstrabitur quàm sanguis: manifesto, & quidè maximi momenti errore, vt eius infœlicissimæ memoriæ hominis, & Germaniæ totius ἀλάζονος [?], Flaccij videlicet impudētia ostēdit, qui enūtiatū illud nō aliter intelligi cōtēdit, quàm illud Mosis de pecuino sanguine, Exo.14.8. ECCE SANGVIS MEVS.
units.tr: The same must be understood of the other statement, This is my blood, or "This (cup) is my blood." That this passage must be so translated appears both from Luke, who repeats the word [illegible], and from the matter itself. For if it is read, as in the Latin Vulgate translator in Matthew and Mark, "This is my blood," without the word "cup" being repeated or supplied, the proposition will be an identity, and nothing will be shown but blood. That is a manifest and a most serious error, as the impudence of that most unfortunate man, and of all Germany's boaster, Flacius, shows, who contends that the statement cannot be understood otherwise than as that saying of Moses about the blood of the covenant, Exod. 24.8: "Behold my blood."

units.la: Vere igitur, cum nulla cuiusquam iniuria, colligere mihi posse videor, tantùm abesse vt posita eiusmodi siue Transsubstantiatione siue Consubstantiatione, seruetur formulæ institutionis Cœnæ Domini τὸ ῥῆμα [?], in vtroque illo toto Christi enuntiato: vt è contrario, singulæ illorum voces, aliter quàm propria & natiua sua significatione sic accipiantur.
units.tr: Truly, then, since I seem entitled to conclude, without wronging anyone, that under either Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation the form of the institution of the Lord's Supper is so far from being preserved, in that whole statement of Christ, that on the contrary each of its individual words is taken otherwise than in its proper and natural meaning. [the word: τὸ ῥῆμα]

units.la: Sed alia sunt præterea quæ velim, & ab iis diligenter expendi, qui corporis & sanguinis voces sic vrgent, vt inde absque tropo vllo, totam hanc actionem æstimari velint. vnum, quùnam poculi nomen, pro vino, quod poculo continetur, accipi, & HOC POCVLVM, Esse NOVVM ILLVD TESTAMENTVM, dici absque metonymia: illud quidem, continentis pro contento: hoc autem, rei significataæ pro signo, possit.Luc.22.20.
units.tr: But there are other points as well, which I would wish to be carefully weighed by those who press the words body and blood so hard that they want the whole action judged from them without any trope at all. First, by what right is the name of the cup taken for the wine contained in the cup, and THIS CUP IS THE NEW COVENANT said without metonymy? The former would be container for contents; the latter, thing signified for sign. Luke 22.20.

units.la: Alterum, quum corpus & sanguis duobus in hac actione, non tantum distinctis, sed etiam inter se separatis signis, distribuantur (quæ separatio quoq; nobis analogicè cruentam illam Christi mortem fidei nostræ considerandam proponit) an τὸ ῥητὸν[?] dici possunt Transubstantiatores seruare, qui corporis nomine ipsum quoque sanguinem intelligentes, altera huius actionis parte Laicos, sic ab ipsis dictos priuarunt?
units.tr: Second, since the body and blood are distributed in this action by two signs that are not only distinct but also separated from each other (a separation which also analogically sets before our faith that bloody death of Christ to be considered), can the Transubstantiators be said to keep the saying? They understand the blood itself by the name of body, and they deprived the laity, as they call them, of the other part of this action.

units.la: Tertiò quæro, si quemadmodū illud ipsum corpus pro nobis traditum, sic quoque ille ipse sanguis pro nobis effusus, reipsa & actua-liter, atque adeo per indistantiam, in terris præsens & ore bibendus, sicuti verba sonant, adesse dicatur: unde constare possit illum fuisse à quoquam recollectum & asseruatum, ut inde nunc quoque depromatur: vel, si neque recollectus est neque asseruatus, sed eo factum est quod Deus voluit, unde nam sic realiter nunc adesse, & bibi possit. Fuisse vero à Christo reassumptum, & resurgenti corpori rursus inditù, quā nā vel leuissima suspicione existimabimus? Christum enim constat animalem illam priorem vitam in sanguine positā, minimè reassumpsisse, sed in spiritualem & coelestem illam, salua tamen ipsa corporea natura & substantia, transmutasse. Sed hæc sunt, inquient illi, curiosa: immò talia sunt, ut, quum illius inexistentia & indistantia essentialis stare, nisi positis illis nequeat, vel sint dissoluenda, vel pro salsissimis habenda, ex quibus tam absurda necessariò consequantur. Et de istis quidem hactenus, ex quibus plus satis intelligi potest, quàm sit facile, dormientibus agricolis, Zizania in agro Domini serere, quæ postea sit difficillimum, atque adeò hominibus ἀδυνάτων[?], euellere, sicut his temporibus, in hoc præsertim argumento, experimur.
units.tr: Third, I ask: if that very body given for us is present on earth, and to be drunk with the mouth as the words sound, in actual and real fact, and therefore by indistant presence, just as that blood poured out for us is also said to be present, then how can it be established that it was gathered up and kept by anyone, so that it can now be drawn out from there? Or, if it was neither gathered up nor kept, but this came about because God willed it, then how can it now be really present and drunk? But that it was taken up again by Christ and put back into his rising body, on what even the slightest suspicion shall we think so? For it is clear that Christ did not take up again that former animal life, which lay in the blood, but changed it into that spiritual and heavenly life, while keeping the bodily nature and substance itself intact. But these things, they will say, are curious. Indeed they are of such a kind that, since his inexistence and essential indistant presence cannot stand unless those things are posited, either they must be dissolved, or they must be regarded as utterly absurd, since such absurdities follow of necessity from them. And so far, on these matters, enough can be understood of how easy it is, while the farmers are asleep, to sow tares in the Lord's field, which afterwards is most difficult and, for men, almost impossible to pull up, as we are experiencing in these times, especially in this matter.

units.la: Optimo iure igitur damnatum fuit illud Transsub-stantiationis dogma, & pro illis accidetibus sine subiecto, repositus est substantialis panis: & pro illo corporis ex Transsub-stantiato pane creati spectro, substantiale cor-pus Christi, & substantialis ille vere sanguis restitutus. Et ut inam huic rei declarandæ sic ad-hibita esset Cosubstantiationis appellatio, ut & simul fuisset vera illa signorum & rerum significatarum coniunctio Sacramentalis explicata: illi reali in terris rerum Sacramen-taliter significatarum per indistantiam præ-sentiæ opposita: & ei respondens spiritualis illa, non nostris hic corporibus, sed mentibus per signorum analogiam proposita, tum præ-bitio, tum per fidem receptio, ad spiritualem illam nostri cum ipso Christo κοινωνίαν, in no-bis sanciendam diuinitus ordinata. Jam tum enim pro asperrimis istis cótentionibus quæ nullum pæne remedium nunc patiuntur, omnes Ecclesiæ ab Antichristi tyrannide asser-tæ, simul omnes in hac verissima veritate con-sensissent.
units.tr: Most rightly, therefore, that dogma of Transubstantiation was condemned, and in place of accidents without a subject, substantial bread was restored; and in place of that specter of a body created from the transubstantiated bread, the substantial body of Christ and his substantial blood were restored. And would that the name Consubstantiation had been used to declare this matter, so that the true sacramental conjunction of signs and things signified had been explained at the same time: opposed to that real presence on earth of the things sacramentally signified, through indistant presence, and corresponding to it that spiritual presence, set forth not in our bodies here but in minds through the analogy of signs, both the offering and the reception by faith, divinely ordained to be sealed in us for that spiritual communion [κοινωνία] with Christ himself. For already then, in view of those most bitter contentions which now admit almost no remedy, all the Churches asserted against the tyranny of Antichrist would have agreed together in this most true truth.

units.la: Sed aliter Opt.Max.Deo visum est, patefa-ctæ Euangelicæ suæ veritatis contemptum, & hominum gratuitam peccatorum remis-sionem a vera & seria resipiscentia separantium impuritatem iustissimè vlcisenti: donec tandem, ad vbiquitatem vsque progressa est, vtrinque disputatium fatalis intemperies.
units.tr: But it seemed otherwise to God, the Best and Greatest, who justly punishes the contempt of the Gospel truth which he revealed, and the impurity of those who separate men's free forgiveness of sins from true and earnest repentance. So at last the fatal intemperance of the dispute on both sides advanced even to ubiquity.

units.la: Quibus autem illa gradibus emerserit, etsi mihi nunc propositum non est explicare, ne tantorum malorum memoriam renouare videar, cuius potius ἀμνηστίαν[?] malim meo ipsius sanguine redimere: tamen reticere nequeo, mirum mihi non videri, quòd aliquot demum post paroxismum illum priorem annis Vbiquitas ista irruperit: sed mirari me potius cur non statim emerserit. Quod enim tandem mecum iudicaturos spero, quicunque sine praeiudicio, & sedatioribus animis, quid ex quo necessario consequatur secum expenderint: nec essentialis & realis illa per indistantiam praesentia, nec oralis tum signorum tum ipsius Christi eius & potus, siue Transsub-stantiatione siue Consubstantiatione posita, stare absque illa Vbiquitate poterit.
units.tr: By what steps it arose, although I do not now intend to explain it, lest I seem to renew the memory of such great evils, whose oblivion [ἀμνηστία] I would rather buy back with my own blood, nevertheless I cannot keep silent that it does not seem strange to me that this ubiquity broke in only some years after that first outburst; rather, I wonder why it did not emerge at once. For I hope that all who weigh with an unprejudiced mind and calmer spirits what follows of necessity from what will finally judge with me: neither that essential and real presence through indistance, nor the oral eating and drinking of the signs and of Christ himself, whether Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation is posited, can stand without that ubiquity.

units.la: Et hæc quidem vsque adeo non latuerunt scholasticos Doctores illorum temporum, minimè profectò obtusi ingenij plerosque, vt memores iampridem aduersus Eutychianos, Monothelitas, Monophysitas gestorum, hanc ipsam Vbiquitatem passim iugularint. Sed iidem, sic tum ferete Spiritus erroris effi-cacia, & illo tunc regnante Transsubstantiationis dogmate, nihilominus ad omnipotentiae Dei latibulū refugere, & ad eum tanquam scopulum facere naufragiū maluerunt, quàm ab eo semel errore discedere unde tam absurda nascebantur.
units.tr: Indeed these things did not escape the scholastic Doctors of those times, most of whom were by no means dull of wit, so that, mindful of what had been done long before against the Eutychians, Monothelites and Monophysites, they everywhere throttled this very ubiquity. But they, so strong was then the efficacy of the spirit of error, and with the dogma of Transubstantiation reigning at that time, nonetheless preferred to take refuge in the hiding place of God's omnipotence, and to make shipwreck on it as on a rock, rather than depart once for all from that error whence such absurdities were born.

units.la: D.autem Lutherus, cuius naevos deplorare longe profecto aliud est, quàm maximis eius laboribus & egregiis donis quicquam detra-here, Ubiquitatem sibi inter disputandum subinde occurrentem, usque adeo tanquam importunam, & alieno negotio sese immiscentem refugit: ut in Confessione illa sua maiore scribere, maluerit, ad hunc modum esse & posse esse Christum in pane, definitiua, quam vocant, praesentia, quomodo, inquit, Angeli & animae nostrae sunt in locis, & legio diabolorum erat in homine, de quo scriptum est Matthaei 8. perperam id quidem, sed ex quo tamen minimè colligi possit Ubiquitas, quum & Angeli & animae nostrae, etsi nulla loci circumscriptione, tamen ubicunque sunt, proprietate naturę suae terminentur. Sed quod idem ille itidem tradit, nempe, quod panis fit, idipsum vere & PROPRIE, corpori Christi, propter Sacramentalem coniunctionem tribui, & Nicolaum Papam laudat, profitentem, non solum Sacramentum (id est panem & vinum) sed etiam verum corpus & sanguinem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sensualiter, & in veritate, manibus Sacerdotum tractari & frangi, & fidelium DENTIBVS ATTERI, credat qui volet. Nam profecto ne in hypostatica quidem unione, vel Deitas de Humanitate, vel de Deitate Humanitas, vel unius naturæ proprietates de altera, abstractis, quas vocant, vocibus dici sine manifesta Eutychia-na impietate possunt. Immo ne in concretis quidem nominibus, vel Deus, & Dei propria de Homine, vel Homo & Hominis propria de Deo, aliter quàm κατ' ἄλλο, idque propter personæ unitatem, & per κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων orthodoxè adversus Nestorium dicuntur.
units.tr: Dr Luther, whose blemishes it is certainly a very different thing to deplore than to take anything away from his very great labours and outstanding gifts, shrank so much from ubiquity, which kept presenting itself to him in disputation as troublesome and meddling in another's business, that in his larger Confession he preferred to write that Christ is in the bread in this way, and can be, by what they call definitive presence, just as angels and our souls are in places, and as the legion of devils was in the man of whom it is written in Matthew 8. This is certainly wrongly said, yet from it ubiquity cannot be inferred, since both angels and our souls, although without any circumscription of place, nevertheless are wherever they are, bounded by the property of their nature. But what the same man likewise teaches, namely that what is of the bread is truly and PROPERLY attributed to the body of Christ, on account of the sacramental conjunction, and he praises Pope Nicholas for professing that not only the sacrament (that is, the bread and wine) but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are sensually and in truth handled and broken by the hands of priests, and ground by the TEETH of the faithful, let whoever wishes believe it. For certainly not even in the hypostatic union can the attributes of the Deity be said of the humanity, or the attributes of the humanity of the Deity, or the properties of one nature of the other, in what are called abstract terms, without manifest Eutychian impiety. Indeed not even in concrete names can God and the properties of God be said of man, or man and the properties of man of God, otherwise than according to the other [κατ' ἄλλο], and that on account of the unity of the person and through the communion of properties [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων], as is said orthodoxly against Nestorius.

units.la: Denique quod idem scribit, quoniâ Chri-stus eiusmodi homo est qui supernaturaliter cum Deo una persona sit, Christi etiam quatenus homo est plena-esse omnia, etsi ambi-guè dicitur, tamen si commoda interpreta-tione emolliatur (id est, si istud QUATENUS HOMO EST, non ad ipsam humanam naturam abstractè, sed ad hominem concretè, & κατ' ἄλλο consideratum, ut & ista repletio referatur) minimè favet Ubiquitati, sed orthodoxè scriptum fuit.
units.tr: Finally, what the same man writes, that since Christ is such a man as is supernaturally one person with God, Christ, in so far as he is man, is also everywhere full: although this is ambiguously said, nevertheless if it is softened by a fair interpretation (that is, if this INSOFAR AS HE IS MAN is referred not to the human nature abstractly but to the man concretely, and considered according to the other [κατ' ἄλλο], so that this filling is referred to it as well), it does not favour ubiquity in the least, but was written orthodoxly.

units.la: Huius autem discriminis, quo fit ut neque Deitati quicquid de Deo dicitur tribui, nec de Humanitate dici possit quicquid de Homine dicitur, hæc causa est, quòd abstractis Deitatis & Humanitatis vocibus naturæ no-tantur quales sunt & manent etiam unitæ: concretis autem Dei & hominis nominibus unitas personæ intelligitur, ut præclarè inter cæteros annotavit Damascenus. Itaque quàm vera sunt hæc & his similia enùtiata de Chri-sto adversus Nestorium, naturas & earum proprietates diuidentem, Deus est Homo. Maria est Deipara, propter vnitatem personae: & Deus gloriae est passus & crucifixus κατ' ἄλλο, siue per id quod homo, & per ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίαν: vt & illa, Homo est Deus, & Deus est filius Mariae, & Homo pendens in cruce erat in cœlis: tam sunt falsa aduersus Eutychē & alias haereses, naturas & earum proprietates con-fundentes, haec enuntiata, Deus est Humani-tas: Maria est mater Deitatis, Deitas est passa & crucifixa, vt & illa, Humanitas est Deus, Deitas est filia Mariae, & Humanitas pendens in cruce, erat in cœlis. Et hinc fit, vt in Trini-tate quidem, fit concretè Alius & Alius pro-pter tres personas, suis proprietatibus distin-ctas:non autem Aliud & Aliud, propter vnitatem & identitatem essentiae diuinae. Contrà verò in persona Christi est Aliud & Aliud propter duas diuersas naturas suis proprieta-tibus, incommunicabiliter aduersus Euty-chen, etiam in vnione distinctas: non autem Alius & Alius, propter personae vnitatem ad-uersus Nestorium.
units.tr: The cause of this distinction, by which it comes about that neither whatever is said of God is attributed to the Deity, nor whatever is said of man can be said of the Humanity, is that abstract terms of Deity and Humanity mark the natures, such as they are and remain even when united; whereas by the concrete names of God and man the unity of the person is understood, as Damascene has excellently noted among others. Therefore, just as true are these and similar statements about Christ against Nestorius, who divides the natures and their properties: God is man. Mary is the God-bearer, on account of the unity of the person; and the Lord of glory suffered and was crucified according to the other [κατ' ἄλλο], that is, through what he is as man, and through the communion of properties; and also these: Man is God, and God is the son of Mary, and the man hanging on the cross was in heaven; so false, against Eutyches and the other heresies that confuse the natures and their properties, are these statements: God is humanity; Mary is the mother of deity; the deity suffered and was crucified, and also these: Humanity is God; deity is the daughter of Mary; and humanity hanging on the cross was in heaven. And hence it comes about that in the Trinity, indeed, another and another is said concretely on account of the three persons, distinguished by their own properties; but not another thing and another thing, on account of the unity and identity of the divine essence. On the contrary, in the person of Christ there is another thing and another thing on account of the two diverse natures, distinguished by their own properties, incommunicably, even in the union, against Eutyches; but not another and another, on account of the unity of the person, against Nestorius.

units.la: Sane igitur tam sunt quoque haec vera ad-uersus Nestorium, de Christo, Homo est vbi-que, omni praesens, omniscius, omnipotens, atque a-deo immensus, aeternus, infinitus, nempe, κατ' ἄλλο, siue per id quod Deus est, vnitate personae non naturarum, aduersus Nestorium: quàm ista in Vbiquitariorum Scriptis passim occurrentia, salsissima sunt & Eutychiana: Chri-stus secundum humanam etiam naturam, siue, Humanitas etiam ipsa Christi est vbique: est per indistantiam vel inexistentiam, in, sub, vel, cum pane essentialiter: est Omniprasens, Omnipotens. & cætera eiusmodi.
units.tr: Therefore these things are indeed just as true against Nestorius concerning Christ: Man is everywhere, present in all places, all-knowing, almighty, and so immense, eternal, infinite, namely κατ' ἄλλο [according to another], that is, through that which God is, by the unity of the person and not of the natures, against Nestorius. How much more are those statements, which occur everywhere in the writings of the Ubiquitarians, most absurd and Eutychian: Christ according to the human nature also, or the humanity itself of Christ is everywhere: it is present by non-distance or inexistence, in, under, or with the bread essentially: it is omnipresent, omnipotent, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Etsi enim quædam excipere coguntur, ve-luti Æternitatem principio temporis carentem, Immensitatem, Infinitatem denique: ta-men postea tribuentes huic Humanitati ge-neraliter in sue Ubiquitatis definitione, essen-tiales omnes Deitatis proprietates, quæ sunt ipsiusmet essentia, ac proinde, prorsus in ipsa quoque hypostatica unitione, incommunica-biles: utinam tandem aliquando animaduer-tant intolerabilem illum errorem, quo tum abstracta non distinguunt à concretis, tum unitionem ipsam naturarum pro coniunctione quæ ex illa exoritur accipiunt: tum pro-prietates illas Dei essentiales & prorsus in-communicabiles,non discernunt à qualitati-bus & donis illis creatis,& in assumptam Hu-manitatem, (non statim tamen, sed peracto demum infirmitatis quoque suæ pro nobis assumptæ mysterio,) plenissime, & abundan-tissimè, per sessionem ad gloriam patris effu-sis: ideoque etsi non directè & totidem ver-bis,tamen consequutionis necessitate,Huma-nitatem in nouam alteram creatam & secun-dariam:idque(quod pene incredibile est)pe-tito ab ipsa usque hypostaticæ unitionis fun-damento,transformant,qua tamen prorsus o-mnis illa proprietatum essentialium unius in alteram effusio expresse tollitur.
units.tr: For although they are compelled to except some things, such as eternity without beginning in time, immensity, and finally infinity, yet afterwards, in the definition of their Ubiquity, they generally attribute to this humanity all the essential properties of the Deity, which are the very essence of God and therefore, by their very nature, incommunicable even in the hypostatic union itself. Would that they might at last notice that intolerable error by which they on the one hand do not distinguish abstract terms from concrete ones, and on the other hand take the union of the natures itself for the conjunction that arises from it; by which they do not distinguish those essential and wholly incommunicable properties of God from those created qualities and gifts, and pour them into the assumed humanity (not immediately, but only when the mystery of his weakness, also assumed for us, had been completed, through the sitting at the Father's glory), most fully and most abundantly. Therefore, even if they do not say it directly and in so many words, yet by the necessity of the consequence they transform the humanity into a new, second, created nature, and that (which is almost incredible) from the very foundation of the hypostatic union itself, although by this the whole outpouring of the essential properties of the one into the other is expressly removed.

units.la: Ut autem quæ sit illorum sententia, qui Vbiquitatem humanæ naturæ Christi tuetur plane intelligamus, agedum ista non certè D. Lutheri, ac multò minus D. Philippi, sed Bretiana verba, singulis pænè paginis funestæ ipsius quam vocat Recognitionis, amarulentissimè inculcata, velim ab omnibus veritatis inquirendæ, & pacis Ecclesiarum conciliandæ studiosis expendi.
units.tr: So that we may clearly understand what the opinion is of those who defend the Ubiquity of the human nature of Christ, I would like all who are eager to seek the truth and to reconcile the peace of the Churches to weigh these words, which are not indeed those of Dr. Luther, and much less of Dr. Philip, but of Brenz, repeatedly and most bitterly pressed in almost every page of his baneful so-called Recognition.

units.la: Ex pagina 40. Huius dicti, & VERBVM CARO FACTVM EST, non potest alia esse sententia quam qua hoc dictum uni & soli Iesu Christo sic competit, ut ita declaretur, quod sit inter Christum, & alios omnes homines discrimen. Recte, si de Christo ὅλως consid-erato, istud intelligis, aut etiam ut de homine, sed concretè istud accipiatur, & ut θεανθρώπῳ [?]. Et tunc in eo positum erit hoc discrimen, quòd hic solus homo fit verus ille Deus suâ in filio illo Dei subsistentiâ. Sin vero de humana ipsa natura abstractè istud accipiatur, (vti sanè ab Vbiquitariis accipitur,) quis non videat Nestorium in illis reuixisse? Sic enim ille pagina 41. In Christo inhabitat diuinitas, eáque tota, secundum essentiam, potentiam, & præsentiam, sed & sic tota inhabitat in Petro. & pag. 90. Christus illam Maiestatem quam habet ab æterno habet communem cum omnibus hominibus, imò cum omnibus creaturis: vbicunque enim est Deus, ibi totus est. En rursus Nestorium rediuiuum, hypostatica vnitione in [illegible, ~12 letters] & Deitatem in Diuinitatem (sic enim θεότης Latinè quoque nunc ad istā Vbiquitariam ὁ μονωνυμίαν [?]. vitandam Deitas à Diuinitate discerneda est, ipso Apostolo istud nos docente Coloss.2.9.) disertis verbis transmutata. Sic enim ille rursus, multò etiam apertius, pag.44. Filius Dei etsi Petrum sua essentia implet sicut & hominem Christum, nempe in Humana ipsius natura & abstracte, (quoniam alioqui, nullus esset isti comparationi locus) non tamen communicat Petro omnes suas proprietates, sed tantum nonnullas. Ergo, si hæc nobis credenda sunt, Deus erit Christus ut & Petrus, aut alius quivis verè sanctificatus, sed ille quidem ut omnes, isti ve-ro nonnullas Deitatis proprietates habetes in se effusas. Et quis ista propius considerata por-tenta ferat? nisi fortasse quid hic dicatur, non satis intelligo. Nam si per has proprietates intelligi volunt ipsam Dei essentiam (sicuti sanè intelligi debent, nisi qualitates Deitati quoque tribuantur) qui has totas humanæ Christi naturæ, aliis verò sanctis nonnullas tantum communicari volunt, annon essentiam Dei diuidunt? Sic enim idem ille argumentatur pag.75.&76. Si ob hanc causam est, inquit, Omniprasentia seu Vbiquitas incommunicabilis proprietas, quoniam sit essentia Dei: nihil certè quod est in Deo, erit communicabile. Atqui Deus omnia ad participatum suæ bonitatis, & in primis hominem ad participatum suæ sapientiæ, iustitiæ, & fœlicitatis condidit, & quidem speciatim ut qui credunt in Christum, fiant consortes divinæ naturæ iuxta suam quisque mensuram. Ipsum autem Christum voluit esse capace omnium suorum bonorum fine vlla mefura. Cedò vero quid istud rei est? non posse istum, aut nolle, inter essentialia Dei attributa & illorum effecta, id est, qualitates inde creatas, & qua libuit mensura definitas, & in hos vel illos, prout ipsi visum est, distributas, discrimen statuere? Et quis hic rursus, nisi discrimen hoc statuatur, non audit Eutychen renatum? quum praesertim qui nunc ista conantur emollire, hac omniprasentiam & Ubiquitatem velint sic effusam in assumptam humanitatem fuisse, ut tamen ei non insit subiectiuè, nec formaliter, nec habitualiter: quae necessariò contradictoria, viderint an unquam magis inter se possint quam lux cum tenebris conciliari.
