Deinde si nec subiectiuè, nec formaliter, nec habitualiter istae proprietates omnes in humanam Christi naturam effusae dicantur, in Petrum verò atque adeò in res omnes creatas, quaecunque effunduntur, insunt illis, quod negari nulla ratione potest, subiectiuè, sive formaliter, sive habitualiter: utrinque certè non different effusiones istae, secundum plus vel minus, quod tamen iste prius asseruit: sed in Christo quidem statuetur Nestoriana περιχώρησις[?], in aliis verò, realis & formalis, magis quam Eutychiana communicatio: & plus illae res quàm Christus ipse diuinitus acceperint: quum maius quiddam sit, nonnullas essentiales Dei proprietates, (si quidem id fieri posset) subiectiuè & formaliter, quàm externa quaedam sola adsistentia recepisse. Praeterea mirum est eos quibus ista omnium Deitatis proprietatum essentialium Eutychiana communicatio tantopere placet, saltem non animaduertisse Omni-praesentiam fuisse necessario excipiendam, tum quoniam ita non ornaretur, sed destrueretur humana natura vere & necessario creata, ac proinde finita: tum quoniam inseparabiliter mutuo sese consequentibus Infinitate & Omni-praesentia, sic plura statuerentur infinita, quod ne ipsi quidem (opinor) aussint imaginari.
units.tr: From page 40: No other meaning can be given to this saying, THE WORD BECAME FLESH, than that this saying belongs to Jesus Christ alone in such a way that it is declared that there is a difference between Christ and all other men. Rightly so, if you understand this of Christ taken wholly, or even as of a man, but taken concretely, and as of the God-man [θεανθρώπῳ]. Then this difference will consist in this, that this man alone becomes that true God by his subsistence in that Son of God. But if this is taken abstractly, of the human nature itself (as indeed the Ubiquitarians take it), who does not see that Nestorius has revived in them? For thus he says on page 41: In Christ the divinity dwells, and that whole, according to essence, power, and presence; but in this way it also dwells wholly in Peter. And on page 90: Christ has that majesty which he has from eternity in common with all men, indeed with all creatures; for wherever God is, there he is wholly. Behold again the revived Nestorius, with the Deity transformed by the hypostatic union into the Divinity, in express words (for θεότης [Deity] must now also in Latin be distinguished from Divinity, to avoid this Ubiquitarian ... [ὁ μονωνυμίαν], as the Apostle himself teaches us in Colossians 2:9). For thus he again says, far more openly, on page 44: The Son of God, although he fills Peter with his essence as he fills the man Christ, namely in his human nature and abstractly, (since otherwise there would be no place for this comparison) does not yet communicate to Peter all his properties, but only some. Therefore, if these things are to be believed by us, God will be Christ and Peter alike, or any other truly sanctified person, but Christ indeed will have all the properties of the Deity poured into him, while those others will have only some of them poured into them. And who could bear these monstrosities when they are considered more closely? Unless perhaps I do not understand what is being said here. For if by these properties they mean the very essence of God (as indeed they must be understood, unless qualities are also attributed to the Deity), why, when they want all of them communicated to the human nature of Christ but only some to other saints, do they not divide the essence of God? For the same author argues thus on pages 75 and 76: If, he says, omnipresence or ubiquity is an incommunicable property because it is the essence of God, then certainly nothing that is in God will be communicable. But God created all things for participation in his goodness, and above all man for participation in his wisdom, justice, and happiness, and indeed especially so that those who believe in Christ become partakers of the divine nature, each according to his own measure. But he willed that Christ himself be capable of all his good things without any measure. But tell me, what is this matter? Is it that he cannot, or will not, establish a distinction between the essential attributes of God and their effects, that is, the qualities created from them, and defined by such measure as he pleased, and distributed to these or those, as seemed good to him? And who here, unless this distinction is established, does not hear Eutyches reborn? Especially since those who now try to soften these things want this omnipresence and Ubiquity to have been so poured into the assumed humanity that yet it does not inhere in it subjectively, nor formally, nor habitually: which things are necessarily contradictory, and let them see whether light can ever be reconciled with darkness more than these can. Next, if it is said that all these properties were poured into the human nature of Christ neither subjectively, nor formally, nor habitually, but that they do inhere in Peter, and indeed in all created things into which they are poured, subjectively, either formally or habitually, which cannot be denied by any reasoning: then certainly these outpourings do not differ according to more or less, which yet the former author asserted. But in Christ a Nestorian [περιχώρησις] perichoresis will be established, while in others a real and formal communication will be established, more Eutychian than the Eutychian one; and those things will have received more than Christ himself received from the divinity, since it is a greater thing to have received some essential properties of God, if indeed this could happen, subjectively and formally, than to have received some external presence alone. Moreover, it is strange that those who are so greatly pleased by this Eutychian communication of all the essential properties of the Deity have at least not noticed that omnipresence had to be necessarily excepted; otherwise the human nature, truly and necessarily created and therefore finite, would not be adorned but destroyed; and further, since infinity and omnipresence necessarily follow one another inseparably, there would thus be posited several infinites, which (I suppose) they would not even dare to imagine.

units.la: Sed quorsum plura? Vt omnes tandé intelligant qualem nobis Christi Deitatem hæc Vbiquitas relinquat, ecce totidem illius Scriptoris verba ex pag.illiusRecognitionis 41.&c 42. Non est nec propter inhabitationem Dei, nec propter miracula, discrimen inter Christum & Petrum, quod ille sit Deus, hic autem nō sit Deus. Vterque enim est homo, & in utroque est Deus: & Petrus edidit quoque miracula potentia divina, eaque non longe absente, sed omnino praesente. Sed num Deitas fuit Petro hypostaticè vnita? Quantum autem sit inter istas inhabitationes in reipsa discrimen, oportuit saltem ex eo intelligere, quo homo à Dæmone obsessus, ab homine animato differt. Et nū [?] Petrus vel sibi insita, an verò extra ipsum ac prorsus externa vi vllum edidit miraculum? Si sua, vel etiam si diuinitus sibi communicata, ergo in sese Petrus quoque fuerit Deus. Petro verò vel alteri cuiquam vnquam datam fuisse, aut deinceps dandam edendorum verè sic appellatorum miraculorum potestatem, non tantum stultum, verùm etiam impium existimare. Nam in miraculis etiam à Christo, vero Deo editis, quanuis unum & idem sit ἀπο-τέλεσμα,[?] tamen ipsæ naturæ ut suis οὐσίαις, sic etiam ἐνεργείας & ἐνεργήμασι distinguedæ sunt necessario adversus Eutychen: Deitate videlicet, quæ Deitatis incommunicabiliter propria sunt, humana verò natura partim Deitati instrumentaliter subserviente, partim sua vi quæ humana sunt agente, citrà ullam personæ vel actionis ὅλως consideratæ divisionem vel confusionem: ut est adversus Nestorium & Eutychianos, & ex illa schola exortos Monotheletas, & Monophysitas, tot iam ante seculis, communi omnium orthodoxarum Ecclesiarum consensu, ex Dei verbo definitum.
units.tr: But why more? So that everyone may at last understand what kind of Deity of Christ this Ubiquity leaves us, behold so many words of that author from page 41 and 42 of the same Recognition: There is no difference between Christ and Peter, either because of the indwelling of God or because of miracles, that he is God and the other is not God. For both are men, and in both is God; and Peter also performed miracles by divine power, and these not from afar, but altogether present. But was the Deity hypostatically united to Peter? How great the difference between these indwellings is in reality ought at least to be understood from that by which a man possessed by a demon differs from an animated man. And did Peter perform any miracle by his own power, or rather by a force entirely external to himself? If by his own, or even if by a power communicated to him by God, then Peter too would be God in himself. But to suppose that the power of performing truly so called miracles was ever given to Peter or to anyone else, or will be given hereafter, is not only foolish but also impious. For in miracles even those performed by Christ, the true God, although the effect is one and the same, nevertheless the natures must necessarily be distinguished, as to their essences, so also as to their energies and operations: that is, the Deity performs those things which are wholly proper to the incommunicable Deity, while the human nature, partly serving the Deity as an instrument and partly acting by its own power, which is human, without any division or confusion of the person or of the action considered as a whole. This is against Nestorius and the Eutychians, and the Monothelites and Monophysites who arose from that school so many centuries ago, and it has been defined from the Word of God by the common consent of all orthodox Churches.

units.la: Denique ne videar hîc quicquam calumniatus, & ut nouerimus quo sensu Scriptor ille passim agnoscat Filium hominis fuisse à filio Dei in unam personam assumptum, (quæ phrasis rursum est manifestè Nestoriana) Christus, inquit, pag.90. est filius Dei, tum Maiestate Diuinitatis istius, quam habet à patre suo ab æterno, & QUAM HABET COMMUNEM CUM OMNIBUS HOMINIBUS IMMO CUM OMNIBUS CREATURIS, tum etiam illius quam filio Hominis in unam personam assumpto, in tempore plenitudinis communicauit, ut impleat non mille tantum aut duo millia locorum, sed cœlum & terram. Nam (inquit idem pag.166.) Assumi in Deum, non aliud est quam quam in cœlesti & diuina gloria collocari.
units.tr: Finally, lest I seem to be slandering him here, and so that we may know in what sense that writer repeatedly acknowledges that the Son of Man was assumed by the Son of God into one person (a phrase again manifestly Nestorian), he says on p. 90: Christ is the Son of God, both by the Majesty of that Divinity which he has from his Father from eternity, AND WHICH HE HAS IN COMMON WITH ALL MEN, INDEED WITH ALL CREATURES, and also by that which he communicated to the Son of Man assumed into one person, in the fullness of time, so that he might fill not merely a thousand or two thousand places, but heaven and earth. For (he says again, p. 166) to be assumed into God is nothing other than to be placed in the heavenly and divine glory.

units.la: Et hæc quidem ille totidem verbis, quæ si tam vera essent quàm nó sunt, Christus (quod absit) quantum ad illam veră & vnicam Deitatem attinet, (qua ne patri quidem & spiritui sancto orthodoxe dici potest συνούσιος[?], sed ὁμοούσιος[?]) non fuerit, (horresco referens,) aliter Deus quàm ἀπερίγραπτος[?] & ea quidem ipsi cum rebus creatis omnibus communi, quod ne-scio an ausus fit ipse Neftorius euomere: quā-tum verò ad dona in ipsius humanam natu-ram effusa, fuerit itidem hac adscititia & crea-ta Deitate à beatis omnibus sola gloriæ illius Vbiquitariæ summo gradu discernendus.
units.tr: These are his words, word for word. If they were as true as they are false, Christ (which God forbid) would not be, as far as that true and only Deity is concerned (which cannot be rightly called co-essential [συνούσιος] with the Father and the Holy Spirit in orthodox terms, but consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος]), God in any other way than uncircumscribed [ἀπερίγραπτος]. And that he would share this even with all created things, which I do not know whether Nestorius himself dared to vomit forth. As for the gifts poured into his human nature, he would likewise have to be distinguished, by this added and created Deity, from all the blessed, by that Ubiquitarian glory alone, at its highest degree.

units.la: Quid amplius? Si vera est Vbiquitas, ec-quod fidei Christianæ caput contradictio-nem non implicabit, ac proinde ridiculum euadet? Simul enim humana Christi natura fuerit in utero & extra uterum virginis, nata simul & non nata: simul fuerit in cruce patiés, & extra crucem vbique nihil patiens: simul resurrexit, & fuerit in sepulchro: Immò quî-nam sepulchro manente obturato, foras exie-rit vbi iam erat? & quorsum, ianuis clausis, in-trarit ad discipulos, si iam intus apud illos e-rat? & quînam abierit ad patrem, qui apud di-scipulos manserit? & quînam verè suprà cœ-los ascenderit corpus illud, quod quum vbiq; esset, locum certè mutare, nisi per præstigias, non potuit? & quînam è cœlis vltimo illo Die vere redituram illam carnem speramus in il-la carne sua conspicuam, si à nobis nó recessit? & quînam émigrare ad illum Paulus optarit, quem præsentem in terris habuit? Denique, quid nobis in Historia tota Euágelica saluum manebit. Et hæc omnia scilicet, positis simul, & in eodem instanti, tot ἀναγκαίως & ἀμέσως contradictoriis consistent.
units.tr: What more? If the ubiquity is true, will not the chief article of the Christian faith be entangled in contradiction, and so become ridiculous? For at the same time the human nature of Christ would be in the womb and outside the womb of the virgin, born and not born at once; at the same time he would be suffering on the cross, and outside the cross suffering nothing anywhere; at the same time he rose and was in the sepulchre. Indeed, how could he have come forth from the sepulchre, which remained sealed, to where he already was? And why, with the doors shut, did he enter to the disciples, if he was already inside among them? And how did he depart to the Father, if he remained with the disciples? And how did that body truly ascend above the heavens, when, since it was everywhere, it certainly could not change place except by trickery? And how, on the last day, do we hope that that flesh will truly return from heaven and be seen in its own flesh, if it has not departed from us? And how did Paul desire to depart to be with him, whom he had present on earth? Finally, what will remain safe for us in the whole Gospel history? And all these things, placed together and at the same instant, will stand as so many contradictions that are necessarily and immediately opposed.

units.la: Viderint autem qua nos incuria immeren-tes afficiant, qui nobis incredulitatem obii-ciunt: quasi quiduis affirmantibus credere te-neantur Christiani, ac nō potiùs ad Capitum Christianæ Religionis analogiam omnia exi-gere, vt verum teneant, dissentanea repu-dient.
units.tr: Let them see, however, with what carelessness they burden us, who object unbelief to us, as if Christians were bound to believe whatever is affirmed, and not rather to demand that all things be brought into agreement with the analogy of the chief points of the Christian religion, so that they hold what is true and reject what is discordant.

units.la: Viderint etiâ qua conscientia illud, quo-modo, Saraæ, Zachariæ, Capernaitarum, nobis imputent: quasi Christi dictorum sententiam aduersus hæreses, ad fidei analogiam, sobriè & reuerenter, & collatis Scripturarum locis examinare, idem sit atque de Omnipotentia Dei ambigere.
units.tr: Let them also see with what conscience they impute to us that thing about Sarah, Zechariah and the Capernaites: as if to examine the sense of Christ's words soberly and reverently against heresies, according to the analogy of faith, and by comparing passages of Scripture, were the same as to doubt the omnipotence of God.

units.la: Et de his quidem plus satis vt spero apud eos quidem qui nullis præiudiciis abripi sese patientur, quum præsertim legitimam, libe-ram, pacatam, sanctam de istis & aliis controuersiis omnibus συζήτησιν, non modo nunquam defugerimus, verum etiam semper perpetuum Ecclesiæ purae morem secuti, ex-petierimus.
units.tr: And of these matters, I hope, there has been more than enough, at least for those who will not allow themselves to be carried away by any prejudices. Especially since we have never shunned a lawful, free, peaceful and holy discussion of these and all other controversies, but have always, following the constant custom of the pure Church, sought it out.

units.la: Superest autem vt repudiatis illorum sententiis explicemus quid nobis de hoc argumento, id est, de Sacramentalium signorum cum rebus significatis coniunctione videatur: qua in re primum omnium fundamentum quoddam, vt minimè controuersum, & vt in Sacramentis essentiale, nobis concedi postulamus.
units.tr: It remains, then, that, having rejected their opinions, we explain what we think about this subject, that is, about the conjunction of the sacramental signs with the things signified. In this matter, first of all, we ask that a certain foundation be granted us, as not open to dispute and as essential to the sacraments.

units.la: Nempe quòd in his mysteriis neque panis, neque vinum simpliciter & proprie, quatenus sunt res substantiales: Immo ne simpliciter quidem & per se, quatenus illorum cibo & potu corpora nostra nutriuntur, sed relatè consideranda proponuntur: quatenus videlicet fides, non in ipsorum natura, sed in sacramentalis institutionis verbo illas intuens, illis vt signis mouetur: & ad panem illum vitæ, & vinum illud verè cor hominis lætificans, spiritualiter magis ac magis apprehendenda excitatur.
units.tr: Namely, that in these mysteries neither the bread nor the wine is set forth to be considered simply and properly, as substances; nor even simply and in itself, insofar as our bodies are nourished by their food and drink, but to be considered relatively. That is, faith, looking upon them not in their own nature but in the word of the sacramental institution, is moved by them as signs, and is stirred to lay hold on that bread of life and that wine which truly gladdens the heart of man, more and more spiritually.

units.la: Nam per signorum & rerum significatarum analogiam, ne res quidem ipsæ significatæ, (putà verum illud corpus, & verus ille sanguis Domini) quàuis res sint verè substantiales, simpliciter tamen, & per se, in hac sacra & spirituali actione, à fideli mente spectantur & concipiuntur, sed qualitatis suæ respectu: quatenus videlicet corpus illud traditum pro nobis, & sanguis ille fusus pro nobis fuit, præbentur nobis, vt spiritualis & perennis vitæ alimonia. Hoc enim ipsa prædicatorum in verbis Institutionis determinatio, expressis verbis sonat. Nam sicut verè non fuisset mortuum Christi corpus, nisi verum fuisset corpus: nec vera fuisset illa huius sanguinis ad mortem vsque effusio, nisi verus fuisset ille sanguis; sic nec illud corpus, nec ille sanguis sunt nobis aliter viuifica,quàm huius pro nobis mactationis & effusionis respectu. Idem autem de rebus per ritus ipsos sacramentales significatis multò magis statuimus, vtpote quae sui natura non subsistant.
units.tr: For by the analogy of the signs and the things signified, not even the things signified themselves (namely the true body and the true blood of the Lord), although they are truly substantial things, are nevertheless viewed and conceived by the faithful mind simply and in themselves in this holy and spiritual action, but with respect to their quality: insofar as that body which was given for us, and that blood which was poured out for us, are offered to us as the nourishment of spiritual and everlasting life. For the very determination of the preachers in the words of institution declares this in express terms. For just as Christ's body would not truly have died unless it was a true body, nor would that shedding of his blood unto death have been true unless that blood was true; so neither that body nor that blood is life-giving to us otherwise than in respect of this sacrifice and effusion for us. We hold the same, much more strongly, concerning the things signified by the sacramental rites themselves, since by their nature they do not subsist.

units.la: Sunt igitur & signa illa & res illae duae materiales significatae,si per se & in sese spectentur, verè Entia quae vocant: sed in[?] his mysteriis, non per se,verùm vt Entia rationis, non quidem ex sua natura, sed ex diuina ordinatione, quae natura est relatorum. Nec aliud spectauit Irenaeus,scribens hanc actionem(sic enim accipiendum est Eucharistiae nomen)ex re terrena & re coelesti constare,mutuis videlicet correlatiuis. Quinam igitur Coena Domini fuerit materiale quippiam ex pluribus substantiis, per substantialem inexistentiam vel indistantiam,συνημμένον[?]?
units.tr: Therefore those signs and those two material things signified are, if they are considered in themselves and by themselves, truly beings, as they call them; but in these mysteries they are not considered by themselves, but as beings of reason, not indeed from their own nature, but from the divine ordination, which is the nature of relatives. Irenaeus also looked to nothing else when he wrote that this action (for so the name Eucharist is to be understood) consists of an earthly thing and a heavenly thing, that is, of mutual correlatives. What then is the Lord's Supper, as some material thing made up of several substances, joined [συνημμένον] by substantial inexistence or indistance?

units.la: His autem demonstratis,per quae omnis illa Consubstantialis praesentia, Humanitatis Christi veritatem à consequenti necessario tollens,vel ἀμεταθετον[?] contradictionem implicans, & pro relatis substantias per se consideratas substituens,prorsus euertitur:facile iam fuerit intelligere qualis sit ista signorum & rerum significatarum coniunctio formalis: nempe merè σχετικόν[?], id est tota in eo posita, quòd, ex diuina ordinatione, verbo institutionis Coenae Domini declarata, res istae mutua & reciproca inter se relatione spirituali, spiritualiter itidem per fidem considerandae & obsignandae,simul praebeantur, signa nimirum ab iis qui legitimè Coenam administrant; res ipsè vero à Patre & Christo, cooperante Spiritu sancto, donatæ. Sed hanc σχέσιν[?] simul observandum est, non ex pacto humano, de rebus humanis, (qualia multa inter se homines adhibitis confirmationis causa signis & testeris pacisccuntur,) sed à mere divino fœdere & voluntate verbo Dei testata, oriri, & credentes ad spiritualem metam perducere.
units.tr: These things having been demonstrated, by which that whole consubstantial presence, by a necessary consequence, removes the truth of Christ's humanity, or involves an unchangeable contradiction [ἀμετάθετον], and substitutes substances considered in themselves for relatives, is utterly overthrown; it will now be easy to understand what sort of formal conjunction the signs have with the things signified: namely, purely relative [σχετικόν], that is, consisting wholly in this, that by divine ordination, declared by the word of the institution of the Lord's Supper, those things are offered together, in a mutual and reciprocal spiritual relation to one another, which are likewise to be considered and sealed spiritually through faith: the signs indeed by those who administer the Supper lawfully, the things themselves by the Father and Christ, the Holy Spirit cooperating, given. But this relation [σχέσιν] must be observed as arising not from a human agreement about human things (such as men often make with one another, using signs and witnesses to confirm the bargain), but from a purely divine covenant and will attested by the word of God, and leading believers to their spiritual goal.

units.la: Itaque Coenam Domini minimè exina-niunt qui, non corpus tropicum nescio quod Christo affingunt, (vt nonnulli calumniantur) sed verum illud corpus, & verum illum sanguinem Domini in Coenæ actione, licet nonnisi mystica σχέσει[?], tamen certissimè, &, nisi indignitas accedentium impediat, efficacissimè credentium mentibus Christum vbi nunc est, id est supra coelos quærentibus & amplectentibus adesse profitentur: vt ipsa omnium Sacramentorum definitio & natura dictat. Contrà verò grauissimè peccant, Coenam Domini meris chimæris infarcientes, qui Consubstantiationem per inhærentiam siue indistantiam, in sacramentali coniunctione imaginantur.
units.tr: Accordingly, those do not in the least empty the Lord's Supper who attribute to Christ I know not what tropical body (as some slander us), but profess that in the action of the Supper the true body and the true blood of the Lord, although only by a mystical relation [σχέσει], are yet most certainly and, unless the unworthiness of those who come hinders, most effectually present to the minds of believers, that is, of those who seek and embrace Christ where he now is, above the heavens. So the very definition and nature of all the sacraments dictates. On the contrary, those sin most gravely who stuff the Lord's Supper with mere chimeras, imagining a consubstantiation through inherence or indistance in the sacramental conjunction.

units.la: Negamus igitur res significatas, id est verum illud corpus, & verum illum sanguinem Christi, vllo alio quàm minimè vanæ illius Sacramentalis relationis modo adesse illi ipsi pani & vino: nedum vt substantialiter illis per inexistentiam aut indistatiam adhæreant, siue consubstantientur. Quod enim ait Dominus de Sabbato, verum est, & de sacramentis: nempe quòd sacramenta sint propter homines, non homines propter sacramenta. Hæc autem profecto; si transsubstantiarentur, id est, si vere mutarentur in illud substantiale ipsummet corpus, & ipsummet sanguinem Christi, tanto potiore essent quàm nos conditione, quató plus est ipsummet reipsa Christum esse, quàm mysticè illi adhærere. Itidem si per inexistentiam vel indistantiam illa consubstantiarentur: rursus potiores in eo essent quàm nos, quòd licet ipsius membra mystica fiamus, tamen ab ipso manemus reipsa separata ὑφισταμένα [?]: nisi forte quispiam eò usque insaniat, vt imaginari velit ipsummet illud verum corpus, & ipsum illum sanguinem Christi, substantia sua (abolitis etiam per concoctionem & assimilationem pane & vino) more substantiarum intra viscera nostra versari ac persistere: quod ne Transsubstantiatores quidem ipsi credunt.
units.tr: We deny, therefore, that the things signified, that is, the true body and the true blood of Christ, are present with that bread and wine in any way other than through that utterly empty sacramental relation. Much less do they cleave to the bread and wine substantially, by inexistence or indistance, or become consubstantiated with them. What the Lord said about the Sabbath is true, and true of the sacraments as well: sacraments exist for the sake of men, not men for the sake of sacraments. Yet if the bread and wine were transsubstantiated, that is, truly changed into that very substantial body and very blood of Christ, the believers would be in a far better condition than we are, since being Christ himself is much more than cleaving to him mystically. Likewise, if they were consubstantiated with the body and blood by inexistence or indistance, the believers would again be in a better position than we are. Although we become his mystical members, we remain in reality separate from him, subsisting [ὑφισταμένα]. Unless perhaps someone is so mad as to imagine that that true body and that very blood of Christ, in their own substance (the bread and wine having been abolished by digestion and assimilation), dwell and persist within our bowels in the manner of substances, which not even the Transsubstantiationists themselves believe.

units.la: Habent autem, fateor, Relata minimum Entitatis, vt in scholis loquuntur, sed maximæ tamen sunt efficaciæ, prout vera & solida sunt eorum subiecta & obiecta, in rebus etiā merè naturalibus: vt, pater & filius: Dominus & seruus. Sed hoc maximè verum est in rebus merè diuinis, vt sunt in Deitate Pater & Filius: quorum relatio, in essentia diuina, rationem & similitudinem quandam habet indiuiduantis proprietatis, vt loquitur Thomas.
units.tr: I grant that relations have, as the schoolmen say, the least of being, yet they are of the greatest efficacy, provided their subjects and objects are real and solid, even in things that are purely natural, such as father and son, lord and servant. But this is especially true in things that are purely divine, such as Father and Son in the Godhead, whose relation, in the divine essence, has something of the character and likeness of an individuating property, as Thomas puts it.

units.la: Sic etiam Sacramentalis hæc relatio subie[?]ctum & obiectum habet firmissimum & im-mutabile,nempe,ex Christi ordinatione,Hu-manitatem pro nobis in ara crucis oblatam.
units.tr: So too this sacramental relation has a firm and unchangeable subject and object, namely, by Christ's appointment, the humanity offered for us on the altar of the cross.

units.la: Deinde & illud est hoc loco summè obser-uandum, quòd quanto minus habet Entitatis relata, id est, quantò simpliciora sunt, tantò sunt significandis meré spiritualibus mysteriis accommodatiora: quod discrimen inter Sa-cramenta veterum & nostra Augustinus re-ctissimè annotauit. Præterea & illud maximè spectandum est, nempe Dominum non tan-tum dixisse.Hoc est corpus meum quod frangitur pro vobis, &c, Hoc est sanguis meus qui funditur pro vobis:sed addidisse:Accipite, comedite,bibi-te, nempe vt nouerimus,res illas signis illis i-ta nobis relatè significari, non duntaxat vt in illis signis, tum substatialibus, tum ritualibus quasi tabellis quibusdam depictæ, nobis in cogitationem veniant:sed vt simul spirituali-ter quidem & per fidei instrumetum, sed ve-rissima tamen & efficacissima communica-tione in nobis ad æternam nostram salutem obsignentur. His autem sic positis, seruata semper omnium nostræ Religionis capitum veritate, ex omnium etiam veterum sacra-mentorum natura, neque humanæ Christi naturæ dignitati,qua supra res omnes creatas verè tandem euecta est, & secundùm quàm Christus est seipso secundùm Deitatem suam nunc etiam minor, vt tota vetus orthodoxa Ecclesia loquuta est,quicquà detrahentes:sed τὰ ὑπερφυσικά[?], quibus hæc ipsius humanitas tantotā[?]topere exaltatur,ab antiphysicis quibus de-struerētur, distinguentes: illa institutionis Coenae Domini verba sic perspicuè explicamus. HOC (id est hic panis, quem Christus suis manibus fractum discipulis suis porrigebat) EST, (non certè sui essentia, sed Sacramentali, nō simpliciter significatiua, sed etiā, licet spiritualiter, tamen realiter sub fidei conditione exhibitiua) IPSVMMET ILLVD CORPVS MEVM. Nec aliter illud enuntiatū, Hoc est sanguis meus, i. HOC, vel, HIC (ΚΑΛΙΧ)[?] EST SANGVIS MEVS, interpretamur. Cur autem Dominus hac phrasi EST CORPVS MEVM, & EST SANGVIS MEVS, vti maluerit, quàm dicere, Hoc significat, corpus meum, & sanguinem meum, id est vti Metonymia omnibus Sacramentis vsitatissima, hęc causa est: quòd leuiculum illi merito visum est simplex significandi verbum: & expressius ita declarare voluit, signa illa non proponi, vt qualia sunt in se considerentur, sed accedentes oportere, fidelis mentis oculis, ea demum in illis quæ per illa menti repræsentantur, ac si panis ille, & vinum illud non illarum rerum signa, sed illę ipsæ res essent quas significant, intueri & spiritualiter apprehendere.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be carefully observed in this place that the less being a relation has, that is, the simpler it is, the better it is suited to signify purely spiritual mysteries. Augustine rightly noted this difference between the sacraments of the old covenant and ours. Moreover, we must especially note that the Lord did not merely say, This is my body which is broken for you, etc., This is my blood which is shed for you, but added, Take, eat, drink, so that we might know that those things are signified to us by those signs in such a relative way that they do not only come to mind through the signs, both the substantial and the ritual, as though painted on certain tablets, but are at the same time sealed in us spiritually, indeed through the instrument of faith, yet by a most true and most effective communication, for our eternal salvation. With these things thus laid down, and always preserving the truth of all the chief articles of our religion, and without detracting from the nature of all the ancient sacraments, or from the dignity of Christ's human nature, by which it has truly been raised above all created things, and according to which Christ, even now, in his Godhead, is himself lesser (as the whole ancient orthodox Church has taught), but distinguishing the supernatural [τὰ ὑπερφυσικά], by which this humanity is so greatly exalted, from the unnatural by which it would be destroyed, we explain the words of the institution of the Lord's Supper clearly as follows. THIS (that is, this bread, which Christ broke with his own hands and handed to his disciples) IS (not indeed of its essence, but sacramentally: not merely signifying, but also, though spiritually, yet really, exhibiting under the condition of faith) THAT VERY BODY OF MINE. Nor do we interpret the sentence, This is my blood, otherwise: THIS, or HERE, [ΚΑΛΙΧ] IS MY BLOOD. Why the Lord preferred to use this phrase, IS MY BODY and IS MY BLOOD, rather than say, This signifies my body and my blood, that is, as a metonymy most common in all sacraments, the reason is this: the simple verb of signifying seemed to him rightly too slight, and he wished to declare more expressly that those signs are not set forth to be considered as they are in themselves, but that those who come must, with the eyes of a faithful mind, look upon and spiritually grasp, in those signs, the things represented to the mind through them, as if that bread and that wine were not signs of those things but the very things they signify.

units.la: Hinc illa, ab vltima vsque vetustate, in Ecclesiis omnibus vsurpata formulâ, SVRSVM CORDA, respondente populo HABEMVS ad DOMINVM: ineptè id quidem & ridiculè, si deorsum adhuc, siue in accidentibus sine subiecto, siue in, sub, vel cum hoc pane essentia[?] sua praesens quaerendum esset nobis corpus illud & sanguis ille Domini: ac non potius nobis (sicut, inter caeteros tam ecstaticis hyperbolis nos admonet Chrysostomus) non amplius esset in illa actione in terris consistendum, sed e vestigio, sicuti monet Augustinus, ibi demum fidei manu magis ac magis tangeda, & apprehendeda esset illa ipsa caro pro nobis olim tradita, & sanguis ille pro nobis effusus. Idem autem de rebus similiter per Sacramentales ritus significatis intelligimus: in-ter quas alia certe nulla iure potest, quam inter panem illum, & vinum illud, cum corpore & sanguine coniunctio statui, in vno & eodem Coenae Domini mysterio.
units.tr: Hence the formula used in all the churches from the most ancient times, Lift up your hearts, with the people answering, We have them lifted up to the Lord. This would be foolish and ridiculous indeed, if we still had to seek that body and that blood of the Lord below, present in their substance, whether in accidents without a subject, or in, under, or with this bread. Rather, as Chrysostom reminds us, among many other ecstatic hyperboles, we need not remain on earth during that action, but, as Augustine advises, we must at once seek and grasp, by the hand of faith, that very flesh once given for us and that blood poured out for us. We understand the same about the things signified by the sacramental rites in a similar way. Among these, there is surely no other thing that can rightly be joined, in the one and same mystery of the Lord's Supper, with the body and blood, except that bread and that wine.

units.la: Rogatibus autem in quibus horum enuntiatorum particulis & metonymia ponatur, respondeo mystice totam hanc actione intel-ligendam esse: ac proinde, nullomodo variata sententia, metonymiam, & toti enuntiato, & tum subiectis tum praedicatis sigillatim tribui posse. Nam neque panis aut vinum hic censentur esse id quod sui natura sunt, sed ut signa eorum quibus per analogiam signifi-candis in hac actione adhibentur: & corpus & sanguis Domini, non res sensibus externis praesentes, sed ut intellectui soli per verbum & analogiam significatae, & per fidem appre-hendendae, proponuntur: nec alia ratione panis illi, & illi vino, attribuuntur. Verbum au-tem EST, non alio sensu intelligi potest illa inter se copulare, quam ut signa, & res signi-ficatas, ficatas,ac proinde in hac præcipuè & propriè particula hanc constituendam esse metonymiam res ipsa ostendit.
units.tr: As to the questions about where the particles and the metonymy are placed in these statements, I answer that this whole action must be understood mystically, and therefore, without any change in the meaning, the metonymy can be attributed both to the whole sentence and separately to the subjects and the predicates. For here the bread or the wine is not taken to be what it is by its own nature, but as signs of those things which, by analogy, are signified in this action. And the body and blood of the Lord are set forth not as things present to the external senses, but as things signified to the intellect alone through the word and by analogy, and to be grasped by faith. Nor are the bread and the wine ascribed to them on any other ground. The word IS cannot be understood to join these things together in any sense other than as signs and things signified. The thing itself shows that the metonymy must be located chiefly and properly in this particle.

units.la: Quid autem præterea ad huius Sacramenti integritatem συςατικλῶ[?], & ad fructum eius percipiendum merito requiratur: nec Consubstantiatores nec Ubiquitatis defensores facilè ostenderint: eo uno excepto, de quo fortasse posteritas inter Christianos ambigi potuisse mirabitur, nempe an ad hoc, ut quod significatur tam verè spiritualiter communicari fideli menti possit, quàm verè signa corporaliter percipiuntur, essentialis rerum significatarum per indistantiam præsentia requiratur.
units.tr: What else, moreover, is rightly required for the integrity of this sacrament [συστατικῷ], and for receiving its fruit, neither the Consubstantiationists nor the defenders of Ubiquity will easily show. With one exception, about which posterity may marvel that there could have been any dispute among Christians: namely, whether, for what is signified to be communicated to the faithful mind as truly spiritually as the signs are truly perceived bodily, the essential presence of the things signified through indistance is required.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De rerum Sacramentaliter significatarum perceptionis modo.
units.tr: On the manner in which the things sacramentally signified are perceived.

units.la: FIDES, inquit Apostolus, est ex verbi divini auditu, cui verbo si statim assentiri nos pateretur illud Carnis φρόνημα, mox quoque fieremus divinarum promissionum participes. Egemus ergo divini spiritus illius nobis aures ad audientium tribuentis dono ad ea percipienda, quæ ne cogitare quidem ex nobis possumus, prorsus necessario, & κυρίῳ αἰτίῳ. Rursus autem hic misertus noster Dominus, ut nihil possent homines suæ incredulitati prætexere, visibilia quoque & in ipsos oculos nostros incurrentia signa verbo illi suo adiunxit, in sacris illis mysteriis, quæ Latinè vocare Sacramenta consueuimus.
units.tr: Faith, says the Apostle, comes from hearing the divine word. If the mind of the flesh [φρόνημα] did not let us assent to that word at once, we would immediately also become partakers of the divine promises. We therefore need that divine Spirit, who gives ears to those who hear, as the gift by which we perceive things we could not even think of by ourselves; this is absolutely necessary, and he is the chief cause [κυρίῳ αἰτίῳ]. Then again, our merciful Lord, so that people could plead nothing in excuse for their unbelief, added to his word visible signs that fall under our very eyes, in those sacred mysteries which we customarily call sacraments in Latin.

units.la: Oportuisse vero semper ipsi diuino verbo reipsa & actu adesse res promissas, &, (siquidem substantiales res essent,) in ipsas audientium manus tradi: ac non potius debuisse intellectu percipi, & fide apprehendi, nescio an quisquam vnquam ante Antichristianæ huius cæcitatis tenebras existimauerit. Nam certè si tum requisita fuisset ista rerum promissarum præsentia, quum caro illa Christi θεανθρώπου, ante mille sexcentos annos, nondum in rerum natura extaret, cuius vnius sanguinis aspersione vera seruati sunt à condito mundo quicunque seruati sunt, actum fuisset de patrum omnium illorum salute. Adfuit igitur jam tum, ut apud Deum, cui præsentia sunt omnia, sic & in credentium intelligentia, Christus ille θεάνθρωπος: cuius diem propterea, licet tot demum postea seculis in rerum natura extituri, vidisse scribitur Abrahamus: adeo quidem efficaciter, ut vere fuerit quoque illius imputata iustitia, iustificatus. Sic cæteri patres credentes, licet eminus, & in legalibus illis umbris, illum quasi delitescentem oculis fidei conspicati, verissimè tamen & efficacissimè agnouerunt, & vera fide sunt facti corporis eius & sanguinis κοινωνοί[?] : in quo uno ratę semper fuerunt omnes æternæ vitę promissiones: vanę tamen & inanes habendæ, si essentialis illa ipsius cum verbo prædicato, & veteribus Sacramentis præsen-tia,tum fuisset necessaria.
units.tr: I do not know whether anyone, before the darkness of this Antichristian blindness, ever thought that the promised things ought always to have been present in fact and in act alongside the divine word itself, and, if they were substantial things, delivered into the hands of the hearers, rather than being grasped by the understanding and apprehended by faith. For certainly, if that presence of the promised things had been required at that time, when that flesh of Christ, the God-man, did not yet exist in nature, by whose blood alone sprinkled all who have been saved since the foundation of the world were saved, the salvation of all those fathers would have been undone. Therefore Christ, the God-man, was already present then, as he is to God, to whom all things are present, and so also in the understanding of believers. Abraham is written to have seen his day, although it was to come into existence in nature so many centuries later; so effectively, indeed, that his righteousness was truly imputed to him and he was justified. In the same way the other believing fathers, although from afar and in those legal shadows, saw him as though hidden from the eyes of faith, yet recognized him most truly and most effectively, and by true faith became partakers of his body and blood. In him alone all the promises of eternal life were always certain; yet they would have to be counted vain and empty if that essential presence of him, joined to the preached word and to the old sacraments, had then been necessary.

units.la: At enim,inquiunt contra quos hic agimus, alia nostra nunc conditio est, extante nunc illa Christi humanitate, & actu peracta no-strorum peccatorum expiatione. Id ego vero fateor, at non quo isti volunt sensu. Tam e-nim Christus secundum carnem, & quod ad essentialem illam præsentiam attinet, à terris ac proinde à verbo auribus nostris sonante, & à Sacramentorum nostrorum signis nunc abest, quàm patrum illorum veterum temporibus. Nam verè discipulis illis suis,non com-mentitia illa inuisibilitate & disparitione, sed vera loci mutatione dixit illud, ME NON SEMPER VOBISCVM HABEBITIS: præ-fatus etiam hac sui corporis in terris præsen-tia, fidem suorum nō modò non promotum, verùm è contrario ad terrenas cogitationes sic deuolutum iri: & si modo credimus illum verè postea supra cœlos omnes penetrasse, nec minùs verè testatum inde sese ante vlti-mum illum diem non esse in terras reuersu-rum.
units.tr: "But," they say, against whom we argue here, "our condition is now different, since that humanity of Christ now exists and the expiation of our sins has been accomplished in act." I admit this, but not in the sense they intend. For Christ, according to the flesh and as far as that essential presence is concerned, is now absent from the earth, and therefore from the word sounding in our ears and from the signs of our sacraments, just as he was in the times of those old fathers. For he truly said to his disciples, not with that fictitious invisibility and vanishing but with a real change of place: YOU WILL NOT ALWAYS HAVE ME WITH YOU. He also foretold that by this bodily presence on earth the faith of his people would not only not be advanced, but would on the contrary sink into earthly thoughts. And if we believe that he afterwards truly penetrated all the heavens, we likewise believe that he truly testified he would not return to earth before that last day.

units.la: Quid amplius? ne hic quidem horrenda il-la spiritus erroris, inter ipsos, præsertim Ec-clesiæ Christianæ ψευδοπροφητευομένας[?], substitit: sed, iusto sic ferente Dei iudicio, quo factum olim fuit vt à nullis minùs agnitus, & nullis magis exosus, fuerit vnicus ille noster Seruatore quàm Sacerdotum principibus: persuasit miseris Christi ouiculis, non illam modò salsissimam præsentiam, quæ tandem ad Vbiquitatem vsque progressa fuit, sed illud etiam ipsum quod ne superstitiosissimis quidem Ægyptiis allia & cepe adoratibus persuasum fuisse Cicero annotauit: nempe id ipsum esse Deum, quo vescerentur. Annon enim hæc ipsa est eorum qui Transubstantiatione tuentur fides ? Alter autem ille num minus crassus est error, qui nunc horrendas istas turbas excitat, Germanicas præsertim Ecclesias & Academias floretissimas deuastás?Hoc enim factū est vt qui illum ipsum, magnū alioqui virum, vsque in hæc deuia à spiritu contentionis abreptum sunt secuti, à quo cognominari gaudent, credi velint illud ipsum Christi corpus pro nobis traditum, & illum ipsum sanguinem pro nobis effusum, ore ipso, inuisibiliter quidem, sed tam verè tamen, & tam proprie actualiter ac reipsa, quàm panem, illum & vinum illud, non tantùm edi & bibi, verùm etiã manducantium quoruuis DENTIBVS SENSVALITER ATTERI ? optante etiam illo vt tam verè Christiani fuerint omnes Romani Pontifices quàm fuit impurissimus, ille Nicolaus, qui hanc palinodiam, Berengario misero præscripsit.
units.tr: What more? Not even here did that horrible spirit of error stop, especially among the false prophets of the Christian Church. By God's just judgment, which once ordained that this unique Saviour of ours should be recognized by no one less, and hated by no one more, than by the chief priests, he has persuaded Christ's poor little sheep not only of that most salty presence which at last advanced even to ubiquity, but also of that very thing which Cicero noted the most superstitious Egyptians, who worship garlic and onions, were persuaded of: namely, that the very thing they eat is God. Is not this the belief of those who defend transubstantiation? And is that other error, which now stirs up those horrible tumults and devastates especially the German churches and the most flourishing academies, any less gross? For it has come about that those who followed that very man, otherwise a great man, carried away into these devious paths by a spirit of contention, and from whom they delight to take their name, want it believed that the very body of Christ delivered for us, and the very blood shed for us, are eaten with the mouth itself, invisibly indeed, but as truly, as properly, and as actually and in fact as that bread and that wine. Not only are they eaten and drunk, but they are even ground by the teeth of whoever communicates, in a sensible way. They also wish that all the Roman pontiffs were as truly Christian as that most impure Nicholas, who prescribed this palinode to the unhappy Berengar.

units.la: Hic verò mihi fas fit, licet feruorũ Dei ἐλά- χίσῳ[?], vos omnes huius tā portentosi dogmatis, tantis,tantis cum offendiculis defensores, petita reuerenter venia,per verum illum,& vnicum verè Θεάνθρωπον Mediatorem obtestari, vt, pacatis tandem animis, nobiscum, qui & ipsi à Papismo vobiscum asserti,nihil aliud quàm integram Euangelicæ veritatis instaurationem dies & noctes optamus, dignemini quid hoc rei sit propius expendere.Quod enim,metuitis ne dissoluatur Christi persona, nisi vbicūque est Christus,secundum Deitatem (est autem hæc Deitas vbique) ibi etiam essentialiter adsit eiusdem caro,frustrà metuitis. Nam si vbique tota est, non per partes, nec vt in loco Deitas, à qua personaliter hæc natura nostra assumpta est,non autem in vnam naturam conflata:quînam fieri possit,vt Deitas vspiam ab illa humana natura dici possit sepa-rata,quanuis ipsa suo tantùm loco, sicuti fert inuiolabilis ipsius veritas,contineatur?
units.tr: Here, although I am a lowly one among the servants of God, I may, with due respect, beg your pardon and entreat you all, defenders of this so portentous a dogma with such great stumbling blocks, by that true and unique God-man Mediator: that, with your minds at last calmed, you would deign to weigh more closely what this matter really is. We, who have been asserted by you as coming from Papism too, wish day and night for nothing other than the full restoration of Evangelical truth. As for your fear that the person of Christ will be dissolved unless, wherever Christ is according to the Deity (and this Deity is everywhere), his flesh is also essentially present there, you fear in vain. For if the Deity is wholly everywhere, not in parts, and not as the Deity is in a place, from which this nature of ours was personally assumed, yet not fused into one nature with it, how could it happen that the Deity could be said to be separated from that human nature anywhere, even though the human nature is contained only in its own place, as the inviolable truth itself declares?

units.la: Omnipotentiam autem illam Dei,iis vt v- trinque veris asserendis, quæ contradictionem necessariam implicant, prætexere, quid aliud fuerit quàm, (quod absit,) Deum, eò quòd sit Omnipotens,mentiri posse affirmare? Nec sanè ignoratis quoties istud fuerit ab orthodoxis patribus,aduersus varias hæreses responsum.
units.tr: But to invoke that omnipotence of God in order to assert things which are both true, while implying a necessary contradiction, what else would that be than affirming, God forbid, that God, because he is omnipotent, can lie? Nor are you unaware how often the orthodox fathers answered this against various heresies.

units.la: Nec minùs certè vanum est,quod existima tis euacuari Christi Cœnam, vel solùm ipsius Christi obedientiæ meritum, pro veri illius corporis & sanguinis communione separatim substitui, nisi vobiscum essen-tiam illam præsentiam & oralem istam manducationem agnoscamus, quæ tamen res ipsa clamat, cum carnis Christi, & secundùm sub-stantiam, & secundum omnes eius carnis essentiales, etiam post glorificationem, proprietates, quibus sublatis corpus verè organicum esse desineret, non magis posse quàm veritatem cum falsitate consistere. Nam è contrario quum negari iusta ratione nequeat, panem illum & vinum illud, non quidem quatenus panis & Vinum sunt, sed ut signa: ac proinde corpus ipsum & sanguinem Christi, non simpliciter & quatenus in sese res sunt subsisten-tes, sed Sacramentaliter, id est, non fictè sed verè, intellectualiter tamen consideranda, in his mysteriis proponi: nec sit sensuum vel ipsius corporis, sed unius intellectus opus, res-ullas, vel ut significantes, vel ut significatas considerare, nedum fide amplecti: quis non videt, neque præsentiam illam essentialem si-gnorum cum rebus significatis, neque oralem hanc manducationem signis & rebus signifi-catis communem, Sacramentorum naturæ & scopo, de quo postea differemus, convenire? neque veram nostri cum ipsa carne & ipso sanguine Christi, [?]κοινωνίαν imminui vel tolli, quum menti, non corpori: fidei, non sensibus, res illas significatas, mente, quoque & sola fide sumendas præberi dicimus, quàuis revera tam procul abesse essentialiter à signis & à nobis, quàm cœlum à terra? At è contrario vestra illa præsentia & manducatio tum Physicè tum Theologicè contradictionem implicat, ipsa quoque Marcionitica δοκήσει [?]tãto[?] intolerabi-liorem, quanto crassior est error, ex duobus contradictoriis(cuiusmodi sunt QVANTVM ET NON QVANTVM, VISIBILE ET IN-VISIBILE, LOCALITER ET ILLOCA-LITER simul & in eodem instanti, corpori Christi, id est, corpori simul & non corpori, attributa) alterum licet falsum ponere, quàm duo illa, ἀμέσως, & omni necessitate contra-dictoria, simul vera esse velle.
units.tr: It is certainly no less vain to think that the Lord's Supper is emptied, or that the merit of Christ's obedience alone is substituted separately for communion with his true body and blood, unless we acknowledge with you that essential presence and that oral eating. The thing itself cries out that the flesh of Christ, both in substance and in all its essential properties (even after glorification, which if removed would make the body cease to be truly organic), cannot be any more possible than that truth should coexist with falsehood. For on the contrary, since it cannot rightly be denied that that bread and that wine are set forth in these mysteries not indeed as bread and wine are, but as signs, and therefore that the body itself and blood of Christ are to be considered not simply and as things subsisting in themselves, but sacramentally, that is, not fictitiously but truly, yet intellectually; and since to consider things, either as signifying or as signified, and still more to embrace them by faith, is the work not of the senses nor of the body itself but of the one intellect: who does not see that neither that essential presence of the signs with the things signified, nor this oral eating common to signs and things signified, agrees with the nature and purpose of the sacraments, of which we will speak later? Nor is our true communion with the very flesh and very blood of Christ diminished or removed, since we say that those signified things are offered to the mind and not the body, to be received by the mind and by faith alone, even though in reality they are as far from the signs and from us essentially as heaven is from earth. But on the contrary, your presence and eating both physically and theologically imply a contradiction, a Marcionite illusion too, all the more intolerable as the error is grosser. For you ascribe to the body of Christ, that is, to a body that is simultaneously and not a body, two contradictory pairs of attributes (of which kinds are QUANTUM AND NOT QUANTUM, VISIBLE AND INVISIBLE, LOCALLY AND ILLOCALLY), simultaneously and in the same instant. It is one thing to posit one of the two as false; it is another to want those two, which are immediately and by every necessity contradictory, to be true at once.

units.la: Neque verò firma est hæc conclusio. Iubet Christus hoc ipsum accipi, comedi, bibi quod dixit esse corpus illud suum & verum illum suum sanguinem: Ergo iussit etiam tam panè illum & suum corpus, ore comedi, quàm vinum illud & suum sanguinem ore bibi. Præ-supponitur enim in illo antecedente, quod naturam Sacramentorum non pati paulò an-tè diximus: nempe tum panem & vinum, tum corpus & sanguinem Domini, similiter, ut res sunt natura sui subsistentes, in his mysteriis proponi, & uni eidemque obiecto, nempe accedentium ori, modo corporali sumenda præberi. Hoc autem falsum esse ex eo constat, quòd in Sacramentis, aliud sit quod videtur, ideoque ori sumendum præbetur: quàm id quod, ut illo significatum, sola mente intelligitur: ac proinde menti soli præbitum, ab illa sola per fidem apprehenditur. Qua igitur ratione voces corporis & sanguinis pani illi & illi vino metonymicè tribuuntur, (nempe non quòd re ipsa & essentia sui panis ille, & vinum illud sint ipsum corpus & ipse sanguis Domini(quod ne Cossubstantiatio[?] quidé ipsa patitur)sed vt nouerimus in hac actio" ne non minus vere menti praeberi res significatas, quàm signa ori praebentur: ita quoque verba ACCIPITE,COMEDITE,BIBITE, interpretanda sunt: actionibus videlicet illis quæ proprie sunt corporeę,ad mentis & fidei spiritualem operationem, per metonymiam sacramentis conuenientissimam translatis.
units.tr: Nor is this conclusion firm. Christ commands that what he said was his body and his true blood be taken, eaten and drunk. Therefore he also commanded that the bread, which is his body, be eaten with the mouth, just as the wine, which is his blood, be drunk with the mouth. The argument assumes what we said a little earlier the nature of the sacraments does not allow: that both the bread and wine and the body and blood of the Lord are set forth in these mysteries in the same way, as things subsisting in their own nature, and are offered to one and the same object, namely the mouths of those who approach, to be taken in a bodily manner. But that this is false is clear from the fact that in the sacraments the thing that is seen is one thing, and so is offered to the mouth to be taken, while the thing signified by it is another, understood by the mind alone, and therefore offered to the mind alone and grasped by it alone through faith. So the words "body" and "blood" are attributed metonymically to that bread and that wine. This does not mean that the bread and wine are in reality and in their substance the very body and blood of the Lord, which not even consubstantiation allows. It means that we may know that in this action the things signified are offered to the mind no less truly than the signs are offered to the mouth. In the same way the words TAKE, EAT, DRINK must be interpreted: namely as those actions which are properly bodily, transferred by metonymy, most suitably to the sacraments, to the spiritual operation of mind and faith.

units.la: Præterquàm quòd autem istis loquutioni-bus à corpore ad animum translatis nihil est, in sacris etiam literis, & in quotidiano sermone usitatius, rectè obseruat Chrysostomus discipulos propterea ad hunc Christi sermonem idcirco non exhorruisse, quòd hæc spiritualiter esse intelligenda ex eiusdem ore, Capernaitarum crassitiem reprehendentis, intellexissent: nunquam alioqui sanguinem contra tam expressum legis interdictum, ne cibo quidem permixtum sumpturi. Et, quæ-so, veteres illos Christianos, quibus immanis illa & Cyclopica,siue visibilis,siue inuisibilis, σαρκοφαγία obiiciebatur, quis absoluisset, si realem illam præsentiam & oralem manducationem approbassent?
units.tr: Moreover, such expressions transferred from the body to the soul are found not only in Holy Scripture but are more common in everyday speech as well. Chrysostom rightly observes that the disciples did not shrink from this saying of Christ for the reason that they had understood from his own mouth, when he rebuked the crassness of the Capernaites, that these things were to be understood spiritually. Otherwise they would never have been about to drink blood, not even mixed with food, against the law's so explicit prohibition. And I ask: who would have absolved those early Christians, against whom that monstrous and Cyclopean eating of flesh, whether visible or invisible, was objected, if they had approved of that real presence and oral manducation?

units.la: Non sunt igitur aliter quàm hæc ipsa Chri-sti verba accipiendæ orthodoxorum patrum hyperbolæ, veluti quum Corpus Domini in os nostrum intrare, & Lingua sanguine Christi in-cruentari, & ipsummet Christum in hac actione videri & tangi scribunt: nihil minùs profecto quàm de portentis illis cogitantes:nec qualis sit, merè nimirum intellectualis, & spiritualis istius rerum significatarum praebitionis & perceptionis modus, sed quàm certum sit & efficax istius communicationis effectum istis expressissimis phrasibus metonymicis indicantes. Hoc autem ita esse sufficiat nunc pauculis testibus omni paenè exceptione maioribus ostendere. Sic igitur Augustinus in Epist.Iohan.Tractatu,1.Nos, inquit, Christum in coelis sedentem manu contrectare non possumus (num autem ore ipso manducare?) sed Christum fide contingere possumus.Et Tractatu in Iohann.50.Ascendit in coelum corpus Christi. Respondeat aliquis, Quomodo tenebo absentem? Quomodo in coelum manus mittam, ut ibi sedentem (non igitur vbique corpore suo essentialiter praesentem) teneam? Fidem mitte & tenuisti: Sed & Ambrosius,Maximè, inquit,(Fidelicet) videtur quod oculis nimirum non videtur.&Chryfostomus,nos non ad Vbiquitatem remittens, sed in coelos, vbi demùm nunc,non autem in terris,est humana Christi natura, subuehens, lib.3.de Sacerdotio haec ipsa de re loquês.Etiamne te, inquit,intermortales versari,atque in terra consistere existimas. ac non potiùs in coelum, è vestigio transferris? annon carnis omnem cogitationem abiiciens, inde animo & meramente circunspicis quae in coelo sunt?
units.tr: The hyperboles of the orthodox Fathers are therefore not to be understood otherwise than these very words of Christ. When they write that "the body of the Lord enters into our mouth," that "the tongue is made bloodless by the blood of Christ," and that "Christ himself is seen and touched in this action," they are thinking nothing less than of those portents. They are not describing what kind of manner this purely intellectual and spiritual offering and perception of the things signified is. They are indicating how certain and effective this communication is, by these most explicit metonymic phrases. That this is so is enough to show now by a few witnesses, almost all of whom are beyond any exception. Thus Augustine, in his Tractate 1 on the Epistle of John: "We," he says, "cannot handle with the hand Christ sitting in heaven" (but can we eat him with the mouth itself?), "yet we can touch Christ by faith." And in Tractate 50 on John: "The body of Christ ascended into heaven. Someone will answer: How shall I hold the absent one? How shall I send my hand into heaven to hold him sitting there?" (therefore not present everywhere essentially with his body?) "Send faith, and you have held him." Ambrose too: "Chiefly," he says, "that is seen which is not seen by the eyes." And Chrysostom, who does not refer us to ubiquity but lifts us up into heaven, where the human nature of Christ now is at last, and not on earth, speaks of this very matter in Book 3 On the Priesthood: "Do you think you dwell among mortals and stand on the earth? Are you not rather at once transported into heaven? Do you not, casting off all thought of the flesh, look around with your mind alone at what is in heaven?"

units.la: Nec est quod nobis hic obiiciatur carnis cogitatio, quasi dum ab humanę naturae quantumuis glorificatae proprietatibus essentialibus & perpetuis ὑπερφυσικὰ quidem seruates, ἀντιφυσικὰ vero inficiantes, argumenta desumimus, Physicis legibus hæc mysteria subii ciamus. Christi n. certè hac in re vestigia sequimur, qui vt veritatis carnis suæ fidè faceret, videte me, inquit, & palpate: quo i argumetu nisi καθ' αὐτὸ de vero organico corpore dicatur, & quidè inseparabiliter, ἀσυλλόγιστον fuisset. Hinc autè etiā apparet, quàm parum vere & commodè nonnulli Vbiquitatis defensores, illud ἀφανῶς ἐγένετο de Christo dictum, & quo subita & hyperphysica discessio significatur Luc.24.31. illi non dissimilis, quæ de Philippo describitur Act.8.38.&39.ad ipsius substantiæ inuisibilitatem & illocalitate transferant. Carnis denique Christi perpetua & immutabilis veritas, ac proinde vera Circunscriptio, & hac necessario consequens Localitas, negari non potest, quin Physicum simul & Theologicum sit necessario retinendum principium, quo negato corpus illud Christi aut prorsus esse desinat, aut in Marcionititicum & Eutychianum spectrum transformetur.
units.tr: Nor should the objection of carnal thought be raised against us here, as if, in drawing arguments from the essential and perpetual properties of human nature, however glorified, we preserved the supernatural properties but denied the contrary-to-nature ones, and so subjected these mysteries to physical laws. In this matter we certainly follow the footsteps of Christ, who, to make them believe in the truth of his flesh, said: "See me, and handle me." That argument would have been inconclusive unless it were said of the true organic body in its proper sense, and indeed inseparably. From this it also appears how little truly and fittingly some defenders of ubiquity apply to illocality and the invisibility of his substance that phrase said of Christ, "he vanished from sight" [ἀφανῶς ἐγένετο], which signifies a sudden and supernatural departure, Luke 24:31, similar to what is described of Philip in Acts 8:38–39. Finally, the perpetual and unchangeable truth of Christ's flesh cannot be denied, and with it true circumscription, and the locality that necessarily follows from it. So the physical and theological principle must necessarily be retained together. If it is denied, that body of Christ either ceases altogether to be, or is transformed into a Marcionite and Eutychian phantom.

units.la: Peto præterea, annum oralem illam manducationem salsissima ista & absurdissima, necessario consequantur. Primum posito illo orali esu & potu, annon ineuitabiliter oportet vel corpus & sanguinem Christi, quod ad sui substantiam attinet, in hac Cœnæ Domini actione simul sumi, & simul euanescere: ac proinde corporalem illam Christi cum sumenfumentium corporibus vnitionem, ista oris manducatione terminari : vel quod sic ore sumptum est intra viscera, (nisi panem illum & vinum illud caro & sanguis Christi mox deserant,) naturali facultate concoqui, digeri,& tandem assimilari. Ad hæc autem monstra qui non aliter respondent quàm vt illa tanquam profana detestentur, seipsos profecto deridendos propinant: quum,vt tunc nondum expediant, ostendere potius illos oportuerit,posita orali manducatione, ista necessario non colligi.
units.tr: I ask further whether those most absurd and salty consequences do not necessarily follow from that oral manducation. First, given oral eating and drinking, must it not inevitably follow either that the body and blood of Christ, so far as their substance is concerned, are taken together in this action of the Lord's Supper and at the same moment vanish, so that the corporeal union of Christ with the bodies of those who receive him ends in this eating with the mouth? Or else, what has been taken thus into the bowels (unless that bread and wine, the flesh and blood of Christ, immediately leave it) is digested by natural faculty, concocted, and at last assimilated. Those who answer these monstrosities by nothing other than detesting them as profane only make themselves a laughing-stock. Since they cannot yet do otherwise, they ought rather to have shown that, given oral manducation, these things do not necessarily follow.

units.la: Deinde si orali manducatione fimus Christo συμφυεῖ & concorporamur,vt qualis est il lius perceptio,tale sit eius effectum : quinam mysticum inde corpus Ecclesiæ oriatur,tot reipsa, nimirum, substantia & numero separatis manetibus personis,quot sunt homines Christo spiritualiter adhærentes?ac non potius inde monstrosissimum & inauditum corpus conficiatur, ex tot hominibus velut in vnum ὑφισταμένον conflatum , quot homines illo corporali nexus modo , cum Christo coaluerint.
units.tr: Then, if by oral manducation we are joined with Christ and made one body with him, so that the effect is of the same kind as the reception, what mystical body of the Church would arise from this? So many persons would remain in reality, separate in substance and number, as there are men spiritually adhering to Christ. Would not rather a most monstrous and unheard-of body be formed, as if fused into one subsisting thing from so many men, as many men as have coalesced with Christ in that corporeal bond?

units.la: Præterea quum non tantùm distinctis, sed etiam separatis signis, corpus & sanguis Domini in his mysteriis præbeantur: si, τῷ ῥητῷ præcisè seruato, realis & essentialis ista consubstantiatio, præsentia, præbitio, manducatio, & potio, statuatur: certè necesse quoque fuerit quot locis ista separatim præbentur, & àquot personis sic oraliter sumuntur, toties Christi humanitatem, veri sui corporis & veri sui sanguinis, per veram distantiam, separatione, essentialiter ac reipsa diuidi.
units.tr: Moreover, since the body and blood of the Lord are offered in these mysteries not only by distinct signs but by separate ones, if this real and essential consubstantiation, presence, offering, eating and drinking is established by keeping strictly to the words [τῷ ῥητῷ], then it would also necessarily follow that in as many places as these are offered separately, and as often as they are orally taken by as many persons, the humanity of Christ, of his true body and true blood, would be divided essentially and in reality by a true distance and separation.

units.la: Hoc autem absurdissimum somnium declinantes Pontificij Transsubstantiatores, fictitio Concomitantiæ commento, illa Sacramentaria verba HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, ET HOC EST SANGVIS MEVS σωματικ[?]ῶς interpretati, (quasi videlicet illic quidem sanguis cum corpore, hic vero corpus cum sanguine intelligatur) hoc demum prætextu suum illud scelus excusant quo Laicos, ab ipsis vocatos, altera horum mysteriorum parte priuarunt.
units.tr: But the Papist Transubstantiators, avoiding this most absurd dream, have recourse to the fictitious invention of concomitance. They interpret those sacramentarian words, THIS IS MY BODY, AND THIS IS MY BLOOD, bodily [σωματικῶς], as if in the one case blood were understood along with the body, and in the other body along with the blood. With this pretext they excuse that crime of theirs by which they deprived the laity, as they call them, of the other part of these mysteries.

units.la: Sed alia præterea nobis longè maximi momenti salsissima falsitas, hic occurrit. Nam si, ut hi volunt, vna & eadem est signorum & rerum significatarum, id est ipsius Christi & omnium eius beneficiorum perceptio, tum digne, tum indigne accedentibus communis: efficietur communem etiam esse ut risque illis corporis & sanguinis Domini κοινωνίαν: ac proinde, sicut signa, sic etiam Christum ipsum ab aliis cum fide ad salutem, ab aliis sine fide ad iudicium sumi. At quæ tandem societas est lucis cum tenebris: & vitæ cum morte? Et contra constat, sicut non aliter quàm fide Christus ipse nobis communicatur, sic illum incredulitate repelli. Deinde sic ipsius Christi sumptio in incredulis ab ipsius beneficiorum perceptione, perabsurde & impie separabitur: quæ tamen ostendimus in his mysteriis non minus signis suis, quàm pa-ne illo & vino illo Christu ipsum Sacramen-taliter significari, & sumendum præberi. Quod autem ad hanc obiectionem nonnulli responderunt, Christum non tantùm vt Seruatorem, sed etiam vt iudicem, vt in simplici prædicato verbo, sic in Sacramentis etiam considerâri, nihil ad rem facit: immo illud ipsum præsupponit de quo controuertitur, Christum videlicet, & vt Seruatorem à digne accedentibus, & vt iudicem ab indigne accedentibus sumi: quod de signorum quidem externa sumptione, his & illis communi, verum est, quæ propterea aliis saluti aliis iudicio cedit: de ipso autem Christo salsissimum est, vtpote qui non sumptus, sed repudiatus, indigne accedentes condemnet.
units.tr: But here there presents itself another most salty falsehood, of the greatest importance to us. For if, as these men wish, there is one and the same perception of the signs and of the things signified, that is of Christ himself and of all his benefits, common to those who approach worthily and unworthily, then it will follow that the fellowship [κοινωνία] of the body and blood of the Lord is common to both as well. And so, just as the signs are taken, so Christ himself is taken by some with faith to salvation, and by others without faith to judgment. But what fellowship, after all, is there between light and darkness, or life and death? On the contrary, it is certain that just as Christ is communicated to us only by faith, so he is repelled by unbelief. Then the taking of Christ himself by unbelievers would be separated from the perception of his benefits in a most absurd and impious way, even though we have shown that in these mysteries he is signified sacramentally and offered to be taken no less than the bread and wine are by their signs. As for the answer some have given to this objection, that Christ is to be considered not only as Saviour but also as judge, as in the preached word, so also in the sacraments, this has nothing to do with the point. Indeed it presupposes the very thing in dispute, namely that Christ is taken as Saviour by those who approach worthily, and as judge by those who approach unworthily. That is true of the external taking of the signs, which is common to these and those, and which therefore falls to some for salvation and to others for judgment. But of Christ himself it is most false, since he is not taken but rejected, and he condemns those who approach unworthily.

units.la: Et de ista quidem orali manducatione falsam illam præsentiam ac etiam vbiquitatem præsupponente, & vtraque Christianæ religionis fundamentum partim directè, partim exconsequenti subuertente, ipsam denique sacramentalis Institutionis Cœnæ Domini formulam ὅλως & κατὰ μέρη corrumpente, hactenus dictum esto. Nos autem, etsi nullum hic ἀντιφωνικὸν & proprie appellatum miraculum agnoscimus, recte ab Augustino præmoniti, honorem hæc habe-re posse vt religiosa, non autem stuporem vt admiranda: tamen cum Apostolo, ve-re magnum esse hoc mysterium agnosci-mus, id est, totam hanc actionem cœlestem[?], supernaturalem, spiritualem esse a-gnoscimus quòd ad res signis siue sub-stantialibus, siue in actione positis si-gnificatas & præbitas attinet: & siue res i-psas quæ communicantur, siue communi-cationis modum: siue finem & scopum i-stius actionis spectemus. Duplex hic est igitur, id est in Sacramentorum administra-tione, præbitio, perceptioque necessario sta-tueda. Vna, videlicet externa, signorum, qua-tenus in externos sensus incurrunt: altera vero interna, & mentis fide præditæ propria, qua fit vt & signa, quatenus signa sunt, & multò magis res ipsæ significatæ, diuina Omnipotentis Dei virtute, ex Euangelico pacto, per fidei in-strumentum, verè à nobis percipiantur. Sic e-tiam in Sacramentali Circuncifionis actione duplex fuit circuncifio, vna præputij, altera cordis. Sic in Baptismo alia est Pastoris aqua sacramentaliter baptisantis, alia Patris in Christo per Sp.Sanctum suum intus baptisantis, id est, peccata abluentis, & nos regeneran-tis, actio. Nec propterea multiplicatur Circu-cisio vel Baptismus, quum longè sit aliud rem quampiam multiplicare, quàm in suas partes distinguere. Nec etiam hinc consequitur Sa-cramentorum vsum ad solam mentem spectare. Nam è contrario, sicut in simplici quoqne verbo Euangelico prædicato vsuuenit, vt quâ-uis sola mens per fidei in-strumentum rem per verbum externum significatam, (id est, Chri-stum, cum suis omnibus beneficiis saluificis) percipercipiat, tamen Euangelium hac sola fideli mente prehensum, sit potens Dei instrumentum ad totius credentis salutem: ita quoque de legitimo Sacramentorum usu statuamus oportet. Nam & externum ipsum verbum simplex signi appellatione comprehenditur, quum naturalia quoque ῥήματα[?], sicut recte inquit Philosophus, sint τὰ ἐν τῇ λαλουμένῃ[?] ψυχῇ[?] παθημάτων σημεῖα[?] : & Sacramentalia signa idcirco verbo simplici praedicato diuinitus adiiciantur, ut ad eundem finem & usum illi per fidei excitationem subserviant.
units.tr: Having said so much about this oral eating, which presupposes that false presence and even ubiquity, which overturns both foundations of the Christian religion, directly in part and by consequence in part, and which finally corrupts the very wording of the sacramental institution of the Lord's Supper both as a whole and in its parts, let this suffice. We, however, although we acknowledge here no miracle that is properly called paradoxical [ἀντιφωνικὸν], are rightly warned by Augustine that these things can be held to deserve honour as sacred, but not astonishment as wonders. Yet with the Apostle we acknowledge that this is truly a great mystery: that is, we acknowledge that this whole action is heavenly, supernatural and spiritual, so far as it concerns the things signified and offered by the signs, whether substantial or contained in the action, and whether we look at the things themselves that are communicated, or at the manner of communication, or at the end and purpose of this action. There must therefore be a twofold offering and receiving in the administration of the sacraments. One is external, of the signs, in so far as they fall under the external senses; the other is internal, and proper to the mind endowed with faith, by which both the signs, in so far as they are signs, and, much more, the things signified themselves, are truly received by us through the divine power of Almighty God, from the evangelical covenant, by the instrument of faith. So also in the sacramental action of circumcision there was a twofold circumcision, one of the foreskin, the other of the heart. So in baptism there is one action of the minister baptizing sacramentally with water, and another action of the Father baptizing within through his Holy Spirit in Christ, that is, washing away sins and regenerating us. Nor for that reason is circumcision or baptism multiplied, since it is one thing to multiply something and quite another to distinguish it into its parts. Nor does it follow from this that the use of the sacraments concerns the mind alone. On the contrary, just as it happens in the simple preaching of the evangelical word that the mind alone, by the instrument of faith, perceives the thing signified through the external word (that is, Christ with all his saving benefits), and yet the Gospel, grasped by this faithful mind alone, is the powerful instrument of God for the salvation of every believer, so we must likewise hold concerning the lawful use of the sacraments. For the external word itself is also comprehended under the simple name of sign, since natural words, as the Philosopher rightly says, are the signs of the affections of the soul [τὰ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σημεῖα]; and the sacramental signs are therefore added by divine appointment to the simple preaching of the word, so that they may serve the same end and use by stirring up faith.

units.la: CAPVT V. De Sacramenti Cœna Domini, legitimè administratæ, fine & effectis.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the Lord's Supper, rightly administered: its end and effects.

units.la: Hoc etiam caput, ad quod dirigenda est tota superior disputatio, spiritus erroris miris modis depravauit, quò magis fidis omnibus seruis Dei enitedum est, ut de hac quoque doctrinæ parte liquido in Ecclesia Dei constet. Sumemus autem ad hoc explicandum argumentum, duos in primis Apostoli locos: unum, ex Roman. 4. ii. vbi duabus voculis, nempe Signi & Sigilli, propo-sito Circuncisionis exemplo, Apostolus tum quæ sit in genere formalis Sacramētorum causa, tum quis fit illorum visus declarat: Alterum, ex 1.Cor. 10. 16. quo proprius & peculiaris sacræ Domini Cœnæ finis & effectus explicatur.
units.tr: Spirit of error has corrupted this chapter, to which the whole of the preceding discussion is directed, in many strange ways. For this reason all faithful servants of God must strive all the more that this part of doctrine also be clearly settled in the Church of God.
