To explain this subject, we shall take two passages of the Apostle in particular: the first from Romans 4:11, where, by two little words, namely "of the sign" and "of the seal," and by the example of circumcision set forth, the Apostle declares both what the formal cause of the sacraments is in general and what their purpose is. The second is from 1 Corinthians 10:16, where the proper and peculiar end and effect of the holy Lord's Supper is explained.

units.la: Horum igitur locorum priore varii maximi errores refelluntur, nempe quibus factum est, ut alii plus, alii minus quàm par erat, sacris istis mysteriis tribuerint. Prioris hac in re peccati rei sunt qui, præpostero quodam zelo, hæc signa diuinitus, & de rebus diuinis ordinata, non contenti à communibus rebus, sancta quadam reuerentia, distinguere: nec animaduertentes Deum, cuius mandato standum fuit, ipsa materiæ & rituum simplicitate, in noui Testamenti Sacramentis, occurrere humanis cogitationibus & iudiciis voluisse: infinitis pœne ritibus sacra ista mysteria certè non ornarunt, sed contaminarunt: qui quum nec ad honestatis ordinem nec ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ quicquam faciant, immò paulatim maxima ex parte, in ἐθελοθρησκείας, atque adeò in idolomaniam degenerarint, qualis est præsertim illa Chrismatis confectio & adoratio: partim etiam per inscitiam vel negligentiam irrepserint, ut Exorcismus ex Energumenorum adiuratione, in quotidianum Baptismum: & fidei Christianæ confessio, ab adultorum Baptismo in Pædobaptismum introducta, & similia eiusmodi: viderint quid agant qui de rebus istis retinendis controuersias mouent, nec Baptismum illum verè Apostolicum plenè instaurari patiuntur. Illa verò sacra Domini Cœna, quibus primùm ineptiis ac tandem impietatibus sit profanata, quis satis possit deplorare? quas impurissimas sordes, mihi religio est pluribus contrectare. Sed ista certè quantumuis horrenda satis execrari, nec possumus, nec debemus: quòd nimirùm signis illis sacris in ipsummet Christum transmutatis, sacra hæc Cœna (idcirco instituta ut adhibita solenni mortis Christi annuntiatione, & gratiarum actione, illius nobiscum communio intra nos sanciatur) sit in idolomaniam, qua nihil unquam indignius Sol aspexit, ac tandem ex Sacramento in sacrificium expiatorium, idque pro vivis & mortuis, transformata. Et utinā videant qui in tanta Euangelij luce adhuc ἐπιδείξιν[?] & alia nō dissimilia retinent, à quibus certum est cœpisse illius adorationis βδέλυγμα, quàm prudenter sibi & posteris suis caveant. Viderint quoque Consubstantiatores, præsertim Vbiquitarij, annon tantorum malorum semen & fomitem retineant. Sed de istis sordibus plus satis, de quibus ne cogitare quidem sine horrore verè pij omnes possunt, quantacunque antiquitatis specie fucatis.
units.tr: From the first of these passages, then, several very great errors are refuted, namely those by which some have attributed too much, and others too little, to these holy mysteries. Those who have sinned by excess are guilty in this matter: out of a certain misguided zeal, they were not content to distinguish these signs, ordained by God and concerning divine things, from common things by a holy reverence. Nor did they notice that God, whose command had to be obeyed, wished by the very simplicity of matter and rites in the sacraments of the New Testament to meet human thoughts and judgments. They have certainly not adorned these holy mysteries with almost endless rites; they have defiled them. These rites contribute nothing either to the order of decency or to the edification of the Church. Indeed, gradually, for the most part, they have degenerated into self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία], and so into idolatry, as is especially the case with the consecration and adoration of the chrism. Partly, too, through ignorance or negligence, some things have crept in, such as exorcism, taken from the adjuration of the possessed, into the daily baptism, and the confession of the Christian faith, introduced into infant baptism from the baptism of adults, and other things of this kind. Let those who stir up controversies about retaining such things see to what they are doing, and who do not allow that baptism, truly apostolic, be fully restored. As for the holy Lord's Supper, who could sufficiently lament with what follies, and at last with what impieties, it has been profaned? I scruple to handle at length the most impure filth of these abuses. Yet such things, however horrible, neither can nor should be sufficiently execrated. For, with those holy signs changed into Christ himself, this holy Supper (instituted so that, with the solemn proclamation of Christ's death and the giving of thanks, communion with him might be confirmed within us) has been turned into idolatry, than which the sun has never looked upon anything more unworthy, and finally from a sacrament into an expiatory sacrifice, and that for the living and the dead. And would that those who, in so great a light of the Gospel, still retain display [ἐπίδειξις] and other not dissimilar things, from which it is certain that the abomination [βδέλυγμα] of that adoration began, would take prudent care for themselves and their posterity! Let the Consubstantiationists, especially the Ubiquitarians, also see whether they retain the seed and fuel of such great evils. But enough about these filths, which no truly pious person can even think of without horror, however much they may be disguised with a show of antiquity.

units.la: Minùs autem multò quàm par sit Sacra-mentis tribuunt, qui, neglectis quæ ad ordi-nem, & sanctam quandam in omni diuino cultu obseruandam reuerentiam faciunt, sacras istas actiones irreuerenter, & non aliter quàm res communes & quotidianas exercét.
units.tr: Those who attribute much less to the sacraments than they ought, however, are also guilty. They neglect what pertains to order and to the holy reverence to be observed in all divine worship, and they perform these sacred actions irreverently, no differently than common and everyday things.

units.la: Itidem qui Sacramentalem significationem pro nudis quasi picturis & spectaculis habet, quibus duntaxat ad recoledam Christi mortis memoriam excitentur: qui liberum sibi esse putant ad Coenam Domini accedere, vel ab ea abstinere, quum sit diuini cultus pars, non minima diuinitus mandatae: qui deniq; haec mysteria non pro sigillis habent diuinitus ad obsignandam in animis nostris Christi communionem ordinata, sed pro externis tantum notis ac tesseris[?], quibus qui Christianos se profitentur, a prophanis aliis gentibus discernuntur.
units.tr: Likewise, those who regard the sacramental signification as mere pictures and spectacles, by which people are merely stirred to recall the memory of Christ's death; those who think it is free for them to approach the Lord's Supper or to abstain from it, although it is a part, and no small part, of divine worship commanded by God; and finally, those who do not regard these mysteries as seals ordained by God for sealing Christ's communion in our souls, but only as external marks and tokens by which those who profess themselves Christians are distinguished from other profane nations.

units.la: Quid autem & quantum sit huic Sacrosanctae actioni tribuendum non possimus, neque rectius, neque certius quam ex istis diui-nissimis Apostoli verbis,intelligere, panis ille quem frangimus, communio corporis Christi est, & poculum illud benedictionis cui benedicimus communio sanguinis Christi est. Haec autem verba, primum declarant materialem causam, sive, ut magis perspicue loquamur, partes hanc actionem constituentes: nempe panem illum & poculum illud, (id est vinum illo poculo comprehensum, ut etiam capitales illi tro-porum hostes, hic cogantur metonymiam continentis pro contento agnoscere) & illa quidem non ut res vulgares, & communi e-fui & potui destinatas, sed ut peculiari Dei ordinatione, & sacris certis ritibus, ad usum plane cœlestem ordinatas, quos Benedictionis & Fractionis nominibus συνεχδοχικῶς intelligit. Altera autem pars eaque praecipua, corpus & sanguis Domini est, id est, ipsemet Christus,rursum συνεκδοχικῶς[?] ab ea sui natura denominatus,qua proprie frater noster est: & quidem non simpliciter, sed quatenus effuso suo sanguine tradidit sese pro nobis. Verbum autem EST, non est opinor quisquam satis sani iudicij qui sic interpretari possit, quasi panis ille, & vinum illud, sint ὑπαρκτικῶς[?] illa ipsa communio: nec etiam quasi panis ille & vinum illud,& tota haec actio, sit causa huius communionis efficiens, quae est Pater Filium suis in eo electis,& suos vicissim filio suo do-nans:Filius seipsum suaque omnia ad salutem nobis comparandam necessaria communi-cans: Spiritus sanctus denique hanc Patris & Filij liberalitatem intra nos per creatum in nobis Fidei instrumetum insinuans. Declarat igitur hoc in loco haec copula, relata non tantum ad panis & vini nomina, sed etiam con-iunctim ad illa verba, cui BENEDICIMUS, ET QUEM FRANGIMUS, causam istius communionis, tum initrumentalem, quatenus illa exterius adhibentur: tum formalem, quatenus ex diuina ordinatione tum panis, & vinum illud, tum actiones illae Sacramentales, animis credentium repraesentat, quae sicuti diximus Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, in nabis reipsa efficiunt: siue ut Apostoli nobis praeeuntis vestigia sequamur, quatenus sunt Sacramentum, id est σημ-[?] μεῖον & σφραγὶς nostrae illius cum Christo communionis. Ipsa vero Communionis appellatio finem præcipuum, & vltimum isto-rum mysteriorum declarat.
units.tr: What and how much is to be ascribed to this most sacred action we cannot understand more rightly or more certainly than from those most divine words of the Apostle: the bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ, and the cup of blessing which we bless is the communion of the blood of Christ. These words first declare the material cause, or, to speak more plainly, the parts that constitute this action: namely that bread and that cup (that is, the wine contained in that cup, so that even those chief enemies of the tropes must here be compelled to acknowledge a metonymy of the container for the thing contained), and these not as common things destined for ordinary food and drink, but as things set apart by a peculiar ordinance of God and by certain holy rites for a plainly heavenly use, which he understands by the names of Blessing and Breaking, by synecdoche. The other part, and that the principal one, is the body and blood of the Lord, that is, Christ himself, again named by synecdoche from that nature by which he is truly our brother; and this not simply, but insofar as he gave himself up for us by pouring out his blood. Now, I think there is no one of sufficiently sound judgment who could interpret the word IS as if that bread and that wine were substantially that very communion. Nor could it be taken as if that bread and wine, and the whole of this action, were the efficient cause of this communion, which is the Father giving his Son and his own in him to be elect, and in turn giving them to his Son; the Son communicating himself and all he has that is necessary for procuring our salvation; and finally the Holy Spirit inserting this liberality of the Father and the Son within us through the instrument of faith created in us. Therefore the copula here declares a cause of this communion, related not only to the names of bread and wine but also jointly to those words, which WE BLESS AND WHICH WE BREAK: instrumental, insofar as those things are applied outwardly; and formal, insofar as by divine ordinance both that bread and wine and those sacramental actions represent to the minds of believers what, as we have said, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit actually effect in us. Or, to follow the footsteps of the Apostle who leads us, insofar as they are a sacrament, that is, a sign [σημεῖον] and seal [σφραγίς] of our communion with Christ. The very name of Communion declares the chief and final end of these mysteries.

units.la: Cæterum antequàm ad huius vocabuli interpretationem accedam, duo sunt de quibus Lectorem præmonitum velim. Vnum, κοινω-νίας, id est, Communionis appellatione, multò melius hic conuenire quàm Participationis, id est μετοχῆς[?]. Est enim μέτοχή, id est participatio, ad signa, authore Apostolo i.ad Cor. 10.12. proprie referenda, singulis videlicet eodem quidem pane, sed fracto & per partes sigillatim distributo vescentibus. Totum autem Christum vnum & eundem apprehen-dunt & sibi applicant singuli veram fidem adferentes: quum diuisus Christus, Seruator noster esse non possit, quanuis huius cum Christo communionis vim & effecta oportet, ex fidei & donorum particularium men-sura metiri.
units.tr: Furthermore, before I come to the interpretation of this word, there are two things about which I would have the reader forewarned. The first is that the name of communion [κοινωνία] fits here much better than that of participation, that is, of partaking [μετοχή]. For participation [μέτοχη], according to the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10:12, is properly referred to the signs: namely, to those who eat of the same bread, indeed, but broken and distributed individually in portions. However, individual believers, bringing true faith, grasp and apply to themselves the whole Christ, one and the same; since a divided Christ could not be our Savior. Nevertheless, the force and effects of this communion with Christ must be measured by the measure of faith and of the particular gifts.

units.la: Alterum, quum hæc communio sit totius Euagelici fœderis finis, illam ab his mysteriis minimè incipere, nec ad illa esse restringendam, vtpote quæ à simplicis verbi auditu inchoetur, & Sacramentis tanquam sigillis, & quidem specialiter in hac Domini Cœna per peculiarem alimoniæ cœlestis, & terrenæ analogiam sanciatur: adeò quidem vt huius Sacramentalis communionis fructum nemo in his mysteriis percipiat, nisi qui iam illam per fidem obtinuit.
units.tr: The second is that, since this communion is the goal of the whole Evangelical covenant, it does not begin with these mysteries at all, nor is it to be restricted to them. It begins with the mere hearing of the Word, and it is sealed by the sacraments as by seals; and in this Supper of the Lord especially it is sealed through a peculiar analogy with heavenly and earthly nourishment. So much so that no one perceives the fruit of this sacramental communion in these mysteries unless he has already obtained it through faith.

units.la: Quatuor igitur hic considerabimus. Pri-mum quid sit in hoc argumento τὸ κοινωνεῖν, & qualis sit iste communicationis modus:
units.tr: We shall therefore consider four things here. First, what κοινωνεῖν [to communicate] means in this subject, and what kind of communication it is.

units.la: Secundò, Quid sit τὸ κοινωνούμενον,
units.tr: Second, what is the κοινωνούμενον [the thing communicated].

units.la: Tertiò, qui sint hi κοινωνοῦντες[?]:
units.tr: Third, who these κοινωνοῦντες [the communicants] are.

units.la: Quartò, qualis sit hæc communio, illorum videlicet effectum.
units.tr: Fourth, what this communion is like, that is, its effects.

units.la: Hæc autem coniunctim sic paucis expli-co. Et vtinam potius accuratè inter nostros summos ætatis nostræ Theologos de hac κοι-νωνία quæsitum fuisset, quàm de signorum cum rebus significatis præsentia certatum.
units.tr: I shall explain these things together, briefly. I wish that our leading theologians of this age had inquired as carefully into this κοινωνία [communion] as they have contended over the presence of the signs together with the things signified.

units.la: Communicari igitur, vnde oritur Cömunionis nomé, illud dicitur, quòd quum antea alicuius esset proprium, fit inter se pacisc[?]etium commune : cuius communicationis varias species persequi, quoniam nimis longum esset, satis, opinor, fuerit eam de qua hic agitur ex verbo Dei, vt certo & authentico huius pactionis instrumento, eruere, prout in illo variis similitudinibus, nobis adumbratur. Certè quàm arcta hæc sit liquet ex nomine ἕνω-σεως, quod explicans Christus: Peto, inquit, à te, Pater, vt quos dedisti mihi sint vnum, prout & nos. Et huc spectant passim occurrentes illæ similitudines: vt coiugij per quod Ecclesia fit caro ex eius carne, & os ex ossibus eius, de quo magno mysterio pluribus mox agemus: item capitis & membrorum eodem spiritu viuifico deuinctorum: item Insitionis, per quam truncus & insitus surculus in vnicam plantam reipsa coalescunt: item fontis & riuorum: item ædificij ex viuis lapidibus constructi & imo angulari & fundamentali saxo impositi. Et ex his apparet verissimum esse quod Patres non uno loco testatur: nempe non simplicem & superficie tenus esse illam Communionē, sed qua fiat vt qui plures numero sunt, vnum quiddam fiant: non tantùm affectu & consensu (qua ratione dicuntur amici inter se concordes & vnanimes, quòd idem velint & idem nolint,& dicit Lucas credentium vnam fuisse animam & cor vnum) sed reipsa quoque, vt loquitur Chrysostomus, & naturaliter,quod ait Cyrillus,id est ipsa quoque naturę humanę Christi communicatione, Ecclesiam Christo adhærere.
units.tr: To communicate, from which the name communion arises, means that what previously belonged to one person becomes common between two parties who have agreed to it. To pursue the various kinds of this communication would take too long. It will suffice, I think, to draw from the Word of God the kind with which we are concerned here, as from a certain and authentic instrument of this agreement, as it is shadowed forth to us in various likenesses. How close this communion is becomes clear from the name ἕνωσις [unity], which Christ explains: "I ask, Father, that those whom you have given me may be one, as we are." To this point look the likenesses that occur everywhere: that of marriage, by which the Church becomes flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, a great mystery of which we shall speak at length shortly; likewise that of head and members bound together by the same life-giving Spirit; likewise that of grafting, by which the stock and the grafted shoot really grow together into one plant; likewise that of the fountain and its streams; and that of a building constructed of living stones and set upon the chief corner-stone and foundation. From these things it appears most true what the Fathers testify in many places: that this communion is not simple and superficial, but makes those who are many in number become one thing, not only in affection and agreement (in which sense friends are said to be concordant and of one mind, because they will the same and refuse the same, and Luke says the believers had one soul and one heart), but really as well, as Chrysostom says, and naturally, as Cyril says. That is, by the very communication of the human nature of Christ, the Church cleaves to Christ.

units.la: Itaque non est cur eorum calumniis fides habeatur qui nos falsò profecto clamitant nihil credere, hęc mysteria profanare,& quid non? Deus meliora. Domine, ad cuius tribunal ab iistis provocamus, nosti qui simus, apud cuius Tribunal omnes stabimus. Illud interim omnes norint, agnoviisse nos semper & agnoscere, per Dei gratiam, quis sit noster ille Christus, à quo non merito tenus, nec ex parte, sed toto & vnico nostro secundum vtramque naturam Mediatore, per fidem, verissimè & efficacissimè nobis indissolubiliter vnito, tota nostra salus pendet: & cuius mutuæ arctissimæ vnionis magnum illud mysterium, speciatim in sacra Domini Cœna, vt eius peculiari signo & sigillo, in cordibus nostris, quasi ipsius Dei & seruatoris manu, sanctitur.
units.tr: There is therefore no reason to give credence to the calumnies of those who falsely shout that we believe nothing, profane these mysteries, and whatever else. May God grant better things. Lord, before whose tribunal we summon them, you know who we are, and before whose tribunal all of us shall stand. Meanwhile let everyone know that we have always acknowledged, and by God's grace do acknowledge, who our Christ is: not a mediator in part or partially, but the whole and only Mediator according to both natures, who is joined to us most truly and most effectively, indissolubly, through faith, and on whom our whole salvation depends. The great mystery of this most intimate mutual union is sanctioned in our hearts, especially in the holy Lord's Supper, as by its peculiar sign and seal, as it were by the very hand of God and Saviour.

units.la: Non igitur, de eo quod nobis communicatur, catur, Christo videlicet toto, & omnibus i-psius beneficiis: non de huius communionis arctissimo nexu, quo videlicet Christus ipse nobiscum, & nos cum illo unum quiddam si-mus inenarrabili mysterio: non de iis qui hic & corpore & animo copulantur, qui sunt Christus & Ecclesia, nobis esse vobiscum có-trouersia arbitror. Sed tamē ut omnes norint quā procul nihilominus à Libertinorū, Ana-baptistarū, & cæterorū eiusmodi Phanaticorū deliciis absimus, mirificas nescio cuius spiri-tus traductiones & effusiones imaginatium, huius Sacrosanctæ communionis mysterium conabor in primis, quantumquidem nobis est ex Dei verbo patefactum, explicare, pro gratiæ mihi concessæ mensura: ut si quo mo-do forte hac in re, quum omnes ex parte co-gnoscamus, in hac veritate non prorsus con-sentire comperiamur, Christiana collatione mutua alij alios erudiamus: quod à me quidem absit ut unquam repudiem. Deinde verò tandem ad ipsum huius Communionis mo-dum accedam, in quo sanè, fateor, & quidem non sine maximo dolore meo, nos toto cœlo diffidere.
units.tr: Therefore I do not think there is any controversy between us about what is communicated to us, namely Christ entire with all his benefits; nor about the very close bond of this communion, by which Christ himself is with us and we with him are one thing, in an unspeakable mystery; nor about those who are joined here both in body and in soul, who are Christ and the Church. But so that everyone may know how far we are from the delights of the Libertines, the Anabaptists and others of that kind of fanatics, I shall try first to explain the mystery of this most holy communion, as far as it has been revealed to us from the Word of God, in the measure of grace given to me. Then, if perhaps in this matter, although we all know it only in part, we find that we do not wholly agree on this truth, we may instruct one another by mutual Christian conference, which I by no means wish ever to reject. Then at last I shall come to the very mode of this communion, in which, I confess, and not without my greatest grief, we are utterly at odds.

units.la: Primùm igitur verum quidem est funda-mentum huius inter Christum & Eccle-siam, id est verè electorum & credentium suorum coetum unitionis fundamentum esse Filij Dei ἐν σαρκώσει[?], qua factus est unum quiddam specie cum humano toto genere: sed hanc tamen de qua hic agimus unitionem, quiddam esse ab illo cui superstruitur diuersum, & longe minus patens, vtpote quo non cum quibusuis hominibus sed cum electis credentibus & sanctis suis suis duntaxat vnitur, pro quibus propterea, petens a patre vt vnum cum ipse fierent, non rogo, inquit, pro mundo, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt.
units.tr: First, it is indeed true that the foundation of this union between Christ and the Church, that is, the assembly of those who are truly elect and believing, is the Son of God in the incarnation [ἐν σαρκώσει], by which he became one thing in kind with the whole human race. But the union of which we speak here is something different from that on which it is built, and far less extensive, since he is united not with any men whatever but only with his elect believers and saints. For these he prays, asking the Father that they may be made one with him: "I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours."

units.la: Deinde & illud praesupponendum est, in hac inter Christum &Ecclesiam vnitione reciproca, non agi simpliciter de mutua quarumdam rerum externarum communicatione,sicut mercatores inter fe fociatatem in aliquibus negotiis ineunt: sed de mutua ipso-rummet inter fe hic contrahentium, & omnium quae ipsis vere insunt,mutua vnius in alterum traductione:qualem illam postea per partes suas describemus, prout res ista multiplici distinctione indiget ille Christus.
units.tr: Next, this too must be presupposed: in this reciprocal union between Christ and the Church we are not dealing simply with the mutual communication of certain external things, as merchants enter into partnership in some business. We are dealing with the mutual transfer, each into the other, of the very persons contracting and of all the things that truly inhere in them. We shall later describe this part by part, as the matter, with its manifold distinctions, requires.

units.la: Quum enim Christus fit Θεάνθρωπος, eum quidem totum nobiscum communicari vt Mediatorem est necesse, quia nec eius Deitas absque Humanitate,nec eius Humanitas absque Deitate nos reconciliaret: sed aliter nobis consideranda est aduersus phanaticos enthufiaftas,Deitatis quàm Humanitatis ipsius communicatio. Primùm igitur istud tenendum est, Deitatem Christi in hoc negotio ad Filij personam, & quidem vt Mediatoris relatè referendam esse, vt huius communicationis beneficium Ecclesiae proprium ab illa vniuersali rerum omnium creatarum guber-nationatione & conseruatione discernantur. Dein-de illud quoque sciendum est, illam Deitatis Christi nobiscum communionem esse merè ἐνεργητικῶ[?]. Manet enim illa ἕνωσις hypostati-ca per quam ᾧ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος in eo σωματικῶς κατοικεῖ, Christi personæ ἀνθρωπότητος propria. Hæc autem in eo posita est quòd hæc Humanitatem hypostaticè sibi vnitam, & nobis hac vnitione communicatam, reddat nobis tum pro peccatis nostris propitiatoriam, tum æternæ vitæ meritoriam, quod ab Apostolo per verbum ἐνδιάθεσιν[?] declaratur: & ita denique illam nobis secum communem faciat verissimè & efficacissimè, vt ne Filiatio quidem eius excipiatur: minimè quidem illa per diuinissimam illam & coæternam & coessentialem generationem, per quam vnicus est Dei Patris Filius: neque itidem per illam merè spiritualem & plusquàm supernaturalem Humanitatis in vtero virginis conceptionem, per quam Homo ille est vnicus verè Filius Dei, quatenus non in sese, sed in illo vnico Filio Dei personaliter subsistit, aduersus Nestorium: sed per υἱοθεσίας beneficium, &, vt ipse Dominus Nicodemo plenissimè declarauit. Et talis quidem est Christi, quòd ad Deitatem ipsius attinet, communicatio.
units.tr: Since Christ is θεάνθρωπος [God-man], it is necessary that he be communicated to us entire as Mediator, for neither his Deity without his humanity nor his humanity without his Deity would reconcile us. But against the fanatical enthusiasts, the communication of the Deity must be considered differently from that of the humanity itself. First, then, this must be held: in this matter the Deity of Christ is to be referred to the person of the Son, and indeed relatively, as Mediator, so that the benefit proper to the Church in this communion is distinguished from that universal governance and preservation of all created things. Next, this too must be known: this communion of Christ's Deity with us is purely energetic. For that hypostatic union remains, by which all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him, proper to the person of Christ's humanity. This communion, however, consists in this: he makes this humanity, hypostatically united to himself and communicated to us by that union, both propitiatory for our sins and meritorious of eternal life, as the Apostle declares by the word ἐνδιάθεσιν [...]. Thus at last he makes it truly and effectively common to us, so that not even his sonship is excluded. Certainly not that most divine, co-eternal and co-essential generation, through which he is the only Son of God the Father; nor likewise that purely spiritual and more than supernatural conception of the humanity in the Virgin's womb, through which that man is truly the only Son of God, inasmuch as he subsists personally not in himself but in that one Son of God, against Nestorius. Rather it is through the benefit of adoption, as the Lord himself most fully declared to Nicodemus. Such, as far as his Deity is concerned, is the communication of Christ.

units.la: In illius autem Humanitatis communica-tione (illam enim totam συνεκδοχικῶς carnis & sanguinis nominibus, & in simplici verbo Ioh.6. & in Sacramentis intelligi, & nobis ad salutem communicari oportere suo loco docuimus) multiplex distinctio, sine vlla tamen separatione adhibenda est, vt magnum illud ab Apostolo appellatum mysterium, absque vlla aberratione intelligatur. Primum ergo hoc Humanitatis subiectum ab iis quę in ipsa considerantur, non quidem separandum, sed discernendum est: vt vanissimam eorum calumniam esse liquido constet, a quibus dicimur obedientiam & meritum Christi in horum mysteriorum explicatione, ab ipsomet Christo, illorum cerrė perpetuo, & insepara-bili subiecto, separare. Hoc enim commentum non tantum vt ἀξιόλογον[?], verum etiam vt per se ἀξίωσιν[?], est a nobis superius refutatum.
units.tr: In the communication of that humanity (for we have shown in its place that the whole of it is understood synecdochically by the names flesh and blood, both in the simple word of John 6 and in the sacraments, and must be communicated to us for salvation), a manifold distinction must be employed, yet without any separation, so that that great mystery named by the Apostle may be understood without any error. First, then, this subject of the humanity is not to be separated from the things considered in it, but distinguished from them. This makes it clear that the most empty calumny is refuted of those who say that we, in explaining these mysteries, separate Christ's obedience and merit from Christ himself, their inseparable and perpetual subject. For this fiction, which we refuted above, is not only a thing worth mentioning [ἀξιόλογον] but also a claim of worth in itself [ἀξίωσιν].

units.la: Deinde in hac ipsa humanitate Christi distinguenda sunt quę, quum nobis sint propria, in se recepit, ab iis quę ab ipso in hac mutua communicatione recepimus. Sunt autem & hęc & illa non vnius generis.
units.tr: Next, within this very humanity of Christ, we must distinguish what he took into himself as his own from what he received from us in this mutual communion. These, however, are not all of one kind.

units.la: Quędam enim verissimè quidem & effi-cacissimè cum natura nostra assumpsit, sic tamen vt minimè ipsi fuerint subiectiuè insita, sed per solam, ex Euangelico pacto, Imputa-tionem imposita. Eiusmodi sunt tum reatus, tum illa natiua labes, ex primorum parentum lapsu, intra omnes, excepto vnico Christo, illorum posteros inuecta: & omnia, quę inde consequuntur peccata: quę tria fideiussor ille noster sibi imposita in crucem sustulit, factus pro nobis κατάρα[?]. Alia vero nostra, vltra omnes facultates (quas ille simul assumpsit hypostaticè, & simul in sese plenissimè san-ctificauit,) idem ille noster ἔγγυος[?], reipsa subiectiuè intra se recepit: omnes videlicet illas per primum illum lapsum in naturam huma-nam inuectas, excepto tamen omni vitio, in-firmitates ac miserias: & praeterea poenas illas omnes, apud ipsius Patris tribunal illi nostro reatui & corruptioni, cunctis denique inde prodeuntibus peccatis, debitas, & tum ani-ma, tum corpore in ara crucis persoluendas: minimè id quidem vt esset huic oneri obno-xius in aeternum, sed donec iustus pro iniustis mortuus, & sub lege factus, nos liberatos per obedientiam suam in aeternam vitam assereret.
units.tr: For some things he assumed along with our nature, most truly and most effectively, yet in such a way that they were in no sense inherent in him as their subject, but were laid upon him only by imputation, under the gospel covenant. Such are both guilt and that innate stain carried down to all the posterity of our first parents by their fall, excepting Christ alone, and all the sins that follow from them. These three things our surety took upon himself and bore to the cross, made κατάρα [a curse] for us. But our other burdens, beyond all these faculties (which he assumed at the same time hypostatically, and at the same time most fully sanctified in himself), that same surety of ours [ἔγγυος] received in fact and subjectively into himself: namely all those infirmities and miseries introduced into human nature through the first fall, excepting every fault; and besides, all those penalties owed before the Father's tribunal to our guilt and corruption, and finally to all the sins proceeding from them, to be paid in soul and body on the altar of the cross. He did this not so that he should be bound to this burden forever, but until the just one, dying for the unjust and made subject to the law, should declare us freed, and into eternal life through his obedience.

units.la: Istis denique ab illo de nostro, sicuti dixi-mus, partim per Imputationem, partim subie-ctiuè per ipsum receptis, operæpretium est videre quàm ad amussim respondeant illa sua quæ nostra facit. Prout igitur ille nostra quæ-dam,sicuti diximus, per solam imputationem sua effecit: sic ille itidem quædam sua per so-lam imputationem credentibus communia facit, suam nimirum illam perfectissimam iustitiam ex illa obedientia profectam, quam summam & absolutissimam Patri in carne sua ad mortem usque crucis praestitit: & per quam, nobis imputatam, tum debita illa no-stra omnia ad ultimum usque quadrantem, credentium nomine persoluit, ut eos à morte eximeret: tum simul ius ad aeternam adipis-cendam vitam credentibus acquisiuit, victor ipse primus beatissimam illam gloriam assequutus, ultimo demum illo die plenissime nobis communicandam. Deinde, sicut eundem illum ostendimus quaedam nostra, mise-rias illas videlicet, & poenas peccatis nostris debitas, excepto peccato, subiectiuè in se re-cepisse: sic quoque praeter illam imputatam, de qua diximus, iustitiam (à qua pendet in solidum & peccatorum nostrorum expiatio, & æternæ vitæ ius) Sp.Sancti virtute, qua suam ipsius carnem plenissimè sanctificauit, credentes quoque incipit ad spiritualem vitam sanctificare: tum mentes nostras illustrans veræ illius veri Dei saluificæ notitiæ luce: tum voluntatem affectúsque omnes credentium ad verè sanctam & puram vitam informans: ut iam nunc istud spiritualis illius, & æternæ immortalitatis pignus in se habeant, & sentiant. Eius autem consummatio ad ultimum illum diem differtur, in quo demum Christus erit omnia in omnium suorum animabus, & corporibus, per illius gloriosissimæ immortalitatis suæ plenissimam communicationem.
units.tr: Finally, since he has received these things from ours, as we have said, partly by imputation and partly subjectively, it is worth seeing how exactly his own things correspond to those he makes ours. Just as he made some of our things his own by imputation alone, so in the same way he makes some of his own things common to believers by imputation alone: namely that most perfect righteousness proceeding from that obedience, which he rendered to the Father in his flesh, supreme and most complete, even to the death of the cross. Through this righteousness, imputed to us, he paid in the name of believers all those debts of ours down to the last farthing, so as to rescue them from death; and at the same time he acquired for believers the right to attain eternal life, having himself first reached that most blessed glory as victor, to be communicated to us most fully on that last day. Then, just as we have shown that he received into himself, subjectively, some of our things, namely those miseries and penalties owed to our sins, apart from sin itself, so also, besides that imputed righteousness of which we have spoken (on which both the expiation of our sins and the right to eternal life wholly depend), by the power of the Holy Spirit, by which he fully sanctified his own flesh, he begins also to sanctify believers to a spiritual life. He illumines our minds with the light of that true knowledge of the true and saving God, and shapes the will and all the affections of believers to a truly holy and pure life, so that even now they have and feel within themselves that pledge of spiritual and eternal immortality. Its full consummation, however, is deferred to that last day, on which at length Christ will be all in all, in the souls and bodies of his own, through the most full communication of his most glorious immortality.

units.la: In summa igitur in hac mutua Christi & Ecclesiæ Communione siue societate, ille factus nobis ὁμοούσιος, de nostro in se adsciuit, tum naturam nostram, tum naturalia nostra omnia: sed utraque illa in se purissima: nec eo contentus miserias omnes per peccatum in naturam nostram inuectas reipsa acerbissi-ma demum morte cum terribili illo Dei iudicio coniuncta expiandas subiit: imputatis nimirum ipsi, sese vt vadem nostro loco sub-stituenti, tum reatu, tum peccatis inde, id est, ex illo reatu & corruptione illam sequuta, in nos emanantibus.Hæc enim vnica est illa dos apud Ezechielem plenissimè declarata, quam à nobis in illo spirituali coniugio recepit.Idè ille denique nos spiritu suo regenerans,spiri-tualem vitam vltimo demum die consum-mandam intra nos inchoat, beatissimam illam immortalitatem nobiscum tunc quoque communicaturus.
units.tr: In sum, therefore, in this mutual communion or fellowship of Christ and the Church, he, made homoousios [ὁμοούσιος] with us, took into himself from ours both our nature and all our natural things, yet remaining in himself most pure. Not content with this, he underwent all the miseries introduced into our nature through sin, to be expiated in actual fact by a most bitter death joined with that terrible judgment of God. The guilt was imputed to him, as he substituted himself in our place as surety, and with it the sins that followed from that guilt and corruption, flowing into us from them. For this is that one dowry, most fully declared by Ezekiel, which he received from us in that spiritual marriage. Hence he, regenerating us finally by his Spirit, begins within us a spiritual life, to be consummated on the last day, when he will also share with us that most blessed immortality.

units.la: Sed hoc mysterium tam cognitu necessa-rium placet præterea duarum similitudinum ex sacris literis petitarum accurata explicatione illustrare. Quemadmodum igitur ad hoc vt fœmina quæpiam fiat vna caro cum viro, non sufficit humanæ naturæ vnitas in specie, sed coniugij pactionem interuenire necesse est, vt vir ille & fœmina illa legitimè vna caro fiant: sic illa Christi natura humana facit vt Christus quidem recté dicatur vnum quiddam esse, specie essentialiter considera-ta, cum quibusuis hominibus: sed absit vt propterea dicatur Christus quibusuis vnitus, quum propter ipsam quoque naturæ humanæ in non regeneratis deformitatem, vix ac ne vix quidem vnum esse cum illis dicatur, scribente Apostolo, scortatores vnum cum scorto fieri, ac proinde à Christo separatos: nullum esse denique Christo cum dæmonibus commercium.
units.tr: But this mystery, which is so necessary to know, it pleases us to illustrate further by an accurate explanation of two similitudes taken from the Holy Scriptures. Just as, for a woman to become one flesh with a man, the unity of human nature in species is not enough, but a covenant of marriage must intervene, so that that man and that woman may lawfully become one flesh, so Christ's human nature makes it that Christ may rightly be said to be one thing, considered essentially in species, with any men whatever. Yet far be it that for this reason Christ should be said to be united with just any men, since on account of the very deformity of human nature in the unregenerate, they are scarcely, indeed hardly at all, said to be one with him. The Apostle writes that harlots become one with a harlot, and so they are separated from Christ; and finally, there is no fellowship between Christ and demons.

units.la: Coniugio igitur illo spirituali opus est vt Ecclesia fiat caro ex Christi carne, & os ex eiusdem ossibus, casta nimirum illa ipsius vxor. Effector autem est huius sacri coniugij Sp.Sanctus: pronubus vero is est in terris qui fœdus illud Euangelicum, quod est illius coniugij instrumentum, & Sacramenta administrat, hoc de se testante Corinthiis Apostolo. Sicut autem in corporali coniugio vtrinque interuenit stipulatio mutuis signis externis & in sensus ipsos incurrentibus fancita; sic in isto spirituali coniugio mutua tum Christi per Pastorum vocem hoc testatis, & seipsum cum suis bonis omnibus suæ sponsæ donantis, tum credentis vera fide donum illud recipientis, & sese suaque omnia vicissim marito illi suo tradentis, interueniens per fidem consensio, sacram hanc copulam vtrinque ratam facit. Sicut denique ita contractum matrimonium corporale consequitur mutua sancta corporum coniunctio, per quam vir & vxor fiunt corporali modo vna caro, siue vnum corpus, & inde carnales nascuntur liberi: sic ex hac sanctissima & purissima Christi & credetis cuiusuis reciproca communione, (quæ cur spiritualis appelletur, plenissime paulo ante expositum) Spiritualem similiter copulam vnitio, id est, magnum illud mysterium, vt clamat Apostolus Ephes. 5.32. consequitur, cuius plenissima ac plane cœlestis declaratio in illo sancto Canticorum Cantico continetur. Et quoniam qui sic Christo adhæret fit vnus cum ipso Spiritus,propterea non carnis sed Spiritus fructus, sancta videlicet soboles inde liberorum instar gignitur: Galat.6.v.16. & Rom.7.4.Et rursus quoniam credentes,etsi numero plures (nec enim hypostatica est haec vnitio, nec istud inde nascens corpus est, sicut suo loco docuimus, aliquid ex indistantibus coagmentatum) tamen quatenus vna & ea-dem fide per eundem Spiritum capiti suo per efficaciorem & firmiorem Spiritualem nexum, quàm corporali vllo contactu co-haerent: & praeterea vera charitate inter se per eundem Spiritum deuincti, quasi corde vnico & anima vnica viuunt & spirant:idcirco totus hic sanctorum coetus, quasi vnica numero esset persona, vnica illius sponsa vocatur, sponso illo sponsam suam quasi intra viscera sua circumgestante: quod mysterium summi Pontificis. Leuitici Pectorale sub Lege adumbrabat, pretiosissimos illos lapides, nominibus duodecim tribuum insculptos, humeris & pectore gestantis. Quis igitur non videt huic spirituali coniunctioni,quàm ve-rè, & quàm efficaciter vnionis & quidem mutuae nomen conueniat? & quantum huic tanto mysterio detrahant, qui similitudines istas, vix profecto prae ista Spirituali & mystica vnitione vmbrarum istius vnionis ap-pellationem merentes, ad oralem manduca-tionem & corporalem ipsarum substantia-rum copulam detorquent? Quantò verius er-go & quantò rectius Bernardus,Homil.super Cantic. 71. hac ipsa de re agens, & ad sacrae Coenae non illam oralem panis & vini propriam, sed Spiritualem manducationem cuius illa signum est sacramentale, respiciens: Manducat nos Christus, inquit, & maducatur à nobis, quo arctius illi adstringamur. Necsane aliàs vnimur illi. Nam si manduco & non manducor, videbitur ille esse in me, sed nondum in illo ego: quia si manducor quidem nec manduco, me in se habere ille, sed non etiam in me esse videbitur. Nec enim perfecta vnitio in vnoquoque horum. Si enim manducet me vt habeat me in se, & à me vicissim manducetur vt sit in me, quatenus integra firmáque sit connexio, tum ego in eo, & nihilo minus in me ipse erit.
units.tr: Therefore this spiritual marriage requires that the Church become flesh of Christ's flesh and bone of his bones, that is, his chaste wife. The author of this holy marriage is the Holy Spirit; the go-between on earth, however, is he who administers that gospel covenant, which is the instrument of this marriage, and the sacraments, as the Apostle bears witness of himself to the Corinthians. Just as in bodily marriage a contract is made on both sides, ratified by mutual external signs that fall under the senses, so in this spiritual marriage a mutual consent, intervening through faith, makes this sacred bond binding on both sides. On the one side, Christ, declaring this through the voice of the ministers, gives himself with all his goods to his bride; on the other, the believer receives that gift by true faith and in turn delivers herself and all she has to her husband. Finally, just as the bodily marriage so contracted is followed by a holy bodily union, through which husband and wife become one flesh, or one body, in a bodily way, and from which carnal children are born, so from this most holy and pure mutual communion of Christ and any believer (why it is called spiritual has been fully explained a little before) there follows in the same way a spiritual joining, that is, a union. This is that great mystery, as the Apostle cries out (Ephes. 5.32), whose fullest and altogether heavenly declaration is contained in that holy Song of Songs. And since whoever thus cleaves to Christ becomes one spirit with him, holy offspring like children is begotten from this, the fruit not of the flesh but of the Spirit (Galat. 6.v.16 and Rom. 7.4). And again, since believers, though many in number (for this union is not hypostatic, nor is the body born from it something put together from undistinct parts, as we have taught in its place), yet inasmuch as by one and the same faith, through the same Spirit, they cohere with their head by a more effective and firmer spiritual bond than any bodily contact, and moreover, bound to one another in true charity through the same Spirit, they live and breathe as if with one heart and one soul, therefore this whole assembly of the saints is called one bride, as if it were one person in number, the bridegroom carrying his bride as if within his own bowels. This mystery the breastplate of the High Priest foreshadowed under the Law (Leviticus), which he bore on his shoulders and breast, those most precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes. Who, then, does not see how truly and how effectively the name of union, and indeed of mutual union, fits this spiritual conjunction? And how much they detract from so great a mystery, who twist these similitudes, which scarcely deserve, compared with this spiritual and mystical union, the name of shadows of that union, to an oral eating and a bodily joining of the substances themselves! How much more truly, then, and how much more rightly does Bernard, treating this very matter in his Homily 71 on the Song of Songs, look not to that oral eating of the bread and wine proper to the holy Supper, but to the spiritual eating, of which that is the sacramental sign: "Christ eats us, he says, and is eaten by us, so that we may be bound to him more tightly. Certainly we are not otherwise united to him. For if I eat and am not eaten, he will seem to be in me, but I am not yet in him; and if I am eaten but do not eat, he will seem to have me in him, but not to be in me. For the union is not perfect in either of these cases. But if he eats me so that he has me in himself, and is eaten by me so that he is in me, then, so far as the connection is whole and firm, I am in him, and he will be in me no less."

units.la: Id autem planius etiam apparebit ex alia, diuersa quidem, sed idem mysterium adumbrante similitudine, in qua tres personae spe-ctantur: debitor videlicet, is cui obligatus est: & Sponsor, debita illius omnia in suum caput translata persoluens. Vsitata enim est ista in sacris literis, tum nostri vt debitorum: tum Dei, cui nascimur infinitis pene nominibus, nempe & reatus originalis, & corruptionis natiuae, & peccatorum omnium inde emanantiū obstricti: & Sponsoris haec omnia per se persoluenda recipientis, pulcherrima & appositissima similitudo. Quoniā enim in illo spirituali coniugio maritus ille & sponsor, sponsam illa suam non modo non locupletè, sed etiam tu auitis, vt pote auorum suorum haeredem, tum priuatis infinitis nominibus obstrictam in suum thorum recepit, maritus simul & illius nomine sponsor euasit apud illum cui obligatam illam inuenit. Illa verò contrà ab eo coniuge tam adamata, qui non modò debita ipsius omnia ad vltimum vsque quadrantem exsoluit, verùm etiam inenarrabiles opes suas cum illa liberalissimè, immo etiam seipsum, communicauit, ex miserrima debitrice, libera, & ex pauperrima, ditissima facta comperitur. Quis non igitur videt tali reciproca communione duos illos coniuges in vnam veluti personam coiuisse? non quidem numero, sed tum quòd ad debita, & ad eorum persolutionem attinet, quæ maritus sponsor in se recepta persoluit: tum earum opum respectu, quas hæc vxor ex mariti sui liberalitate nacta est.
units.tr: This will appear even more plainly from another likeness, different but shadowing the same mystery, in which three persons are seen: the debtor, namely, the one to whom he is bound, and the surety, who takes all the debts of the debtor upon his own head and pays them. This comparison is common in Holy Scripture, both of our debts and of God, to whom we are born bound by almost countless obligations: the guilt of original sin, the corruption of our birth, and all the sins that flow from these. It is also a most beautiful and fitting picture of the surety who takes on himself and pays all these things in our place. For in that spiritual marriage the husband and surety received his bride, who was not only not wealthy but was bound to him by countless obligations, both inherited, as heir of her ancestors, and personal. At the same time he became her surety, under her name, before the one to whom he found her bound. She, on the other hand, was so loved by that spouse that he not only paid all her debts to the last penny, but also shared with her his unspeakable riches, and even himself, most generously. So she, from the most wretched debtor, was made free, and from the poorest, the richest. Who does not see that by such a mutual fellowship those two spouses have come together, as it were, into one person? Not indeed in number, but in respect of the debts and their payment, which the husband as surety took upon himself and paid, and in respect of the riches which the wife has received from her husband's generosity.

units.la: Nam ex iure quoque non tam ciuili quàm naturali, qui correi sunt, pro vna quodámodo numero persona apud eum habentur, qui vnam & communem aduersus singulos actionem habet: in quorum etiam est numero qui sese pro principali, quem vocant, debitore cuipiam obstrinxit. Sic autem vicissim sponsor, & is pro quo spopondit, persolutione per sponsorem facta & debitori à creditore imputata, simul liberatur, haud secus quàm si vnica essent numero persona.
units.tr: For in law also, not so much civil as natural, those who are jointly liable are regarded as, in a sense, one person in number before the one who has a single common action against them all. Among these are also those who have bound themselves to someone as the principal debtor, as they call him. So too, conversely, when the surety and the man for whom he stood surety are both released, once the payment has been made by the surety and credited by the creditor to the debtor, it is just as if they were one person in number.

units.la: Sed præterea summopere hic est obseruan- dum, nos; qui debitoris persona in hac simi-litudine sustinemus, non aeris alicuius alieni, aut aliarum rerum extra nos positarum debitores esse, sed personis ipsis nostris esse apud Dei seuerissimi exactoris tribunal, tum corporibus, tum animabus ipsis ad poenas laesae diuinae maiestatis ἀναλόγως conuenientes, luendas obstrictos.
units.tr: But moreover, it must be carefully noted here that we, who sustain the part of the debtor in this comparison, are debtors not of some money or other things outside ourselves, but are bound, in our very persons, before the tribunal of the most severe Judge of God, to pay penalties proportionate to the offence against the divine majesty, both in our bodies and in our souls themselves.

units.la: Hinc autem efficitur, no posse nos nisi per sponsorem illum nostrum, non auri, non argenti persoluendi causa, sed horrendas illas poenas in semetipsum vere & proprie recipientem, liberari: vt in hac pro nobis sponsione, ipse quodammodo, (nempe quod ad hanc obligationem attinet,) in nos semetipsum transfuderit: & nos per praestitam ab illo persolutione, in illum ipsum immigrauerimus: nobis certe non illis substantiis nostris, sed ex Euangelico illo pacto, in illo passis & crucifixis, ad poenas nostris peccatis debitas expiandas: quae omnia apud Deum patrem, per & propter sponsorem illum nostrum, per gratuitam imputationem rata sunt: sicut ipsi sponsori debita omnia nostra pater vicissim imputauit.
units.tr: From this it follows that we cannot be freed except through that surety of ours, who undertook to pay not for money or silver, but who truly and properly received upon himself those dreadful punishments. In this suretyship on our behalf, he has in a sense (so far as this obligation is concerned) transferred himself into us, and we, through the payment made by him, have passed over into him. We indeed, not in our own substances, but by that gospel covenant, were in him suffered and crucified, to atone for the punishments due to our sins. All these things are ratified before God the Father, through and on account of that surety of ours, by a gratuitous imputation, just as the Father in turn imputed all our debts to the surety himself.

units.la: Ad haec aute omnia & illud accedit, quod illo suo Spiritu, quo noster maritus ille simul & sponsor, idemque nostrorum debitorum omnium persolutor, & locupletator, plenissime primum seipsum in assumpta natura nostra proluerat, nos quoque, quasi sua ipsius anima nobis communicata, sibi συμμορφωτας: paulatim quidem in nobis agens, sed nunquam ab hoc in nobis opere desiturus, donec vltimo illo die nobiscum prorsus spiritualibus factis, beatissimam quoque illam immortalitatem, vt cohæredibus suis, communicet. Et hoc est alterum illud summum ipsius bonitatis nos hic paulatim regenerantis, & in cœlis tandem nos plenè consummaturi, beneficium, in sacris literis capitis & membrorum, eiusdem Spiritus Christi vinculo, in vnum mysticum corpus connexorum similitudine adumbratum, & in his sacræ Cœnæ mysteriis, in credentium mentibus obsignatum.
units.tr: To all these things there is also added this: that by his Spirit, by which our husband and surety, who is also the payer and enricher of all our debts, first most fully cleansed himself in the nature he had assumed, he also, as if his own soul were communicated to us, conforms us to himself [συμμορφωτάς]. He works this in us gradually, yet will never cease from this work in us until on that last day, when we have been made wholly spiritual with him, he imparts to us also that most blessed immortality, as to his co-heirs. This is the other great benefit of his goodness, which regenerates us here little by little and will at last fully perfect us in heaven. It is shadowed in Holy Scripture by the likeness of the head and members, joined into one mystical body by the bond of the same Spirit of Christ, and it is sealed in the minds of believers in these mysteries of the holy Supper.

units.la: Hæc est igitur, Christiane & amice lector, quisquis es, de ista diuinissima & arctissima cum vnico illo Mediatore nostro communione sententia, ex puro puto Dei verbo, nisi prorsus ignorantia fallimur, deprompta: ex qua satis, opinor, vides quantum ab eo absimus, vt vel ab ipsius Christi nobiscum vnitione quæ ex illo bona percipimus, vel itidé à nostri cum ipso communione quæ à nobis in se transtulit, seperemus. Sed de hoc demum inter illos de quibus hic ago & nos controuertitur, Num fiat reali & actuali carnis Christi cum nostra contactu &σωαφῇ[?] (quo verbo, sed metaphora à corporeis rebus sumpta, vt & corporis & membrorum vocabulis, vtitur Apostolus) ista vnitio: quod eos existimare necesse est, qui eandem & quidem per inexistentiam vel indistantiam signorum cum rebus significatis præsentiam, & realem illi vnitioni respondentem vtrorumque manducationem sibi & aliis persuadent. Mutuo enim necessario nexu hæc præsentia, manducatio, & vnitio inter se cohærent, ex qua non mysticum, sed vere actualiter & essentialiter monstruosissimum corpus ex tot corporum substantiis constatum, nasceretur, quot unquam fuerunt, sunt & erunt vera Christi membra, quod res ipsa clamat, & satis superque fuisse confido manifeste demonstratum. Nos autem e contrario sicut Sacramentalium signorum & rerum significatarum nexum ἐνεργητικὸν[?], & Sacramentalem esum ac potum, metonymice sic vocari ostedimus: sic huius unitionis & communionis modum mere tum suis partibus omnibus, tū suo fine, affirmamus non simpliciter intellectualem, sed plane spiritualem, divinum ac cœlestè esse, cuius τὸ ὅτι quidè, ex Dei verbo, tum simplici, tum Sacramentali, nobis patet, effectum vero, optimo iure, Apostolus magnum mysterium appellat. Utra vero sit vera, id est, capitibus nostræ religionis conueniēs sententia, & an non seipsas collidant ratio-nes ab iis allatæ, quibus eundem modum simul & corporalem, & invisibilem, & incomprehensibilem esse volunt, non recuso, quin ex contrario prolatis utrinque argumentis, ab i-doneis iudicibus dispiciatur.
units.tr: This, then, Christian and friendly reader, whoever you are, is the teaching concerning that most divine and most intimate communion with our one Mediator, drawn, unless we are utterly deceived, from the pure Word of God. From it, I think, you can see well enough how far we are from separating, either the union of Christ with us, from which we receive good things, or our communion with him, by which he has transferred our sins to himself. But this is finally the point in dispute between those of whom I speak and us: whether that union takes place by a real and actual contact [συναφῇ] of Christ's flesh with ours (a word, but a metaphor taken from bodily things, as the Apostle uses both the words body and members). Those must hold this view who, by the indwelling or non-distance of the signs with the things signified, persuade themselves and others of a real presence, corresponding to that union, and of the eating of both. For this presence, eating and union cohere with one another by a necessary mutual bond. From this there would arise not a mystical body but, truly, actually and essentially, a monstrous body made up of the substances of as many bodies as have ever been, are, or will be true members of Christ. The thing itself cries out against this, and I trust I have shown it clearly enough and more than enough. We, on the other hand, have shown that the bond between the sacramental signs and the things signified is called effectual [ἐνεργητικόν], and that the sacramental eating and drinking are so called by metonymy. Thus we affirm that the mode of this union and communion, both in all its parts and in its end, is purely not merely intellectual but plainly spiritual, divine and heavenly. Of its that it is, we are made plain by God's Word, both simple and sacramental, but its effect the Apostle rightly calls a great mystery. Which opinion is true, that is, agrees with the heads of our religion, and whether the arguments brought by those who wish this same mode to be at once corporeal, invisible and incomprehensible do not clash with one another, I do not refuse to have examined by competent judges, with arguments set forth on both sides.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Responsio ad Physica eorum argumenta qui verum Christi corpus essentiale negant, nisi essentialiter in terris adsit, posse vere per fidem apprehensum credentibus communicari.
units.tr: Reply to the physical arguments of those who deny that the true, essential body of Christ can be communicated to believers, who receive it by faith, unless it is essentially present on earth.

units.la: Quis vero non miretur nos Physicis argumentis ab iis peti, qui nos clamitant hæc myste-ria naturalibus principiis me-tiri? Sic enim argutantur. Vultis, inquiunt, corpus Christi in cœlos receptum nec inde ante extremum diem esse rediturū. Sanè ita est, sicut Christianorum Symbolum simpliciter, & κ[?]α̱τὰ τὸ ῥητὸν prorsus intelligendum declarat: ideóque essentialem illam omnipræsentiam, ut dogma Christianæ fidei ex diametro repugnās, detestamur. Fides autem nostra, inquiunt, immo nos ipsi toti deorsum infra in terris fixi hæremus. Sanè ita est, quòd ad nostri situm, & ad externam hanc actionem attinet: quo sensu Apostolus omnipræsentiam illorum Vbiquitariam velut ex professo refellēs, nos dicit, 2. ad Corinth. 5. 6, dum hoc corpus incolimus, peregrè à Domino abesse. Sed absit, ut quod ad interiorem hominem, & opus illud Dei intra nos inchoatum attinet, defixi in terris, in hac præsertim actione, teneamur.
units.tr: Who would not be astonished that we are being met with physical arguments by men who cry out that we measure these mysteries by natural principles? For this is how they reason: You hold that the body of Christ has been received into heaven and will not return from there before the last day. Certainly so, as the creed of the Christians declares, to be understood plainly and strictly according to the letter [κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν]. For that reason we reject that essential omnipresence as a doctrine flatly contrary to the Christian faith. But our faith, they say, or rather we ourselves, are fixed wholly down here, below on earth. Certainly so, as far as our place and this outward action are concerned. In this sense the Apostle, refuting their Ubiquitarian omnipresence expressly, says that while we dwell in this body we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6). But far be it that we are held fixed on earth as regards the inner man and that work of God begun within us, especially in this action.

units.la: Nam è contrario (sicut idem Apostolus diserte verbis testatur, Coloss. 3. 1.) quia cum Christo resurreximus, superna quærimus ubi Christus est, non terrestria: & conversatio nostra eatenus iam nunc est in cœlis: Philipp. 3. 20, licèt adhuc non sanè Omnipræsentem secundùm corpus Christum in terris habentes, sed è cœlis adhuc venturum expectantes. Huc enim nos vocat in his præsertim mysteriis solennis illa formula Sursum Corda, & quò huc nos tanquam aquilas per fidei scalam è vestigio trásferri Chrysostomus iubet, & Augustinus, Fidem, inquit, mitte in cœlis & eum tanquam in terris præsentem tenuisti, iis ipsis respondens, qui quærunt, Quomodo teneo absentem? quomodo in cœlum manum mittam, vt ibi præsentem teneam?
units.tr: On the contrary, as the same Apostle clearly testifies (Col. 3:1), since we have risen with Christ, we seek the things above, where Christ is, not the things on earth; and our citizenship is already in heaven (Phil. 3:20), although we do not yet have Christ present on earth in his bodily omnipresence, but are still waiting for him to come from heaven. For that solemn formula, Lift up your hearts, calls us here, especially in these mysteries, and Chrysostom and Augustine bid us be carried at once up to that place, as eagles, by the ladder of faith. Augustine says, Send your faith into heaven, and you will hold him as if present on earth, answering those very people who ask, How do I hold one who is absent? How shall I send my hand into heaven to hold him there as present?

units.la: In hoc autem errore [illegible, ~7 letters] illorum ψεῦδος[?] est, quòd Communicationem imaginantes suæ illi Omnipræsentiæ & orali manducationi accommodatam, & ex errore in errorem ruentes, hanc Communionem siue Vnitionem imaginantur fieri mutuo reali & actuali substantiarum ipsarum contactu. At nos è contrario, ab Apostolo edocti eos qui Christo agglutinantur vnum esse cum Christo spiritum, ac proinde corporis illius mystici Ecclesiæ & Christi, Eph. 4. 16. & 5. 32. iuncturas omnes esse spirituales: affirmamus, COMMVNICARI idem esse atque Christum NOSTRVM & Nos VICISSIM IPSIVS FIERI: quem contractum, istis sacræ Cœnæ mysteriis speciatim sanciendum, postea non solā eorum quæ tum Christo, tum nobis, partim per imputationem, partim subiectiuè in-sunt, vera communicatione definimus, sed, ex pacti Euangelici tenore, interpretamur: quo nimirum fiat ex immensa illa Seruatoris nostri liberalitate, vt ipsemet quoque Christus vsque adeo arctè noster euadat & nos vi-cissim illius, vt apud Patris tribunal, Christus & Ecclesia quasi, non quidem hypostatica substantiarum unitione, sed quòd ad istam communicationem mutuam attinet, mysticè velut unum & idem ὑφιστάμενον [?] efficacissimè censeamur. Et huc referendas esse varias illas similitudines ostendimus: ita videlicet inter-pretandas, ut (quum aliud sit SIMILE quadà analogia ESSE, quàm substantialiter IDEM ESSE: & spiritualem horum mysteriorum finem, ac proinde spiritualiter accipi oporteat ἀναλόγως, quæ nos ad hunc finem deducunt) in illis similitudinibus explicandis, non quæ spiritualiter intelligenda sunt, rebus corporeis, sed è contrario, quæ à similitudinibus corporeis sumpta sunt, spiritualibus accom-modemus.
units.tr: But in this error [illegible, about seven letters] there is a falsehood [ψεῦδος], namely that they imagine a communion adapted to their own omnipresence and to oral eating, and, falling from error into error, they imagine that this communion or union comes about by a mutual, real and actual contact of the substances themselves. We, on the contrary, taught by the Apostle that those who are joined to Christ are one spirit with Christ, and therefore that all the joints of that mystical body of the Church and of Christ are spiritual (Eph. 4:16; 5:32), affirm that to COMMUNICATE means that Christ becomes OURS and we in turn become HIS. This bond, to be sealed specifically in these mysteries of the holy Supper, we define not only as the true communication of those things which are in Christ and in us, partly by imputation and partly subjectively, but also, by the tenor of the Gospel covenant, we interpret it thus: that by the immense generosity of our Saviour, Christ himself becomes so closely ours, and we so closely his, that before the Father's tribunal Christ and the Church are counted, not indeed by any hypostatic union of substances, but as far as this mutual communication goes, mystically as one and the same hypostasis [ὑφιστάμενον], most effectively. And we have shown that those various similitudes must be referred here, and they must be interpreted so that (since being SIMILAR by some analogy is one thing, and being substantially the SAME is another; and since the spiritual end of these mysteries, and so the way that leads us to this end, must be understood spiritually and analogically) in explaining those similitudes we apply to spiritual things not what must be understood spiritually in bodily terms, but, on the contrary, we apply to spiritual things what has been taken from bodily similitudes.

units.la: Tale est istud illorum argumentum Si cor-pus Christi percipitur sola fide. Ergo vel imagina-rie, id est, nuda quadam ἀναμνήσει [?], vel reipsa. At non reipsa, si est in cœlis absens, Ergo tantum ima-ginarie. Hic ego verò propter harum vocum ὁμωνυμίαν, sic respondeo. SI IMAGINARIE ad qualitatem, id est ad ipsum perceptionis modum, REIPSA verò ad substantiæ prædi-camentum, id est ad rem ipsam perceptam re-feratur: non respondet hæc propositio Logicæ regulæ, præcipienti, ut quæ sic ἀμίσως [?] opponuntur, in eodé prædicameto censean-tur. Sin verò illud utrumque vocabulum, ad ipsum perceptionis modum referatur: nem-pe sic ista opponentur, ut falsum verò, sive, ut in scholis loquuntur, ut ENS Non Enti. Quinà autem non fuerit impietas, Imaginarium siue falsum id vocare, quod Mens per fidem in Verbo Dei intuetur: & (quoniam ei non tantum intelligendum, verum etiam credendum, atque adeo ipsi in promissionis verbo, applicandum praebetur) certissime profecto (nisi forte Deus verax non est,) apprehendat necesse est: siue corporeum illud siue incorporeum: siue situ praesens, siue absens fuerit. Vt autem vniuersam Scripturam Propheticam & Apostolicam euoluamus, quodnam tandem aliud interius in mente nostra situm instrumentum, & quidem diuinitus intra nos creatum, praeter Fidem illam inueniemus? Est enim certe hac si non vna, tamen praecipua & essentiali conditione nobis datus Christus, vt qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam: vsque adeo vt quicquid creditur aut geritur inter Christianos ista fide non συγκεκραμμένον[?], peccatum censeatur.
units.tr: Such is their argument: If the body of Christ is perceived by faith alone, then it is so either imaginarily, that is, by some bare recollection [ἀνάμνησις], or really. But not really, if it is absent in heaven. Therefore only imaginarily. Here, because of the ambiguity of these words, I reply as follows. If IMAGINARILY is referred to the quality, that is, to the very manner of perceiving, and REALLY to the category of substance, that is, to the thing itself perceived, then this proposition does not agree with the rule of logic, which requires that things opposed in such a way be counted in the same category. But if both words are referred to the very manner of perceiving, then they are opposed as false and true, or, as the schools put it, as BEING to NON-BEING. Why would it not be impiety to call imaginary or false what the mind beholds by faith in the Word of God, and what, since it is offered not only to be understood but also to be believed, and so to be applied to the very word of promise, it certainly (unless God is perhaps not true) must grasp, whether that thing is corporeal or incorporeal, and whether it is present in place or absent? But if we go through all of Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture, what other inner instrument placed in our mind, and indeed created in us by God, shall we find besides that Faith? For Christ is given to us, if not the only one, then certainly by this principal and essential condition, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. So much so that whatever is done or believed among Christians without this faith is counted as sin.

units.la: Eiusdem est generis tertium hoc illorum argumentum Fides, inquiunt, vt pote notitia vel assensus, inter habitus animi reponitur. Actio igitur ab ipsa proficiscens intra cerebrum hominis tota perficitur, & nihil reale extra mentem producit: adeo vt fides ei cui fidit non aliter quam cogitatione attenta, & voluntatis erga illum inclinatione, seu spirituali quodam contactu copuletur. Ergo sola fide corpus ipsum Christi re ipsa, nec cum mente nostra, nec cum corporibus nostris vnitur: Atqui contra logices regulas, plus sic concluditur quam praemissa comprehendant. Inepta enim est haec argumentatio, Corpus & sanguis Domini nullo corporali contactu, sed tantum spirituali apprehensio-ne vniuntur. Ergo verè & reipsa non vniuntur. Fallit τὸ ἐπούσιον[?], quoniam intellectualis etiam quaedam est, & ea quidem tanto certior & arctior sani intellectus in rebus quibusvis cognoscendis, & ad suum usum applicandis operatio, quàm sensuum, quanto intellectualia sensibilibus praestant: ne substantiis quidem ipsis rerum subsistentium exceptis.
units.tr: Of the same kind is their third argument: Faith, they say, since it is knowledge or assent, is placed among the habits of the soul. Therefore the action proceeding from it is wholly completed within the man's brain, and produces nothing real outside the mind; so that faith joins the believer to the one in whom he trusts only by attentive thought, by an inclination of the will toward him, or by some spiritual contact. Therefore by faith alone the body of Christ is not really united either with our mind or with our bodies. But against the rules of logic, more is concluded here than the premises contain. For this argument is faulty: the body and blood of the Lord are united with us by no bodily contact, but only by spiritual apprehension; therefore they are not truly and really united. The fallacy lies in the [ἐπούσιον?], since there is also an intellectual operation, and it is indeed the surer and closer operation of a sound mind in knowing things of every kind and applying them to its use, by as much as intellectual things surpass sensible things, not excepting even the substances of subsisting things themselves.

units.la: Rerum enim omnium, siue in ipsis speciebus, siue in specierum indiuiduis considerarum, vera perceptio posita est, quòd ad species attinet, siue corporeas siue incorporeas, ab illarum definitionis notitia. Indiuiduarum verò perceptio ab ipsa indiuiduantium proprietatum recta cognitione dependet: quae tota, vtraque operatio est intellectus: per sensus quidè de iis admoniti quae in sensus incurrunt, sed ita vt proprie tamè nō oculus ipse videat quod videt, nec auris quod audit audiat, sed ipse potius animus videat & audiat, quod de caeteris quoque sensibus est intelligendum: vt motus praeterea merè intellectuales, quū Intellectus nō tātum abstrahit à sensibilibus, sed etiā supra ipsa abstracta ratiocinādo colligit.
units.tr: For the true perception of all things, whether considered in their kinds themselves or in the individuals of those kinds, rests, as far as the kinds go, whether corporeal or incorporeal, on knowledge of their definition. But the perception of individuals depends on right knowledge of the very properties that individuate them; and both of these operations belong wholly to the intellect, which is admonished of those things that fall under the senses through the senses, yet in such a way that properly it is not the eye itself that sees what it sees, nor the ear itself that hears what it hears; rather the mind itself sees and hears. The same must be understood of the other senses. Besides, there are purely intellectual motions, since the intellect not only abstracts from sensible things but also, by reasoning, gathers conclusions above those very abstractions.

units.la: Sed inquient isti, rerum tamen sic intellectu perceptarum substantia, extra ipsum intellectum permanet. Fateor. Nam ne in visionis quidè sensu res visae vt cerni possint, ipsis oculis admo-uetur: immo aliquo distet interuallo oportet, vt commodè cerni possint,nedum vt in ipsos oculos penetrent. Num verò propterea rerum visarum substantias non perspicit animus,& eas sibi applicat? Et,ne istius per phātafmata apprehensionis & applicationis effectum vanum hic efle videatur, fi physicis scriptoribus eruditioribus creditur, substantiæ,fiue corporeæ, fiue incorporeæ, res denique omnes intelleætæ, per imagines ab intellectu agente formatas, sic intellectui vniuntur & inferuntur, vt intellectus vnum quiddā intellectuale cum illis euadat. Cæterum ista nolim sic accipi, quasi istius vnitionis instrumentum vere ὑπερφυσικὸν & diuinum, id est, Fidem Christianam statuam pro Spirituali Intellectualem: sed vt hi difputatores secum expendant etiam atque etiam, fi hæc vis est intellectus naturali tantum luce præditi, quid de Fide statuendum fit, & eius ἐνέργεια [?]: dono, inquam, illo, in ista communicatione & vnitione de quibus hic agimus, non simpliciter intellectuali, sed plus quàm supernaturali : plane denique cœlesti & diuino? quatenus videlicet, mysterium istud non modò naturale non est, sed è contrario tale, vt non renatis mentibus, aliis quidem fit stultitia,aliis fit offendiculum.Sit igitur sane hoc verissimum, substantiam ipsam corporis & sanguinis Christi, neque in mentem ipsam fide præditam,neque in corpus nostrum actualiter magis, immo multo etiam minus, vtpote multo longius dissitam ingre-di di,quàm corpus visum in ipsos corporis oculos: An verò propterea ipsa Christi Humanitas,veluti contactu quodam spirituali, verissimè & efficacissimè credentium animis non vnitur? Non sanè vlla substantiæ vel animæ reali traductione,(quorsum enim hoc ad nostram salutem?) sed verissimo, & efficacissimo,mentis fide præditæ,& spiritualia,tum in simplici verbo Dei, tum in Sacramentis intuentis, conceptu. Quàm autem iste conceptus sit verax & efficax, ex illa admirabili & merè cœlesti credentium cum ipso Christo συμμορφώσει[?] : & infinitis istius fidei effectis, quibus omnis rerum natura cessit, quis ita stupidus est vt non animaduertat? Fruantur ergo qui volent, illa sua orali proprie & sine tropo intellecta perceptione,manducatione, & vnitione:Nobis autem illa interior, non tamen antiphysica, & corporis Christi veritatem tollens,quæ principio nititur physico simul & Theologico,sed supernaturalis ac merè diuina & cœlestis,sufficit: & illa Fides quæ Dei profunda nobis in verbo patefacta,& Sacramentis fancita,scrutatur:quæ mentem Dei de nostræ salutis mysterio tenet:quæ denique Omnipotentis Dei virtute freta, nos in cœlum vsque subuehit: rectè propterea dicente Chrysostomo ad populum Antiochenum hom. 61. nobis Christum sese in his mysteriis præbere,non tantum videndum,sed etiam tangendum ac palpandum. At non certè corporis oculis, manu, vel ore, sed spirituali per fidem contactu: idque non in terris, sed in cœlis, ne sei-psum ille refellat, cuius verba antea citaui-mus.
units.tr: But, they will say, the substance of things so perceived by the intellect still remains outside the intellect itself. I grant it. For even in the sense of sight, things seen are not brought to the eyes themselves so that they may be discerned; indeed they must be at some distance, so that they can be discerned conveniently, let alone that they penetrate into the eyes. But does the mind therefore not perceive the substances of seen things, and apply them to itself? And lest the effect of this apprehension and application through phantasms should seem empty here, if we believe the more learned physical writers, substances, whether corporeal or incorporeal, in short all things understood, are joined and carried into the intellect through images formed by the agent intellect, so that the intellect becomes one intellectual thing with them. Yet I would not have that taken to mean that I set up, as the instrument of this union, a truly supernatural and divine thing, that is, the Christian faith, in place of a spiritual intellectual faculty. Rather, let these disputants weigh again and again, if this is the power of an intellect endowed only with natural light, what must be decided about faith and its operation: that gift, I say, in that communion and union with which we are dealing here, not simply intellectual, but more than supernatural, plainly heavenly and divine. In that sense, indeed, this mystery is not only not natural, but on the contrary such that to unregenerate minds it is foolishness to some and a stumbling block to others. Let it then be granted as most true that the substance itself of the body and blood of Christ does not enter the mind endowed with faith, nor our body, in actuality, any more, indeed much less, since it is far more distant, than a body seen enters the very eyes of the body. But is the humanity of Christ therefore not united, by some spiritual contact, to the souls of believers most truly and most effectively? Certainly not by any real transfer of substance or of soul (for what would that have to do with our salvation?), but by the most true and most effective conception of a mind endowed with faith and contemplating the spiritual things set before it, both in the plain Word of God and in the Sacraments. And how true and effective that conception is, from that wonderful and purely heavenly conformity [συμμόρφωσις] of believers with Christ himself, and from the countless effects of this faith, to which all of nature has yielded, who is so stupid as not to notice? Let those who wish enjoy that oral perception, eating and union, understood properly and without a figure.
